orderingVariable: COURSE ORDER — 4 stages that interleave all ten categories, so each stage adds new kinds of things you can say; within a category, chunks run simple to complex and prerequisites come first.
whyThatVariable: Versatility = spoken frequency (rank in jiten.moe drama subtitles, 3,030 dramas) x spread across topics x reach (how many sentences it attaches to) x speaking need. Casual is the default form (romaji); the polite desu/masu counterpart sits beside it (polite).

conventions.romaji: kotoba's stored spelling: modified Hepburn, lowercase, no macrons, long vowels as spelled (sou, daijoubu, kirei), wa/o/e particles, っ before ch = t (kotchi). Leading hyphen = attaches to a word.
conventions.register: romaji = casual form, learned first; polite = desu/masu counterpart, or null when there is no register difference.
conventions.freqRank: rank in jiten.moe drama frequency list (CC BY-SA 4.0); freqNote explains tokenizer-split forms. null = no usable rank.
conventions.contrastGroup: items sharing a group name are learned side by side; their examples share a base sentence.

stages.name: Stage 1
stages.summary: Greet, thank and apologise, ask what, who and where, and say what you do, have and where you're going today or did yesterday, linked with but and because.

stages.name: Stage 2
stages.summary: Ask favours, say what you want, like, saw, know, said and think, react with e?, hee and sou, and say how often and how soon things happen.

stages.name: Stage 3
stages.summary: Check things with someone, guess and make plans and choices, talk about food, mood and difficulty, use fillers to hold the floor, and say how sure you are.

stages.name: Stage 4
stages.summary: Suggest things, pass on what you heard or what seems true, compare, soften what you say and give advice, and talk about before, after and until.

categories.scope: relative time, aspect/timing adverbs, frequency, time clauses

blocks.label: Yes and no
blocks.rationale: The three ways to answer a yes/no question, which you do in almost every exchange. It's a closed set, so the block stays at three.
blocks.interference: un and uun differ only in length and pitch (a short un against a two-beat, dipping u-un); iya is a firmer no that also corrects or pushes back.

items.use: The casual yes, and also the 'uh-huh' you keep saying while someone talks to show you're following.

examplePolite.ja: はい、行きます。

items.freqNote: うん #49; polite はい #22
items.notes: As a backchannel it shows you're listening, not that you agree; with superiors use hai (ee is the softer conversational polite yes). Trap: un confirms the statement, so to 'ikanai no?' (you're not going?) 'un' means 'right, I'm not going'.

items.use: The casual no to a yes/no question: two beats with a dip in pitch, while a short un means yes.

examplePolite.ja: いいえ、行きません。

items.freqNote: ううん #593; polite いいえ #688
items.notes: A long, flat uun (うーん, #298) means 'hmm'. The romaji is the same but it sounds different. To 'ikanai no?', 'uun, iku yo' means 'no, I AM going'.

items.use: A firmer no than uun: it denies, corrects ('iya, chigau'), or opens a turn with 'well, actually'.

example.romaji: iya, chigau yo. ashita da yo.

examplePolite.ja: いいえ、違います。明日ですよ。
examplePolite.english: No, that's not right. It's tomorrow.

items.freqNote: いや #54, which may also count 嫌 'don't want' written in kana; kanji 嫌 #304
items.notes: This is not the adjective iya 'unpleasant' (D). In polite speech you mostly hear a short ie ('ie, daijoubu desu') or iya itself; full iie mostly answers a direct yes/no question.

blocks.label: Thanks, sorry, please
blocks.rationale: The everyday politeness formulas for thanking, apologising, asking and offering, plus kochira koso, which hands thanks or an apology straight back.
blocks.interference: sumimasen apologises and also thanks, while gomen only apologises. onegai is 'please' when you ask for something; douzo is 'please' when you offer it. kochira koso doesn't mean 'you're welcome': it returns the same thanks, apology or yoroshiku to the speaker.

items.use: Thanks anyone for anything. Add gozaimasu for strangers, coworkers and anyone older.
items.politeJa: ありがとうございます

example.ja: ありがとう、ほんとに助かった。

examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます、本当に助かりました。
examplePolite.english: Thank you, that was a real help.

items.freqNote: ありがとう #128; ありがとうございます #165; clipped ありがと #766
items.notes: The past form arigatou gozaimashita thanks someone for something that's finished, like a meal or a lesson.

items.use: Apologises to friends and family for anything from bumping into them to turning them down; 'gomen ne' is softer.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、遅くなりました。

items.freqNote: ごめん #154; ごめんなさい #254
items.notes: gomen nasai is the earnest middle step: stronger than gomen, less formal than sumimasen.

items.use: Gets a stranger's attention, apologises politely, and thanks someone who went to trouble for you.

example.ja: あ、わざわざすみません。
example.english: Oh, thanks for going to all that trouble.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、これいくらですか？
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, how much is this?

items.freqNote: すみません #289; spoken すいません #416
items.notes: Often pronounced suimasen. Already polite: with friends say gomen to apologise, arigatou to thank, and nee to get attention.

items.use: Turns any noun into a request ('mizu, onegai') or seals an ask. Said on its own to friends, it's a pleading 'please!'.

example.english: Sorry, can you take care of this?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、これお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you take care of this?

items.freqNote: お願い #258; お願いします #183
items.notes: In shops, 'X o onegai shimasu' is the safe all-purpose way to order.

items.use: Offers something, hands it over, or lets someone go first. It's the same in both registers.

examplePolite.ja: はい、こちらどうぞ。

items.freqNote: どうぞ #140
items.notes: It offers or invites; to ask for something, use onegai (douzo yoroshiku is the set phrase where it softens a request).

items.use: Returns whatever the other person just said, whether thanks, an apology or yoroshiku, and is usually followed by that same word.

example.ja: こちらこそ、ありがとうね。

examplePolite.ja: こちらこそ、ありがとうございます。

items.freqNote: こちらこそ #1155; casual こっちこそ has no entry because the tokenizer splits it into こっち #148 + こそ #320, so no rank
items.notes: Friends also say kotchi koso. To yoroshiku, answer kochira koso yoroshiku (onegai shimasu). It isn't 'me too': to say you feel or do the same, use watashi mo.

blocks.label: this/that: things
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do row for things: near me, near you or just said, far or shared, and which.
blocks.interference: sore vs are: sore is near you or just said, are is far or something we both remember; dore is for three or more, dotchi for two.

items.use: Points at a thing near you so you can ask about it or choose it before you know its name; it stands alone and never goes before a noun.

examplePolite.ja: これ、いいですね。

items.notes: Before a noun it becomes kono: kono hon, never kore hon.

items.use: Points at a thing near the listener, and even more often at what they just said, so it is the main way to react to an idea (sore hontou?, sore tte dou iu imi?).

examplePolite.ja: それ、いいですね。

items.notes: Use sore, not are, for something the other person just mentioned.

items.use: Points at something away from both of you or something you both remember, and stands in for a word you can't recall (are, are da yo).

examplePolite.ja: あれはどうなりましたか？

items.freqNote: also counts the surprised 'are?' (G)
items.notes: Calling a person are sounds rude; say ano hito.

items.use: Asks which one out of three or more and takes ga, not wa (dore ga ii?); for a choice between two, use dotchi.

examplePolite.ja: どれがいいですか？

items.notes: dore demo ii = any of them is fine.

blocks.label: Basic enders
blocks.rationale: The plain copula, the three core sentence-final particles (ka, ne, yo) and their most common combination, yo ne. They share one base sentence so that only the ending changes.
blocks.interference: yo and ne get mixed up. yo tells the listener something they don't know, ne treats it as shared, and yo ne checks that it's shared. In a casual question ka sounds blunt or rough, so drop it and use a rising tone.

items.use: Plain 'is' after nouns and na-adjectives. A bare final da is mostly self-talk or a sudden realisation and can sound blunt, so to tell someone, drop it (ashita yasumi) or add yo or ne (ashita yasumi da yo). It stays before ne, yo and kedo. Polite speech has no self-talk, so the polite pair is a plain statement.

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みです

items.notes: It becomes na before n da and no (yasumi na n da) and never follows an i-adjective (takai, not *takai da). Dropping da before yo or ne (yasumi yo, kirei ne) is common but feminine-leaning; da yo / da ne is the neutral form.

items.use: Turns a polite sentence into a question when said with a rising tone. Said falling, polite desu ka is a realisation instead (sou desu ka = I see). Casual questions drop ka and rise, so bare casual ka is mostly heard in musing realisations (sokka, ashita yasumi ka).

example.english: Oh, tomorrow's a day off, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: a, ashita wa yasumi desu ka
examplePolite.ja: あ、明日は休みですか
examplePolite.english: Oh, tomorrow's a day off, I see.

alsoIn: vocab-trainer learner-phrases: ○○ wa nihongo de nan desu ka
items.notes: For a casual question, drop ka and raise the pitch: ashita yasumi? The real polite question is ashita wa yasumi desu ka? with a rising tone. A casual rising ...ka? (daijoubu ka?) sounds rough and masculine. Neutral casual ka appears in musing (sokka), in jaa iku ka (let's get going, then) and inside sentences (nani ga ii ka wakaranai = I don't know what would be good).

items.use: Invites the listener to share or agree with what you say. It softens statements, comments on things you both see, and confirms details.

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですね
examplePolite.english: So tomorrow's a day off, then.

items.notes: A drawn-out nee at the start of a sentence means hey. Mid-sentence ne (ano ne, kinou ne...) just holds the listener's attention. Don't add ne to facts only you know, such as your name or your plans; yo or nothing fits there.

items.use: Marks something the listener doesn't know or needs reminding of, such as news, warnings, corrections or recommendations. Without it, a statement can sound flat.

example.english: Tomorrow's a day off, you know.

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよ
examplePolite.english: Tomorrow's a day off, you know.

items.notes: When correcting a superior, yo can sound like lecturing.

items.use: Checks that the listener shares something you believe, either to confirm it or to agree emphatically (sou da yo ne).

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yasumi desu yo ne?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよね？

items.notes: The order is fixed: always yo ne, never *ne yo.

blocks.label: Good or no good
blocks.rationale: The four basic verdicts (good, OK, no good, bad) that answer 'is this all right?' about anything.
blocks.interference: ii and daijoubu both mean 'OK' and both turn down offers (ii desu / daijoubu desu = no thanks). The shared frame keeps them apart: kore de ii? asks for approval, kore de daijoubu? asks if anything is wrong, and dame flips the frame to kore ja dame?

items.use: The default positive verdict on anything, and 'fine, acceptable' when checking (kore de ii?). When choosing, X ga ii = I'd like X, and X de ii = X will do. It is also the core of -te mo ii (may) and -ta hou ga ii (should).

examplePolite.ja: これでいいですか？

items.freqNote: いい #24; includes reply and -te mo ii uses; formal 良い #1474
items.notes: Only the dictionary form is ii; every other form uses yo-: yokatta, yokunai, yokute. As a reply, ii yo = sure, go ahead, but ii desu to an offer usually means no thanks; accept with onegaishimasu. Choosing a gift or dish, say kore ga ii: kore de ii sounds like settling.

items.use: Says someone or something is OK, safe or not a problem; it is how you check on people (daijoubu?), and daijoubu desu politely declines an offer.

examplePolite.ja: これで大丈夫ですか？

items.freqNote: 大丈夫 #76; rank includes the reply use (daijoubu desu = no thanks)
items.notes: To an offer it usually means 'no thanks' (fukuro wa? / daijoubu desu), but it can also mean 'yes, that's fine', so clerks may check again. To accept clearly, say onegaishimasu.

items.use: Says something is no good, won't work or isn't allowed (rules, plans, broken things, hopeless efforts), and is the base of -cha dame (must not).

examplePolite.ja: これじゃダメですか？

items.freqNote: spelling split: ダメ #596, 駄目 #1901, だめ #3328; combined it is far higher than any one row
items.notes: In the 'is this OK?' frame, de ii becomes ja dame: kore de ii? / kore ja dame?

items.use: Bad in quality, weather, health (guai ga warui) or behaviour, and 'to blame' (X ga warui); the opposite of ii.

example.romaji: kyou, chotto guai warui n da
example.ja: 今日、ちょっと具合悪いんだ

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa chotto guai ga warui n desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日はちょっと具合が悪いんです

items.freqNote: 悪い #139; includes the casual apology 'warui'
items.notes: Casual apology: warui! or warui ne (mostly male), and warui kedo... (sorry, but...), which everyone uses. The polite equivalent is sumimasen / sumimasen ga..., never warui desu.

blocks.label: Question words
blocks.rationale: The bare wh-words for what, who, when, why and how much; each opens a question on any topic.
blocks.interference: nande (why) and nan de (by what) sound the same, so nan de kita? can mean 'how did you get here?'; a question word never takes wa, and as the subject it takes ga.

items.use: Asks what; before d, t and n sounds it shortens to nan (nan da, nan desu ka, nan de), so you need both forms by ear.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nani suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何するんですか？

items.freqNote: 何(なに) #34; 何(なん) #245; bare なん #97
items.notes: nani ga, nani o, but nan desu ka; the switch has to be automatic. nan no hanashi? = what are you talking about?

items.use: Asks who (dare ga), whose (dare no) or with whom (dare to); the answer takes ga.

examplePolite.romaji: donata ni kikeba ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どなたに聞けばいいですか？

items.freqNote: polite どなた #1577
items.notes: dare desu ka is fine with coworkers; donata is the softer choice with strangers and on the phone.

items.use: Asks when, and with kara or made asks since when or until when (itsu kara?, itsu made?).

examplePolite.ja: いつがいいですか？

items.freqNote: いつ #257; 何時(いつ) #2675 counted separately
items.notes: No ni after itsu: itsu iku?, not itsu ni iku?

items.use: The everyday casual 'why', said alone (e, nande?) or in a question ending in no?, and usually answered with kara; it can sound blunt or accusing, so doushite is softer and the safe choice in polite speech.

examplePolite.ja: どうして来なかったんですか？

items.freqNote: なんで #232; 何で #572 (also includes 'by what means'); polite どうして #170
alsoIn: 05-acquisition-order critique: question words incl. nande omitted
items.notes: By ear, nande iku? sounds the same whether it means 'why are you going?' or 'how are you getting there?', and is usually heard as 'why'; to ask for the route, say dou yatte iku? or nani de iku?

items.use: Asks a price or amount (kore ikura?); ikura demo means 'as much as you like' (ikura demo aru), and ikura -te mo means 'no matter how much' (ikura tabete mo futoranai).

examplePolite.ja: 全部でいくらですか？

items.notes: ikura is for price and amount; for 'how many' the word is ikutsu.

blocks.label: Hello and goodbye
blocks.rationale: Fixed greetings for the time of day, first meetings, phone calls and leaving.
blocks.interference: hajimemashite opens a first meeting and yoroshiku closes it. konnichiwa is for people you aren't close to; with friends, say ohayou in the morning and otherwise just start talking. moshimoshi is the hello for phone and video calls, not for greeting someone in person.

items.use: The morning greeting. In shift work (restaurants, TV, some shops) ohayou gozaimasu also opens a shift whatever the hour; elsewhere, after midday, colleagues say otsukaresama desu.

examplePolite.ja: おはようございます、早いですね。

items.freqNote: おはよう #606; おはようございます #583; clipped おはよ #5618

items.use: The daytime hello to neighbours, shop staff and people you don't know well. Friends rarely say it to each other.

example.ja: あ、こんにちは！お買い物？

examplePolite.ja: あ、こんにちは。お買い物ですか？
examplePolite.english: Oh, hello. Are you out shopping?

items.freqNote: こんにちは #537
items.notes: The evening version is konbanwa.

items.use: The everyday goodbye to friends and family; 'mata ne' adds 'see you again'.

examplePolite.ja: では、また明日。失礼します。
examplePolite.english: Well then, see you tomorrow. Goodbye.

items.freqNote: じゃあね #937
items.notes: sayounara sounds final or school-like, and friends almost never say it. Leaving work before others: osaki ni shitsurei shimasu; to coworkers generally: otsukaresama desu.

items.use: Opens a first meeting, before you give your name, and is always followed by yoroshiku.

example.ja: はじめまして、健太です。よろしく！
example.english: Hi, I'm Kenta. Nice to meet you!

examplePolite.romaji: hajimemashite, kenta desu. yoroshiku onegai shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: はじめまして、健太です。よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: How do you do, I'm Kenta. Nice to meet you.

items.freqNote: はじめまして #1596; 初めまして #3524

items.english: glad to know you; thanks ahead
items.use: Closes an introduction ('please treat me well') and any favour you leave in someone's hands.
items.politeJa: よろしくお願いします

example.english: Okay, I'm counting on you tomorrow.

examplePolite.ja: では、明日よろしくお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Well then, thank you in advance for tomorrow.

items.freqNote: よろしく #398; よろしくお願いします #516
items.notes: 'X ni yoroshiku' means 'say hi to X for me'.

items.use: Opens a phone or video call, and checks the line when the other person goes quiet or the sound cuts out; it isn't used to greet someone in person.

examplePolite.ja: もしもし、今大丈夫ですか？
examplePolite.english: Hello, is now a good time?

items.freqNote: もしもし #442
items.notes: Checking the line: moshimoshi? kikoeru? (hello? can you hear me?). When you answer a work phone, say hai, [name] desu rather than moshimoshi. Face to face it's either a joking 'hello? anyone home?' or an older speaker's 'excuse me' to a stranger.

blocks.label: Phrases for occasions
blocks.rationale: Fixed phrases tied to a particular moment: meals, bedtime, the end of shared work, someone heading out, and seeing someone again.
blocks.interference: itadakimasu comes before eating and gochisousama after. oyasumi, otsukare and ki o tsukete are all sign-offs: oyasumi for the night, otsukare after work or study together, and ki o tsukete as someone heads out (it also works as a warning: 'careful!'). hisashiburi greets someone you're meeting again and is never a goodbye.

items.use: Said just before you start eating or drinking, alone or with others. It's already a -masu form, so every register uses it unchanged.

example.ja: うわ、おいしそう！いただきます！

examplePolite.ja: おいしそうですね。いただきます。
examplePolite.english: That looks delicious. Thank you, I'll dig in.

items.freqNote: いただきます #486; 頂きます #2378
items.notes: Also accepts something offered, like a drink or a sweet: jaa, itadakimasu = 'don't mind if I do'.

items.use: Said when you finish eating, and to whoever cooked or paid. To a host or someone who treated you, use gochisousama deshita.

example.ja: ああ、おいしかった！ごちそうさま！
example.english: Ah, that was good! Thanks for the meal!

examplePolite.ja: おいしかったです。ごちそうさまでした。
examplePolite.english: That was delicious. Thank you for the meal.

items.freqNote: ごちそうさま #2052; polite ごちそうさまでした #1827
items.notes: At a restaurant, gochisousama deshita on the way out is the usual thank-you to the staff.

items.use: Said when going to bed, parting late at night, or ending a night-time call or chat. It's only a goodbye, never a greeting.

example.ja: じゃあ、また明日。おやすみ。

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、また明日。おやすみなさい。
examplePolite.english: Well, see you tomorrow. Good night.

items.freqNote: おやすみ #1575; polite おやすみなさい #2270 (お休み #1980 also counts the 'day off' sense)
items.notes: yasumi means 'day off, break', and its polite version is also oyasumi: ashita yasumi = 'I'm off tomorrow'; ashita oyasumi desu ka? = 'are you off tomorrow?'. oyasumi means 'good night' only at bedtime or when parting at night.

items.use: Said to people you work or study with when you finish something together or part for the day. With seniors say otsukaresama desu, or otsukaresama deshita once the work is over.

example.romaji: jaa, kyou wa koko made ni shiyou. otsukare!
example.ja: じゃあ、今日はここまでにしよう。お疲れ！
example.english: Okay, let's call it a day. Good work!

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, kyou wa koko made ni shimashou. otsukaresama deshita.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、今日はここまでにしましょう。お疲れさまでした。
examplePolite.english: Well, let's stop here for today. Thanks for all your work.

items.freqNote: お疲れ #848; お疲れさま #504
items.notes: Comes from tsukareru (get tired). At work it is also a passing 'hi' and the reply to someone who leaves first.

items.use: Greets someone you haven't seen or talked to in a while. It also marks doing something again after a long gap.

example.english: Long time no see! How've you been?

examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気でしたか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time. How have you been?

items.freqNote: 久しぶり #594; polite お久しぶり #1495
items.notes: hisashiburi ni + verb means 'for the first time in ages': hisashiburi ni sushi tabeta.

items.use: Said to anyone heading off (going home at night, driving, on a trip), and as a warning ('careful!'). Adding ne (ki o tsukete ne) makes it warmer.

example.romaji: jaa, mata ashita. ki o tsukete ne.
example.ja: じゃあ、また明日。気をつけてね。
example.english: Okay, see you tomorrow. Take care.

examplePolite.romaji: jaa, mata ashita. ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、また明日。気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Well, see you tomorrow. Please take care.

items.freqNote: 気をつけて #1735 (気を付けて #2563 counted separately); verb 気をつける #1226
items.notes: You learn this one as a set phrase. The verb ki o tsukeru comes later (H-ki-o-tsukeru) and adds ki o tsukete kaette ne (get home safe) and ki o tsukemasu (I'll be careful). As a warning it's often shouted on its own: abunai, ki o tsukete! To see off a customer or a senior, say oki o tsukete (お気をつけて), often as oki o tsukete okaeri kudasai, because bare ki o tsukete kudasai sounds more like an instruction.

blocks.label: Now and nearby days
blocks.rationale: The anchor words for the present moment and the days on either side of it. Plans and catch-ups start here.
blocks.interference: kyou and kinou sound alike: listen for the 'no' in ki-no-u. kinou pairs with past tense, ashita with non-past, and kyou with either.

items.use: Places anything at the present moment, and builds ima kara (from now), ima made (until now) and ima sugu (right now).

examplePolite.ja: 今どこですか？

items.use: Names the current day, and kyou wa makes it the topic for plans and small talk.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は休みですか？

items.freqNote: 今日(きょう) #86
items.notes: Shop and office staff say honjitsu. Recognise it, but you don't need to say it.

items.use: The default word for the next day, used in plans, deadlines and goodbyes (jaa ashita).

examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよ。

items.freqNote: 明日(あした) #367; formal あす #10447
items.notes: Shop and office staff say myounichi, and asu is the news reading. Recognise both; ashita is fine in your own polite speech.

items.use: Names the day before today. Pair it with past tense to report what happened.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は休みでした。

items.freqNote: 昨日(きのう) #319
items.notes: To tell kinou from kyou, listen for the 'no'. Shop and office staff say sakujitsu.

blocks.label: this/that: places
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do row for places: here, where, there by you, over there.
blocks.interference: soko is near the listener, asoko is away from both of you; asoko is the irregular member (not ako).

items.use: Names the place where you are, or 'this part' of something (koko ga muzukashii); takes ni for where things are and de for where things happen.

examplePolite.ja: ここにありますよ。

items.notes: Shop staff say kochira for 'here'; koko is fine in your own polite speech.

items.use: Asks where (doko ni aru?, doko iku?) or which part (doko ga ii?); in casual speech the particle after it is often dropped.

examplePolite.ja: どちらにありますか？

items.notes: doko desu ka is fine in everyday polite speech; dochira is the softer version. dochira also means 'which of two' (dotchi): dochira ni? and dochira kara? ask about a place, dochira ga ii? asks for a choice.

items.use: A place near the listener or one just mentioned, and also 'that point' in a discussion (soko ga mondai).

examplePolite.ja: そこにありますよ。

items.freqNote: 底 'bottom' counted separately (#4174)
items.notes: soko is by the listener; a place far from both of you is asoko.

items.use: A place away from both speakers, either in view or one you both know (asoko no raamenya).

examplePolite.ja: あそこにありますよ。

items.notes: The irregular member: asoko, not ako.

blocks.label: But
blocks.rationale: Three ways to say 'but', from neutral to complaining, learned on one rain sentence.
blocks.interference: demo starts a new sentence, -kedo ends the first clause, -noni adds surprise or complaint and can't lead into a request or plan; the shared 'ame ... iku' sentence keeps only the connector changing.

items.use: Opens a sentence or a turn that pushes back against what was just said; works the same in every register.

example.romaji: ame da ne. demo, iku yo.
example.english: It's raining, huh. But I'm going.

examplePolite.romaji: ame desu ne. demo, ikimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 雨ですね。でも、行きますよ。

items.freqNote: でも #32 (also counts noun + demo 'even / or something')
items.notes: Same sound as noun + demo ('ocha demo' = tea or something); sentence-initial position tells them apart.

items.use: Ends the first clause and contrasts it with the second. Left trailing, it softens a statement ('chotto takai kedo...') or sets up a request ('chotto kikitai n da kedo...'). Fuller keredo; formal ga.
items.politeJa: ですけど / ますけど

examplePolite.ja: 雨ですけど、行きますよ。

items.freqNote: けど #37; fuller けれど #1376
items.notes: A trailing kedo ('sumimasen kedo...') is a soft opener, not a contrast.

items.use: Contrast with surprise, complaint or regret: the result isn't what the first clause should lead to. Nouns and na-adjectives take na noni. Left trailing it's a complaint ('itta noni!' = 'but I told you!'); after -tara / -ba it means 'if only' ('motto hayaku ittara, maniatta noni').

example.english: You're going, even though it's raining?

examplePolite.romaji: ame na noni, iku n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 雨なのに、行くんですか？
examplePolite.english: You're going even though it's raining?

items.freqNote: のに #95 (also counts purpose noni); sentence-initial なのに #274, それなのに #1791
items.notes: Can't end in a request or plan ('...noni, ikou' is wrong); use kedo there.

blocks.label: Because / so
blocks.rationale: The reason family: two clause linkers, two sentence openers and the reason-stacker.
blocks.interference: -kara vs -node differ in softness, not meaning: node sounds objective and suits strangers, and in polite speech it still follows the plain form ('isogashii node, ikemasen'). dakara points forward to the result while datte points back to the reason; kara, dakara and datte share the 'isogashii' reason so only the linker changes.

items.use: Reason clause + kara + result; also ends a sentence as a bare excuse ('isogashii kara'). Nouns and na-adjectives take da kara.
items.politeJa: ですから / ますから

example.english: I'm busy, so I can't go.

examplePolite.romaji: abunai desu kara, ki o tsukete kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 危ないですから、気をつけてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous, so please be careful.

items.freqNote: から #14 (also counts 'from')
items.notes: Reason comes first, then kara, then the result: the reverse of English 'because'. As a polite refusal desu kara sounds pointed; use node there ('isogashii node, ikemasen').

items.use: Same reason-then-result order as kara, but sounds objective and softer; the standard choice for explanations and excuses to strangers. Nouns and na-adjectives take na node.

example.romaji: ashita hayai node, mou neru ne.
example.ja: 明日早いので、もう寝るね。
example.english: I've got an early start tomorrow, so I'm heading to bed.

examplePolite.ja: 忙しいので、行けません。
examplePolite.english: I'm busy, so I can't go.

items.freqNote: ので #156; casual contraction -n de
items.notes: With friends kara is the default; node, when used, often clips to -n de ('isogashii n de'). In polite speech node still follows the plain form; desu node / -masu node is business-formal.

items.use: Starts a sentence that states the result of what came before; said sharply ('dakara!') it means 'like I said'.

example.ja: 忙しいんだ。だから、行けない。
example.english: I'm busy. So I can't go.

examplePolite.ja: 忙しいんです。なので、行けません。
examplePolite.english: I'm busy. So I can't go.

items.freqNote: だから #58; polite なので #652; ですから #269 (can sound insistent)
items.notes: Points forward to the result; datte points back to the reason. In polite speech, desu kara at the start of a sentence can sound insistent ('as I said'); nanode is the softer opener.

items.use: Starts a sentence that justifies yourself or pushes back, usually answering 'why?' or a complaint; the reason follows, often ending in n da (yo / mon).

examplePolite.ja: でも、忙しいんですよ。

items.freqNote: だって #79, also counts 'even / too' datte
items.notes: Sounds sulky to a coworker; there, open with demo and give the reason with ...n desu (yo). Don't confuse it with noun + datte 'even X' or hearsay '...n datte' ('I hear').

items.english: and what's more; since ... and all
items.use: Stacks reasons ('yasui shi, oishii shi'); a single trailing -shi hints there are more, like 'and all'. Nouns and na-adjectives take da shi.

example.english: It's late and all, let's head home.

examplePolite.ja: もう遅いですし、帰りましょう。
examplePolite.english: It's late and all, so let's head home.

items.notes: A trailing -shi gives a reason softly ('mou osoi shi'); it isn't a neutral 'and' for listing facts, use -te for that.

blocks.label: And then
blocks.rationale: Ways to carry on to the next thing: -te inside a sentence; de, jaa and ato at the start of one.
blocks.interference: Sentence-initial de is not the place / means particle de; ato alone means 'also' while ato de means 'later'; jaa overlaps with dattara (If-openers block).

items.use: The te-form chains clauses: one action then the next, or a cause and its result ('tsukarete, neta'). Adjectives join with -kute, nouns and na-adjectives with de.

examplePolite.ja: うちに帰って、寝ました。

items.freqNote: て #458, heavily undercounted: tokenizer usually fuses -te into the verb
items.notes: Tense and politeness go only on the last verb, in polite speech too: 'kaette, nemashita', not 'kaerimashite' (that sounds formal). A -te reason can't lead into a request or invitation ('isogashikute, tetsudatte' is wrong); use kara there.

items.use: Starts a sentence that moves a story to the next step, or prompts the speaker to go on ('de?' = 'and?'). Clipped casual form of sorede.

examplePolite.ja: それで、どうなりましたか？

items.freqNote: rank of それで; sentence-initial で is not separable from particle で (#8); slangy んで #3821
items.notes: Comes first, after a pause; that's how to hear it apart from the particle de. Bare 'de?' can sound impatient; 'de, de?' or 'sorede?' with rising pitch sounds keen.

items.use: Draws a conclusion from what was just said and moves to the next step: deciding, ordering, wrapping up, saying goodbye. Short form ja.

example.english: Okay then, I'll go with this.

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、これにします。
examplePolite.english: Okay then, I'll go with this one.

items.notes: To a clerk or coworker, jaa + masu is normal ('jaa, kore ni shimasu'); dewa is the formal version for meetings, announcements and shop staff.

items.use: Starts a sentence that adds one more item to a list, order or request, often as an afterthought.

examplePolite.ja: あと、これもお願いします。
examplePolite.english: Oh, and this one too, please.

items.freqNote: あと #135, also counts 'after / later / remaining'
items.notes: Ato de = 'later'; ato + amount = 'more / left' ('ato gofun' = five more minutes); bare ato at the start, then a pause = 'oh, and'.

blocks.label: Past, negative, linking
blocks.rationale: The first endings almost every sentence needs: past and negative for verbs and for adjectives/nouns, plus the adjective/noun linking form built on the same -ku stem.
blocks.interference: Verbs and adjectives conjugate differently (neta / isogashikatta, ikanai / isogashikunai), never *isogashii datta; and takai ja nai is a tag ('it's pricey, isn't it?'), never the negative takakunai.

items.use: Puts any verb in the past for what you did or what happened, built with the same sound changes as the -te form (itta, tabeta, shita).

example.english: I went to bed early last night.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は早く寝ました。
examplePolite.english: I went to bed early last night.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer folds た into the verb (standalone た #100752)
items.notes: -ta also covers 'already': mou tabeta? = have you eaten yet? Trap: 'not yet' is mada tabetenai, never *tabenakatta, which means 'I didn't eat (then)'.

items.use: Makes any verb negative for 'don't / won't' (ikanai, wakannai), and is the stem that -nakya, -nakute mo ii and -nai hou ga ii build on.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は行きません。

items.freqNote: ない #43 combines the negative auxiliary and the adjective 'there isn't'
items.notes: Past negative is -nakatta (ikanakatta); casual speech shortens -ranai to -nnai (wakannai). With a rising tone it invites: issho ni ikanai? = want to come? (polite: ikimasen ka?)

items.use: Past tense for descriptions: i-adjectives swap -i for -katta (samukatta, ii -> yokatta), while na-adjectives and nouns take datta (hima datta, ame datta).

examplePolite.ja: 昨日は忙しかったです。

items.freqNote: rank of だった; the tokenizer splits -katta off the adjective, so it has no usable rank of its own
items.notes: Trap: never *takai datta, and in polite speech never *takai deshita; the past goes on the i-adjective itself (takakatta, takakatta desu).

items.use: Negative for descriptions: i-adjectives swap -i for -kunai (takakunai, ii -> yokunai), while na-adjectives and nouns take ja nai (hima ja nai, sou ja nai).

examplePolite.ja: 今日は忙しくないです。

items.freqNote: rank of じゃない, which also counts the tag-question use (ja nai?)
items.notes: Past negative: -kunakatta / ja nakatta (polite -kunakatta desu / ja nakatta desu). Trap: after an i-adjective ja nai is always the tag (takai ja nai = it's pricey, isn't it); more formal polite is -ku arimasen / ja arimasen.

items.use: The -te form of adjectives and nouns, used to link descriptions (yasukute oishii) or give a reason (isogashikute, hima de); negatives use -nakute (jikan ga nakute).

example.ja: この店、安くておいしいよ。
example.english: This place is cheap and the food's good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono omise, yasukute oishii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このお店、安くておいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: This place is cheap and the food's good.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; an inflection the tokenizer splits off
items.notes: Na-adjectives and nouns take de (shizuka de, ame de); ii -> yokute.

blocks.label: Doing and done
blocks.rationale: Four -te auxiliaries that set the shape of an action: ongoing, tried out, finished, done ahead.
blocks.interference: -teru, -chau and -toku are all short contractions on the same -te form; key on the ending: -teru ongoing, -chatta finished, -toku done ahead. Don't mix -toku with -teku (-te iku): kaitoku vs kaiteku. -te miru stays apart as 'try and see'.

items.english: is doing / is in a state
items.use: Attaches to the -te form for an ongoing action (tabeteru), a resulting state (kekkon shiteru, shitteru) or a habit; it is the casual contraction of -te iru.

example.english: I'm writing a report right now.

examplePolite.ja: 今レポート書いてます。
examplePolite.english: I'm writing a report right now.

items.freqNote: rank of contracted てる; full いる #42 also counts the main verb 'be'
items.notes: With change verbs it's a state, not progress: kekkon shiteru = is married. Trap: the negative of shitteru is shiranai, not *shittenai.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to try something out and see how it goes (tabete miru, kiite miru), which also softens plans and suggestions.

example.english: OK, I'll give it a try.

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、食べてみます。
examplePolite.english: OK, I'll give it a try.

items.freqNote: rank of kana みる, mostly the auxiliary (見る #55 is 'see')
items.notes: Not 'attempt and fail': you actually do it to find out.

items.use: Contracted -te shimau, marking something done completely, often with regret or an 'oops' (wasurechatta, tabechatta); -nde verbs take -jau (nonjatta).

example.ja: レポート、もう書いちゃった。

examplePolite.ja: レポート、もう書いちゃいました。

items.freqNote: rank of ちゃう (some Kansai ちゃう 'no, wrong' mixed in); ちゃった #4935, じゃう #9415, full しまう #2285
items.notes: The regret reading is the everyday one: saifu wasurechatta = I forgot my wallet (ugh). Not -cha (= -te wa): kaetchau = I'll end up going home, kaetcha dame = you can't go home. -chaimashita is friendly-polite; with superiors or strangers use -te shimaimashita.

items.use: Contracted -te oku, for doing something now so it's ready later (kattoku) or leaving it as it is (sono mama ni shitoite); -nde verbs take -doku (yondoku).

example.ja: レポート、先に書いとく。
example.english: I'll get the report written first.

examplePolite.ja: レポート、先に書いときます。
examplePolite.english: I'll get the report written first.

items.freqNote: rank of kana おく (mostly the -te oku auxiliary); contracted とく #8852
items.notes: Not -teku (-te iku): kaitoku = write it now so it's done, kaiteku = write it before heading off. Past -toita (kaitoita) sits close to -teta (kaiteta); listen for the o.

blocks.label: Be, have, live
blocks.rationale: The ways to say something is there or that you have it — aru for things, iru for people and animals, motteru for what you own or carry — plus sumu for where you live.
blocks.interference: aru vs iru depends on whether the thing is alive (kasa aru / neko iru), and that holds for 'have' too: kyoudai iru? / inu iru? but jikan aru?; motteru is for what's in your possession or on you (kasa motteru?); iru is where you are now and sunderu where you live (ima doko ni iru? / doko ni sunderu?).

items.use: States that a thing, event or amount exists or is available, and is the default 'have' for time, plans and things (jikan aru?), with the thing marked by ga.

example.english: Do you have an umbrella at home?

examplePolite.romaji: uchi ni kasa ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: うちに傘がありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have an umbrella at home?

items.freqNote: ある #21; includes auxiliary -te aru and copular de aru
items.notes: The negative is the separate word nai (kasa nai), never *aranai.

items.use: Says where a person or animal is or that they exist (ima doko ni iru?), is the 'have' for people and animals (kyoudai iru?, kanojo iru?, inu iru?), and is the base that -teru is built on.

examplePolite.ja: 今うちにいますか？

items.freqNote: いる #42 merges the verb with auxiliary -te iru; 居る #6802 separately
items.notes: Homophone iru 'need' (要る) is godan: iranai, itte.

items.use: Holding or carrying something, and in the -teru form owning or having it on you (kuruma motteru?), with motte iku / motte kuru meaning take / bring.

example.english: Do you have an umbrella on you?

examplePolite.ja: 今傘持ってますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have an umbrella with you?

items.notes: Owning or having it on you is motteru; bare motsu is 'hold / carry' (motou ka? = shall I carry that?) and also 'last' (ashita made motsu, karada ga motanai).

items.use: Says where someone lives, with the place marked by ni; your current home takes the -teru form (doko ni sunderu?), the plain form is for a move ahead (rainen toukyou ni sumu) and -tai for a wish (toukyou ni sumitai).

examplePolite.ja: どこに住んでますか？

items.freqNote: 住む #548; homophone 済む (be over) #671 and kana-written すむ #1535 are separate entries
items.notes: Homophone sumu 'be over, be settled' (済む) also gives sunde, sunda, and its polite negative is sumimasen (sorry), one sound off sumimasu; for where you live now say sundemasu, and 'I don't live there' is sundenai / sundemasen.

blocks.label: Do, can, become, change
blocks.rationale: The structural action verbs — do (suru, casual yaru), can do (dekiru) and become (naru) — that turn nouns and adjectives into events, plus kawaru for something changing on its own.
blocks.interference: suru and yaru overlap as 'do' (nani shiteru / nani yatteru), but only suru builds noun+suru verbs (shinpai suru, renraku suru); 'can do' for those is X dekiru, not a potential form of suru; naru says what something became (samuku natta) while kawaru says it's different from before (kawatta ne) and names the result only with ni (yotei ga raishuu ni kawatta); its transitive partner kaeru (change it) gives kaeta (changed it), one doubled t away from kaetta (went home).

items.use: The all-purpose 'do' and the hinge of every noun+suru verb (benkyou suru, shinpai suru), while X ni suru / -ku suru means 'go with X' or 'make it X'.

example.english: What are you up to right now?

examplePolite.ja: 今何をしてますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you doing right now?

items.freqNote: する #15; also carries every noun+suru compound
items.notes: Irregular: shite, shita, shinai, shiyou.

items.use: Casual-leaning 'do' for activities, hobbies, sports and tasks (yatta!, gitaa yatteru, nani yatteru?); yarimasu is normal in everyday polite talk (watashi ga yarimasu), with shimasu the safer choice in formal settings.

example.ja: なんかスポーツやってる？

examplePolite.ja: 何かスポーツをやってますか？

items.freqNote: やる #45; includes -te yaru
items.notes: yatta! = 'Yay!' for any good news, not only your own success; yaru also means give to pets and plants (mizu yatta?), and -te yaru (doing for someone) sounds rough.

items.english: can do; be ready; come into being
items.use: The 'can' for skills and every noun+suru verb (unten dekiru, nihongo dekiru), with the skill marked by ga; dekita means 'it's ready / done' and also that something new appeared (atarashii mise ga dekita, kareshi dekita?).

examplePolite.romaji: kuruma no unten wa dekimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 車の運転はできますか？

items.freqNote: できる #73 (kana); 出来る #1313 counted separately
items.notes: Only nouns and suru-verbs take dekiru (unten dekiru, never *unten sureru); every other verb uses its potential form: ikeru, taberareru, never *iku dekiru.

items.use: Any change of state, as adjective -ku naru or noun / na-adjective ni naru (samuku natta, genki ni natta), and dou natta? asks how something turned out.

examplePolite.ja: 寒くなりましたね。

items.freqNote: なる #29
items.notes: Past natta reports the new state: samuku natta = it's cold now.

items.use: Says something changed on its own (a person, plan, place or price), with the thing marked by ga; changing it yourself is the transitive kaeru (kaeta).

examplePolite.ja: 変わってませんね。

items.freqNote: 変わる #226; 代わる (take over, swap) #1244 counted separately
items.notes: kawatteru / kawatta often means odd or unusual, not 'is changing' (kawatteru ne = you're a bit unusual; kawatta hito = an odd person). 代わる shares the sound: kawarou ka? = want me to take over?

blocks.label: Coming and going
blocks.rationale: The motion verbs for plans and arrivals: go, come, go home, come back, leave, enter.
blocks.interference: iku/kuru follow the speaker's position, so 'I'll come to your party' is iku yo; kaeru means back to home or base while modoru means back to where you just were.

items.use: Going anywhere, asking about plans (iku?) and inviting (ikou), with the destination marked by ni or e; te-form and past are irregular (itte, itta).

example.ja: 明日のパーティー行く？
example.english: Are you going to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーに行きますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you going to the party tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 行く #40; kana いく #179 separately; both include -te iku
items.notes: Heading to the listener is iku: ima iku ne = 'coming now'.

items.use: Movement toward the speaker or the place being talked about (kite!, kita!), and it is irregular: kita, konai, kite.

example.ja: 明日のパーティー来る？
example.english: Are you coming to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni kimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーに来ますか？
examplePolite.english: Are you coming to the party tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 来る #52; kana くる #429 separately; both include -te kuru
items.notes: The host asks kuru?; the guest answers iku yo.

items.use: Going back home or to your base such as your hometown or country (mou kaeru), and it is godan: kaette, kaetta.

example.english: What time are you heading home?

examplePolite.ja: 何時に帰りますか？
examplePolite.english: What time are you going home?

items.freqNote: 帰る #101; homophone 変える (change) #450 separately
items.notes: Looks ichidan but is godan (kaette); kaeru 'change' is ichidan (kaete).

items.use: Returning to where you just were, or to a topic or earlier state (sugu modoru), without the 'home' meaning of kaeru.

example.english: What time will you be back?

examplePolite.ja: 何時に戻りますか？
examplePolite.english: What time will you be back?

items.use: Leaving a place (ie o deru) and coming out or appearing, as in answering the phone (denwa ni deru), getting a fever (netsu ga deta) or being in a show or match.

examplePolite.ja: もう家を出ましたよ。

items.freqNote: 出る #81
items.notes: Its transitive partner is dasu (put out, hand in).

items.use: Going into a room, bath, club or company, and fitting into a container (kaban ni hairu?), with the place marked by ni.

example.english: Have you had your bath yet?

examplePolite.ja: もうお風呂に入りましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you had your bath yet?

items.notes: Godan despite the -iru ending: haitte, haitta.

blocks.label: this/that + noun
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do row that is always followed by a noun, with the same distances as kore/sore/are.
blocks.interference: kono must have a noun after it (kono mise) while kore stands alone; sono toki is 'then' in a story, ano toki is 'that time we both remember'.

items.use: Goes before a noun to point at something near you or current (kono mise, kono hen = around here) and never stands alone.

examplePolite.ja: この店、おいしいですよ。

items.notes: kono mae usually means 'the other day', not 'before this'.

items.use: Goes before a noun for something near the listener or just mentioned (sono hito, sono toki = at that time), which makes it the main back-reference word in stories.

example.english: That place you mentioned is good.

examplePolite.ja: その店、おいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That place you mentioned is good.

items.freqNote: also counts the hesitation filler sono... (G)
items.notes: Said alone with a pause, sono... is a hesitation filler (G).

items.use: Goes before a noun for something far off, or for something you both remember (ano mise, ano toki = that time).

example.english: That place (you know the one) is good.

examplePolite.ja: あの店、おいしいですよ。
examplePolite.english: That place (you know the one) is good.

items.freqNote: also counts the hesitation filler ano (G)
items.notes: Said alone, ano... is the 'um, excuse me' filler (G).

items.use: Goes before a noun to ask which one of several, mostly inside set frames (dono hen?, dono hito?, dono kurai?).

examplePolite.ja: どのくらいかかりますか？

items.notes: dono kurai? (how long, how much) is its most useful frame.

blocks.label: People
blocks.rationale: The person words every conversation needs: I, the name suffix, everyone and oneself.
blocks.interference: jibun means 'self' for whoever the subject is, not only 'me'; -san never goes on your own name.

items.use: The neutral 'I', safe for anyone in polite speech, though men usually switch to boku or ore casually; it is dropped whenever context makes it clear and used mainly for contrast or 'me too'.

examplePolite.ja: 私も行きます。

items.notes: Saying watashi in every sentence sounds foreign; drop it unless you're contrasting. In casual speech men usually say boku or ore and women watashi or atashi; with desu/masu, watashi suits everyone.

items.use: Attaches to a name, a job or a shop (tanaka-san, omawari-san, panya-san) as the default respectful suffix, but never on your own name, or on your own family when talking to outsiders.

examplePolite.ja: 田中さんはもう来てますか？

items.freqNote: さん #17 (三 'three' counted separately at #2400)
items.notes: Where English says 'you', use the person's name + san (tanaka-san wa dou?); anata sounds distant or presumptuous. -kun (boys, juniors) and -chan (children, close friends) are the casual alternatives.

items.use: Everyone in the group (minna de = all together); in polite speech minasan addresses or refers to other people.

examplePolite.ja: 皆さんお元気ですか？

items.freqNote: polite 皆さん #332
items.notes: Keep minna when you include yourself (minna de ikimashou); minasan is for others.

items.use: A reflexive 'self' for any person: jibun de (by yourself, on your own) and jibun no (your own).

examplePolite.ja: 自分でやります。

items.notes: In Kansai, jibun can also mean 'you'.

blocks.label: Me, us, home
blocks.rationale: Beyond watashi: boku, the softer male 'I' that works casually and with desu/masu, -tachi for 'we' and 'X and the others', and uchi for home and 'our side'.
blocks.interference: boku is for men only; it is fine with desu/masu among coworkers, but watashi is safer with strangers and superiors. -tachi goes on people, never on things. uchi ni (at home) sounds like -uchi ni (while), which follows a verb, an adjective or X no (atsui uchi ni, kyou no uchi ni).

items.use: The softer male 'I': gentle among friends (ore is the rougher, very common one there) and still fine with desu/masu among coworkers. Women don't use it, and with strangers, clients and superiors watashi is the safe choice, so the polite form here is watashi.

examplePolite.ja: 私もそう思います。

items.freqNote: 僕 #123; rougher 俺 ore #44
items.notes: ore is the rougher male 'I' among friends: learn to recognise it and save it until you know the group. Adults also call a small boy boku (boku, namae wa? = what's your name?), so there it means 'you'.

items.use: Attaches to a person word or a name to mean that person and their group: watashitachi (we), kodomotachi (the kids), tanaka-san-tachi (Tanaka and the others). It is used for people (and pets), never for things.

example.ja: 田中さんたちはもう帰ったよ。
example.english: Tanaka and the others already went home.

examplePolite.ja: 田中さんたちはもう帰りましたよ。
examplePolite.english: Tanaka and the others already went home.

items.notes: Men also say bokutachi or bokura, and oretachi or orera (rougher, common among male friends). Plural is optional: kodomo alone can already mean 'the kids', so add -tachi when you want to stress the group.

items.use: Means home, usually your own (uchi ni iru, uchi ni kaeru), and uchi no puts the next noun on your side: uchi no kaisha (our company), uchi no ko (my kid).

example.english: Want to come over to my place today?

examplePolite.ja: 今日、うちに来ませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come over to my place today?

items.freqNote: うち #113, which also counts -uchi ni 'while' (A-uchi-ni); 家 read いえ #152
items.notes: ie means the house as a building. As 'I', uchi is Kansai or young women's speech, so just recognise it.

blocks.label: A bit / more
blocks.rationale: The small-degree dials and their 'more' partners, needed in almost every request or comment.
blocks.interference: chotto and sukoshi share the 'a little' sense; chotto is the spoken default and sukoshi sounds more careful. Only chotto does the social jobs: softening (chotto ii?), getting attention (chotto!) and the soft refusal (chotto…). motto is 'more' and mou chotto is 'a bit more', which makes a softer request.

items.use: Turns a degree or amount down to 'a bit'. It is the everyday spoken default and also softens complaints, requests and refusals.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと高いですね
examplePolite.english: It's a bit pricey, isn't it.

items.freqNote: whole word; rank includes softener and 'excuse me' uses
items.notes: Said alone with a trailing tone ('chotto…'), it is a soft no (see G).

items.use: Means the same 'a little' as chotto but sounds more careful. It is safe in polite speech and also measures amounts (sukoshi dake).

examplePolite.ja: 少し高いですね
examplePolite.english: It's a little expensive, isn't it.

items.notes: Casual talk prefers chotto. Reach for sukoshi with strangers or when chotto might sound evasive.

items.use: Adds 'more' to any adjective, adverb or verb (motto yukkuri, motto hoshii, motto ganbaru).

examplePolite.ja: もっと頑張ります

items.notes: For 'one more' of something use mou (mou hitotsu, mou ikkai), never motto. In a request to a stranger, mou chotto or mou sukoshi sounds softer. For 'too much' the ending is -sugiru (see I).

items.use: Asks for or offers 'a bit more' of anything, and is softer than motto. With de it means 'almost' (mou chotto de owaru).

example.ja: もうちょっとゆっくり話して

examplePolite.ja: もうちょっとゆっくり話してください
examplePolite.english: Please speak a little more slowly.

items.freqNote: kept whole by the tokenizer; もう少し is split and shows only #41735
items.notes: With strangers, mou sukoshi is the slightly more careful version.

blocks.label: Already, still, finally
blocks.rationale: These say where an event stands: done, not yet, ongoing all along, or done after a long wait.
blocks.interference: mou + negative means 'not anymore' and mada + negative means 'not yet'. zutto is an unbroken stretch, and yatto is the moment that stretch finally ends.

items.use: Marks something as done (mou tabeta), or as over for good when the verb is negative (mou ikanai). 'mou ...?' asks whether it has happened yet.

examplePolite.ja: ご飯はもう食べましたか？

items.freqNote: もう #36, all senses (already / anymore / more / exasperated 'mou!')
items.notes: Before an amount, mou means 'more, another': mou ichido (once more), mou sukoshi (a bit more). 'mou!' said alone with a sigh is exasperation, not a time word.

items.use: Says something hasn't changed yet. mada + negative means 'not yet', mada + -teru means 'still doing', and mada alone answers a 'mou ...?' question.

examplePolite.ja: ご飯はまだ食べてません。

items.freqNote: まだ #92
items.notes: 'Haven't X yet' is mada + -te nai (mada tabetenai), or just mada (desu). Not mada tabenakatta (= I didn't eat) and not mada tabenai (= I won't eat yet).

items.use: Stretches a state or action unbroken across time: zutto matteta (waited the whole time), zutto suki (have always liked).

example.english: I've been waiting the whole time.

examplePolite.ja: ずっと待ってましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I've been waiting the whole time.

items.freqNote: ずっと #142, includes the 'by far' comparison sense
items.notes: In comparisons it means 'by far' (zutto ii = much better).

items.use: Shows relief that something long awaited has happened, usually with past tense (yatto owatta).

examplePolite.ja: やっと仕事が終わりました。

items.notes: tsuini is the more dramatic 'at last', the climax of a long build-up, and it can mark a bad end (tsuini kowareta = it finally broke). yatto always sounds relieved, and can also mean 'only just' (yatto ma ni atta = only just made it).

blocks.label: Really / very
blocks.rationale: The intensity dial: five words that each go before the same adjective and set how strong it is.
blocks.interference: kekkou and kanari sit below sugoku: kekkou adds 'more than I expected', and kanari is matter-of-fact. honto ni stresses that it is true rather than how big it is. metcha is casual only.

items.use: The everyday spoken 'very'. It goes before an adjective or verb and works in both casual and polite speech.

examplePolite.ja: これ、すごくおいしいです

items.freqNote: tokenizer lemmatises すごく under すごい (#114, includes adjective uses); すごく as its own entry is a residual #40036
items.notes: Casual speech often uses sugoi as the adverb (sugoi oishii). Natives say it, but it counts as sloppy and slangy: recognise it, produce sugoku, and never use sugoi + adjective in desu/masu speech.

items.use: Adds 'really / truly' to an adjective, verb or thanks (honto ni arigatou). It stresses sincerity more than size.

example.ja: これ、ほんとにおいしい

examplePolite.ja: これ、本当においしいです

items.freqNote: rank of 本当に (all registers); casual spelling ほんとに separately #3240
items.notes: The bare reaction 'honto?' (really?) is a separate item in G.

items.use: Means 'pretty / quite', and signals that the degree is higher than you expected.

examplePolite.romaji: asoko no mise, kekkou oishii desu yo
examplePolite.ja: あそこの店、結構おいしいですよ
examplePolite.english: That place is actually pretty good, you know.

items.freqNote: rank includes the 'kekkou desu' (no thanks / fine) senses
items.notes: Trap: 'kekkou desu' on its own (often with a small hand wave) is a polite 'no thanks' (see G), so never use it to accept an offer; say 'onegai shimasu'. 'Kore de kekkou desu' means 'this will do'. Before an adjective (kekkou oishii) it never means 'no', but never say kekkou oishii to the person who made or chose the food: it implies you expected worse. Use sugoku or hontou ni instead.

items.use: A strong but measured 'considerably'. It sits between kekkou and sugoku and sounds factual rather than excited.

examplePolite.ja: これ、かなりおいしいです

items.use: Casual 'super / so', the strongest everyday intensifier among younger speakers. Switch to totemo or sugoku in polite speech.

example.ja: これ、めっちゃおいしい

examplePolite.ja: これ、とてもおいしいです

items.freqNote: めっちゃ #1170; stronger sibling めちゃくちゃ #1297
items.notes: Kansai in origin, now used nationwide. vocab-trainer spells it meccha. The polite pair totemo sounds stiff among friends (use sugoku there), and with a negative it means 'no way': totemo muri = can't possibly.

blocks.label: Explaining: n da
blocks.rationale: The n/no explanatory frame in four forms: statement, question, soft lead-in and conclusion. All four share one base sentence.
blocks.interference: n da gives the reason and wake da draws the conclusion from it. no? is the question form, and the answer usually comes back with n da. After nouns, all four take na (yasumi na n da, yasumi na no?).

items.use: Frames a statement as the explanation or background to the situation: giving reasons, sharing news, or showing you're personally involved.

examplePolite.ja: 頭が痛いんです
examplePolite.english: I have a headache, you see.

items.freqNote: #20 んだ (polite んです #23)
items.notes: After nouns and na-adjectives it becomes na n da (yasumi na n da). As a question, use no? (casual) or n desu ka (polite); casual n da? sounds rough. n desu ka about someone's actions can sound like a challenge (nani shite iru n desu ka?).

items.use: The everyday casual question that asks about the situation or for an explanation (doushita no?, doko iku no?). It is said with a rising tone and used by everyone.

examplePolite.romaji: atama ga itai n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 頭が痛いんですか？

items.freqNote: rank of なの (na no?); bare の #1 is mostly possessive
items.notes: With a falling tone (atama itai no), it is a soft, feminine-leaning statement version of n da.

items.use: Sets out the background and trails off so the listener can offer help. It is the soft way to open a request, a question or a new topic.

example.romaji: chotto atama itai n da kedo
example.ja: ちょっと頭痛いんだけど
example.english: My head kind of hurts, so...

examplePolite.romaji: chotto atama ga itai n desu kedo
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと頭が痛いんですけど
examplePolite.english: I have a bit of a headache, so...

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of けど #37, the rarer component (んだ #20)
items.notes: Leave the request unsaid, because the listener fills it in. The polite form is the classic opener with clerks.

items.use: Draws the conclusion once the reason is known ('no wonder', 'which means'). It is common as sou iu wake (so that's how it is). dou iu wake? demands an explanation (what's going on here?!); the neutral question is dou iu koto?

example.english: So that's why your head hurts.

examplePolite.romaji: dakara atama ga itai wake desu ne
examplePolite.ja: だから頭が痛いわけですね
examplePolite.english: So that's why your head hurts.

items.freqNote: わけ #272 (all uses; わけじゃない #535 and わけない #449 are separate tokens); わけだ not found
items.notes: Don't confuse it with wake ja nai (it's not that...), which is a separate item.

blocks.label: Thinking aloud
blocks.rationale: Endings for talking half to yourself: exclaiming, wondering, trying to remember, and summing things up loosely.
blocks.interference: kana wonders about something you don't know, while kke tries to recall something you once knew. naa is said to yourself, where ne would draw the listener in (samui naa vs samui ne). tte kanji loosely sums up your own impression; it is not tte koto?, which checks what the other person meant.

items.use: Exclaims or muses to yourself, for envy, admiration or wishes (ii naa, samui naa, ikitai naa). Unlike ne, it isn't aimed at the listener. Polite speech has no self-talk; drawn-out desu nee is the nearest.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は寒いですねえ
examplePolite.english: It's really cold today, isn't it.

items.freqNote: #387 なあ (なー #934); bare な #16 merges prohibitive and attributive na
items.notes: Short na works after adjectives and -tai (samui na, ikitai na). After a dictionary-form verb, short na is a rough prohibition (iku na = don't go!), so stretch it: ame furu naa. Short na aimed at someone in place of ne (sou da na, jaa na) is masculine-leaning.

items.use: Wonders aloud about something you don't know, or softens a guess or request (ii kana? = is it okay?). Because it is half to yourself, the listener can answer or not.

example.english: Is the meeting tomorrow, I wonder?

examplePolite.romaji: kaigi wa ashita desu ka ne
examplePolite.ja: 会議は明日ですかね
examplePolite.english: Is the meeting tomorrow, I wonder?

items.freqNote: #90 かな (polite でしょうか #341)
items.notes: No da before it: ashita kana, not *ashita da kana. deshou ka is the more formal polite option, right for clerks and superiors. kana is common even with coworkers as a soft hedge: ...kana to omoimasu. The feminine kashira is dated and heard mostly in dramas.

items.use: Asks someone to confirm something you once knew but have half-forgotten, like a name, time or plan. It attaches to da / datta or a past verb (nan datta kke?, itta kke?); with a non-past verb, use n da kke (iku n da kke?). It can also be nostalgic self-talk: yoku asonda kke (we used to play a lot).
items.politeJa: でしたっけ／〜ましたっけ

example.english: Wait, is the meeting tomorrow again?

examplePolite.ja: 会議は明日でしたっけ？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, remind me, is the meeting tomorrow?

items.notes: deshita kke is fine with coworkers but a little casual for superiors.

items.use: Sums up a feeling or situation loosely ('it's like...'), so you can approximate when you lack the exact words. sonna kanji means 'something like that', and konna kanji desu (it's like this) is fine at work.

example.english: Eh, it's kind of just okay.

examplePolite.ja: まあ普通って感じです

items.freqNote: rank of 感じ (all uses); って感じ and そんな感じ not found
items.notes: A sentence-final X tte kanji is youthful and sounds vague when overused; sonna / konna kanji is the neutral all-purpose core.

blocks.label: How often
blocks.rationale: The frequency scale for habits, plus nando mo for one thing repeated again and again. Every one of these goes ahead of the verb phrase it describes.
blocks.interference: Keep the habit words on one scale: itsumo > yoku > tokidoki > tama ni. mainichi literally means every day, not 'always'. nando mo sits off the scale: it counts repeats of one thing, usually in past tense (nando mo itta = I said it over and over), and 'many times' is nando mo, not takusan.

items.use: Says something happens every single day. It is the backbone of talk about routines.

examplePolite.ja: 毎日歩いて帰ります。

items.notes: The same mai- gives maiasa (every morning), maiban (every night) and maishuu (every week).

items.use: The default word for habits and for doing things as usual. It sits at the top of the frequency scale.

examplePolite.ja: いつも歩いて帰ります。

items.freqNote: いつも #172
items.notes: itsumo no means 'the usual' (itsumo no mise = our usual place).

items.use: The everyday word for 'often', used before any verb to describe a habit (yoku iku).

examplePolite.ja: よく歩いて帰ります。

items.freqNote: よく #143, includes the 'well / thoroughly' sense
items.notes: It is the same word as 'well' (yoku dekita = well done), and yoku wakaranai means 'I'm not really sure'. yoku nai (not good) and yokatta (that's good) come from ii, not from this 'often'.

items.use: The middle of the frequency scale, for things that happen now and then.

examplePolite.ja: 時々歩いて帰ります。

items.use: The low end of the scale, one step below tokidoki. Very common in casual talk about habits and treats.

example.english: I walk home once in a while.

examplePolite.ja: たまに歩いて帰ります。
examplePolite.english: I walk home once in a while.

items.freqNote: たまに #724
items.notes: tama ni wa means 'for a change, every once in a while' (tama ni wa ii ne = nice for a change; tama ni wa renraku shite = get in touch once in a while).

items.use: Says the same thing happened again and again, usually in past tense (nando mo mita = I've seen it loads of times), often with a note of frustration.

example.english: I've told you so many times!

examplePolite.romaji: nando mo itta ja nai desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: 何度も言ったじゃないですか。
examplePolite.english: I've told you so many times!

items.notes: nankai mo means the same and is just as common in casual chat (nankai mo itta jan). ichido mo + negative means 'not even once'. Don't mishear nandemo (anything): nandemo ii = anything's fine.

blocks.label: Times of day
blocks.rationale: The parts of the day that routines and plans hang on, plus kesa and konban for this morning and tonight.
blocks.interference: kesa and konban always mean this morning and tonight. Bare asa and yoru just name the part of the day, and context picks which day: yoru denwa suru ne said at lunch means tonight, and asa denwa suru ne said at night means tomorrow morning. konban wa hima? starts exactly like the greeting konbanwa. If more words follow, it means tonight.

items.use: The morning as a part of the day, for routines (asa hayaku, asagohan) and spans like asa kara (since the morning).

example.english: I'll call you in the morning.

examplePolite.ja: 朝電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you in the morning.

items.notes: For 'this morning' say kesa or kyou no asa.

items.use: Midday and the daytime as opposed to yoru, mostly in set phrases: hiru made (till noon), hiru kara (from noon), hirusugi (just after noon), hirugohan (lunch). Casually, bare hiru also means lunch (hiru nani taberu?).

examplePolite.ja: 昼まで寝てました。

items.notes: For 'at lunchtime' say ohiru ni (ohiru ni denwa suru ne). ohiru on its own also means lunch, and hiruma means the daytime hours. For the afternoon say gogo (午後, #1394): gogo wa hima?

items.use: Evening and night, for plans and routines. kyou no yoru is a common casual way to say tonight.

examplePolite.ja: 夜電話しますね。

items.notes: ban (晩, #4729) is a near-synonym that lives in set words: konban, konbanwa, bangohan (dinner), maiban (every night). For late afternoon to dusk say yuugata (夕方, #2124); yoru starts once it is dark.

items.use: One word for kyou no asa. It often looks back at earlier this morning with past tense (kesa nani tabeta?), but while it is still morning non-past is fine too: kesa wa samui ne.

example.english: It was cold this morning, huh.

examplePolite.ja: 今朝は寒かったですね。
examplePolite.english: It was cold this morning, wasn't it?

items.notes: An irregular word (not kon-asa). Like kyou, it takes no ni. kyou no asa means the same and is always safe.

items.use: Tonight, for evening plans and invitations. It has the same kon- ('this') as konshuu and kongetsu.

example.english: Want to go for a drink tonight?

examplePolite.ja: 今晩飲みに行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to go for a drink tonight?

items.freqNote: 今晩(こんばん) #3984; same-meaning 今夜(こんや) #770
items.notes: konya (今夜) means the same and is more frequent in dramas, so recognise it. Among friends, plain kyou often covers tonight: kyou nomi ni ikanai? For last night say yuube (ゆうべ, #2525) or kinou no yoru.

blocks.label: Last, this, next week
blocks.rationale: kinou, kyou and ashita stretched to weeks: sen- is last, kon- is this, rai- is next. Plus the weekend that everyone asks about.
blocks.interference: senshuu, konshuu and raishuu differ only in the first syllable. sen- goes with past tense like kinou, and rai- with plans like ashita. Like kinou and ashita, all three take no ni: raishuu iku, not raishuu ni iku. shuumatsu is the weekend, and the tense tells you which one; it can take ni or go without.

items.use: Last week, for recaps. Like kinou, it pairs with past tense, and the same sen- gives sengetsu.

examplePolite.ja: 先週は忙しかったです。

items.freqNote: 先週(せんしゅう) #2652

items.use: This week. It works like kyou, taking past or non-past tense, and the same kon- gives kongetsu and konban.

example.romaji: konshuu wa chotto isogashii n da.
example.ja: 今週はちょっと忙しいんだ。
example.english: I'm kind of busy this week.

examplePolite.romaji: konshuu wa chotto isogashii n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 今週はちょっと忙しいんです。
examplePolite.english: I'm a bit busy this week.

items.freqNote: 今週(こんしゅう) #2825

items.use: Next week, a scheduling staple. Like ashita, it pairs with non-past tense, and the same rai- gives raigetsu and rainen.

examplePolite.ja: 来週は忙しいですか？

items.freqNote: 来週(らいしゅう) #1291

items.use: The weekend, mostly in small-talk questions. Non-past (nani suru?) asks about the coming weekend, past (nani shita?) about the one just gone, and -teru about habit: shuumatsu wa nani shiteru no? (what do you usually do at weekends?).

example.english: What are you doing this weekend?

examplePolite.ja: 週末は何しますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you doing this weekend?

items.freqNote: 週末(しゅうまつ) #3278
items.notes: To pin down which weekend, say konshuumatsu (今週末) or raishuumatsu (来週末), one word each. konshuu no shuumatsu also works.

blocks.label: Like & dislike
blocks.rationale: The ways to say how you feel about a thing, from love and like through 'not my thing' to dislike and can't stand; all take the X ga ___ frame.
blocks.interference: kirai is a settled dislike of a thing or person; iya is a gut rejection, 'I don't want this / this is unpleasant', usually about what is happening now. Drill 'ame no hi, kirai' (rainy days in general) against 'mata ame? iya da naa' (the rain today). iya also sounds like the interjection iya ('no / well', G): the interjection is soft and opens a reply (iya, chigau yo), while the adjective is emphatic and stands alone or ends the sentence (iya!, iya da, iya na yokan). daisuki is just a stronger suki (dai- = big) on the same rainy-days sentence, so add it once suki is solid. nigate is the soft kirai on that same sentence (ame no hi, nigate = rainy days aren't my thing) and the safe choice about food or people, so add it after kirai. It also means 'bad at' about yourself (eigo ga nigate); its opposite is tokui (my strong point), while jouzu (good at, later block) is praise for someone else.

items.use: Says you like something or someone (X ga suki); suki na X means 'the X I like, my favourite X'.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga suki desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が好きです

items.notes: Ends in -i but is a na-adjective: suki ja nai, suki datta (never sukikunai). About a person, suki usually means romantic interest, and 'suki desu' to someone's face is a confession; for friendly liking say ii hito da ne or yasashii ne.

items.use: Says you dislike something or someone (X ga kirai); it sounds strong about people, so polite speech often softens it to amari suki ja nai.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga kirai desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が嫌いです

items.notes: A na-adjective despite ending in -ai: kirai ja nai, kirai datta.

items.use: A gut rejection of a situation or action, 'I don't want this / this is unpleasant' ('iya!', iya da, iku no iya da = I don't want to go); more immediate and emotional than kirai. iya na X = unpleasant X (iya na yokan = a bad feeling).

example.english: Rain again? Ugh, I hate this.

examplePolite.romaji: mata ame desu ne. iya desu ne
examplePolite.ja: また雨ですね。嫌ですね

items.freqNote: 嫌 #304; いや #54 is mostly the interjection 'no / well' (G); casual contraction やだ #777
items.notes: Casually iya da is usually yada: mou yada (I've had enough), yada yo (no way). Polite iya desu in reply to a request is a blunt, childish-sounding refusal; refuse with chotto... or kekkou desu instead. About things like the weather, iya desu ne is fine small talk.

items.use: A stronger suki for food, hobbies and places, in the same X ga ___ frame; like suki it is a na-adjective (daisuki ja nai, daisuki datta). About family, kids or pets it is warm, but daisuki (desu) said to one person's face means 'I love you'.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga daisuki desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が大好きです

items.freqNote: 大好き #579
items.notes: dai- works on kirai too: daikirai = really hate.

items.use: Says something isn't your thing: a food, a type of person, or a task you're weak at (X ga nigate). It is softer and safer than kirai, and it is the modest way to say you're bad at something (eigo ga nigate).

example.english: Rainy days aren't really my thing.

examplePolite.romaji: ame no hi ga nigate desu
examplePolite.ja: 雨の日が苦手です
examplePolite.english: Rainy days aren't really my thing.

items.notes: The opposite is tokui (my strong point). heta (bad at) is fine about yourself but blunt about other people, and nigate also hints you don't enjoy it. Don't mix it up with nigai (bitter): koohii, nigate = I'm not into coffee; koohii, nigai = the coffee's bitter.

blocks.label: Also / only
blocks.rationale: Particles that widen (mo) or fence off (dake, shika, bakkari) whatever comes before them.
blocks.interference: dake, shika and bakkari all mean 'only'. dake is neutral with any verb, shika needs a negative and sounds like 'and that's all', and bakkari complains that it is too much or too often.

items.use: Takes the place of wa, ga or o to mean 'too / also'. After a number it stresses 'as many as' (mittsu mo tabeta).

examplePolite.ja: 私も行きたいです

items.notes: mo replaces wa, ga and o (watashi mo, never watashi wa mo) but follows other particles (nihon ni mo, tomodachi to mo). A mo B mo = both A and B; with a negative, neither. In casual speech men usually say ore mo or boku mo.

items.use: Means 'only / just' after a noun, number or clause (sore dake, chotto dake). Any verb can follow, positive or negative.

example.romaji: kyou wa geemu dake shite owatta
example.ja: 今日はゲームだけして終わった
example.english: Today was just games, and that was it.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa geemu dake shite owarimashita
examplePolite.ja: 今日はゲームだけして終わりました
examplePolite.english: Today was just games, and that was it.

items.notes: 'Kore dake?' (just this?) and 'chotto dake' (just a little) are everyday chunks.

items.use: Means 'nothing but / only' and must be followed by a negative verb. It sounds emphatic or regretful: 'and that's all'.

example.ja: 今日ゲームしかしなかった
example.english: All I did today was play games.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa geemu shika shimasen deshita
examplePolite.ja: 今日はゲームしかしませんでした
examplePolite.english: All I did today was play games.

items.notes: Trap: shika with a positive verb is wrong. Say hitotsu shika nai, never hitotsu shika aru.

items.use: Means 'nothing but', with a sense of too much or too often. It is the complaining 'only' (geemu bakkari).

example.ja: 今日ゲームばっかりしてた
example.english: I did nothing but game all day.

examplePolite.ja: 今日はゲームばかりしてました
examplePolite.english: I spent all day just playing games.

items.freqNote: ばっかり #511; neutral/polite ばかり #448, clipped ばっか #1180
items.notes: It carries judgement, so use dake for a neutral 'only'. bakka is the clipped casual form you'll hear constantly (geemu bakka shiteru). -te bakari and -ta bakari belong to I.

blocks.label: Eat, drink, sleep
blocks.rationale: The body's daily round — eating, drinking, going to bed, getting up, being tired — which comes up in nearly every how's-your-day exchange.
blocks.interference: neru is going to bed, nemuru is actually falling asleep (nerenakatta / nemurenakatta = couldn't sleep); medicine is nomu, never taberu; tsukareta, a past form, is 'I'm tired' now.

items.use: Eating anything and suggesting meals (nani taberu?), and it is the model ichidan verb for pattern drills.

examplePolite.ja: もうご飯を食べましたか？

items.freqNote: 食べる #130

items.use: Drinking anything, taking medicine (kusuri o nomu) and going out drinking (nomi ni iku).

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa nani o nomimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 今日は何を飲みますか？
examplePolite.english: What are you having to drink today?

items.notes: Medicine is nomu, never taberu.

items.use: Going to bed and sleeping (nanji ni neta?), and also lying down.

example.english: What time did you go to bed last night?

examplePolite.ja: 昨日何時に寝ましたか？
examplePolite.english: What time did you go to bed last night?

items.notes: neteru = is asleep; neta = went to bed.

items.use: Waking up or getting up (nanji ni okita?), and also events happening (nani ga okita?).

example.english: What time did you get up this morning?

examplePolite.ja: 今朝何時に起きましたか？
examplePolite.english: What time did you get up this morning?

items.freqNote: 起きる #329
items.notes: okiteru? = 'are you awake?'

items.use: Getting tired, where the past tsukareta is the normal way to say 'I'm tired' right now.

example.ja: 今日はほんとに疲れた。

examplePolite.ja: 今日は本当に疲れました。

items.freqNote: 疲れる #714; 疲れた #1640 also listed as its own entry
items.notes: Present tsukareru says something is tiring (kono shigoto tsukareru = this job wears you out); 'I'm tired' right now is tsukareta, a lasting state is tsukareteru.

blocks.label: Want & need
blocks.rationale: What you want, what you need and what matters, all said with X ga ___.
blocks.interference: hoshii (want) and hitsuyou (need) share the same sentence, so only the word changes (casual hitsuyou adds da na). Remember hoshii is an adjective, not a verb (X ga hoshii, never X o hoshii).

items.use: Says you want a thing (X ga hoshii); it is an adjective, and for wanting to do something use -tai, for wanting someone else to do it -te hoshii.

example.ja: 新しいパソコンがほしい

examplePolite.ja: 新しいパソコンがほしいです

items.freqNote: ほしい #195 (欲しい #420); includes the -te hoshii auxiliary
alsoIn: vocab-trainer core-vocab: Intensifiers (in example of motto)
items.notes: Only for your own wants. Asking a superior 'X ga hoshii desu ka?' sounds too direct. To ask for something in a shop, say X o kudasai or X onegaishimasu, not X ga hoshii desu.

items.use: Says something is needed (X ga hitsuyou) or not needed (hitsuyou nai), for documents, money, time, skills and steps.

example.romaji: atarashii pasokon ga hitsuyou da na
example.ja: 新しいパソコンが必要だな
example.english: I'm going to need a new computer.

examplePolite.ja: 新しいパソコンが必要です

items.freqNote: 必要 #271; casual verb 要る (iru, need) #2729
items.notes: Casual 'need' is usually the verb iru (要る): kore iru? / iranai (no need). It sounds like iru (be there), but the negatives differ: iranai = don't need, inai = isn't here.

items.use: Says something or someone is important or precious (daiji na hanashi = an important matter), and odaiji ni means 'take care' to someone who is ill.

example.romaji: kazoku ga ichiban daiji da yo

examplePolite.romaji: kazoku ga ichiban daiji desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 家族が一番大事ですね

items.freqNote: 大事 #262; synonym 大切 (taisetsu) #578
