items.notes: taisetsu is a synonym that sounds warmer and a little more formal; daiji is the everyday spoken choice.

blocks.label: Hot, cold, ouch, look out
blocks.rationale: How the weather and your body feel, and when something is dangerous: hot, cold, it hurts and watch out. These are the daily small-talk openers and the reports and warnings you have to make on the spot.
blocks.interference: atsui and samui are opposites with the same shape (three beats ending -ui) on the same sentence (kyou, ___ ne), so learn atsui first; per 11-list-adjectives note 9(a), keep samui at least 10 items after atsui in drill order even though they share a block. atsui covers hot air and hot things, but samui is only for the air and how you feel: a cold drink is tsumetai. itai (it hurts) sounds almost the same as iru + -tai (want to stay): atama ga itai vs zutto koko ni itai, and the words before it tell you which. abunai is the warning about the situation, while kowai (scared, later block) is the feeling: shout abunai! to stop someone. abunai ends in -nai but is not a negative (not dangerous = abunakunai), so per 11-list-adjectives #42 add it only once the -kunai negative is solid. As reflex shouts all four clip to the stem: atsu!, samu!, ita!, abuna!

items.use: Says it's hot, about the weather and air (kyou atsui ne) or about food, drinks and things you touch; the top small-talk opener in summer. Written 暑い for weather and 熱い for things, but it is one word by ear.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は暑いですね

items.freqNote: 熱い #1030 (hot to the touch / passionate); 暑い #1990 (weather). Same sound for both.
items.notes: Touching something hot, people clip it to atsu!; atsui 'thick' differs only in pitch.

items.use: Says it's cold, about the weather and how you feel (samui! = I'm cold); not for cold drinks or objects, which are tsumetai.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は寒いですね

items.notes: Often clipped to samu!; the drawled samii! is rough, mostly male speech. samui also means a joke fell flat.

items.use: Reports pain (atama ga itai = my head hurts; doko ga itai? = where does it hurt?) and is the reflex 'ouch!'; figuratively, sore wa itai = that hurts, that's a blow.

example.english: I've got a bit of a headache.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと頭が痛いです
examplePolite.english: I've got a bit of a headache.

items.notes: As a reflex it is clipped to ita! or stretched to ittaa!; itee! / ite! are rough and masculine. About a person or behaviour (ano hito, itai) it is slang for 'cringey'.

items.use: Warns of danger on the spot (abunai! = watch out!) and calls anything risky, from a road to a plan. It also says something is at risk (jikan, abunai = we might not make it; tesuto, abunai = I might fail). After a near miss, abunakatta = that was close.

example.romaji: soko, abunai yo! ki o tsukete
example.ja: そこ、危ないよ！気をつけて

examplePolite.romaji: soko, abunai desu yo. ki o tsukete kudasai
examplePolite.ja: そこ、危ないですよ。気をつけてください
examplePolite.english: It's dangerous there. Please be careful.

items.freqNote: 危ない #513
items.notes: As a shout, abunai! is fine to anyone, strangers included, with no desu; abunee! is the rough, mostly male version. 'Not dangerous' is abunakunai.

blocks.label: Want, can, have done
blocks.rationale: The frames for talking about yourself: what you want to do, what you want others to do, what you can do, and what you've done.
blocks.interference: issho ni ikitai (I want to go) vs issho ni itte hoshii (I want you to go): the -te form hands the action to the other person. -ta koto ga aru needs the past; iku koto ga aru means 'sometimes'.

items.use: Attaches to the verb stem for what you want to do (ikitai, tabetai) and conjugates like an i-adjective (ikitakunai, ikitakatta).

example.english: I want to go with you.

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to go with you.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer folds たい into the verb (standalone たい #5172 badly undercounts)
items.notes: For someone else's wants, quote them (ikitai tte) instead of stating them. Don't offer with -tai desu ka? (nomitai desu ka? sounds nosy); use -masen ka? or ikaga desu ka? instead. The object can take ga: mizu ga nomitai.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to say you want someone else to do something (kite hoshii, yamete hoshii), with the doer marked by ni.

example.english: I want you to come with me.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni itte hoshii n desu kedo...
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行ってほしいんですけど…
examplePolite.english: I was hoping you'd come with me...

items.freqNote: rank of kana ほしい; also counts plain 'want (a thing)'
items.notes: Said straight at someone it presses: soften with n da kedo (casual) or n desu kedo (polite), and to ask a stranger or senior use -te moraemasu ka? instead.

items.use: Turns a verb into 'can': godan verbs change -u to -eru (iku -> ikeru), ichidan verbs swap -ru for -rareru (taberu -> taberareru), suru becomes dekiru; the object often takes ga (nihongo ga hanaseru).

example.ja: 明日のパーティー行ける？
example.english: Can you make it to the party tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no paatii ni ikemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日のパーティーに行けますか？
examplePolite.english: Can you make it to the party tomorrow?

items.freqNote: tokenizer keeps potentials as their own verbs: 言える #291, 行ける #985, 話せる #1219; suppletive できる #73
items.notes: Casual speech drops ra in short verbs: mireru, koreru (ra-nuki); polite speech keeps -rareru. wakaru has no potential (wakareru = break up). mieru / kikoeru = it's visible / audible, vs mirareru / kikeru = get to see / listen.

items.use: Attaches to the past form to ask about or state experience (itta koto aru?, mita koto nai); casual speech drops ga.

example.english: Have you ever been to Okinawa?

examplePolite.romaji: okinawa ni itta koto ga arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 沖縄に行ったことがありますか？
examplePolite.english: Have you ever been to Okinawa?

items.freqNote: rank of fused ことがある; also counts the 'sometimes' use (iku koto ga aru)
items.notes: With the plain present (iku koto ga aru) it means 'sometimes', not experience.

blocks.label: Or / for example
blocks.rationale: Offering choices and examples instead of one definite thing.
blocks.interference: -toka lists things and can trail anything, -tari ... -tari lists actions and closes with suru; both use the same 'eiga' sentence. -tari is not -tara ('if').

items.use: A ka B offers a choice between nouns or clauses; B can take a second ka. Clause + ka dou ka = 'whether or not' ('kuru ka dou ka wakannai').

example.english: Are you free tomorrow or the day after?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ka asatte, jikan arimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日か明後日、時間ありますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you have time tomorrow or the day after?

items.freqNote: か #11, also counts the question particle; sentence-initial それとも #892
items.notes: To offer the second option as its own question, use soretomo ('kotchi? soretomo atchi?').

items.use: Names examples without a full list ('A toka B toka'), or hedges one item so it sounds less blunt ('eiga toka'). '...toka itteta' = 'said something like'.

example.english: I'd like to see a movie or something.

examplePolite.ja: 映画とか見たいですね。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to see a movie or something.

items.freqNote: とか #70
items.notes: In careful speech nado replaces a listing toka ('eiga nado'); the hedging toka can sound vague or young there.

items.use: Introduces an example or a hypothetical; also buys a second to think.

example.english: How about this one, for example?

examplePolite.romaji: tatoeba, kore wa dou desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 例えば、これはどうですか？
examplePolite.english: How about this one, for example?

items.freqNote: 例えば #790

items.use: Lists sample actions without claiming the list is complete; built on the -ta form and closed with suru ('mitari, kaimono shitari suru'). A single -tari softens an invitation or plan ('gohan tabetari shinai?'); casually the closing suru is sometimes dropped.

example.ja: 映画見たり、買い物したりしたい。
example.english: I want to see a movie, go shopping, that kind of thing.

examplePolite.romaji: eiga o mitari, kaimono o shitari shitai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 映画を見たり、買い物をしたりしたいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like to see a movie, do some shopping, things like that.

items.freqNote: たり #2470; tokenizer often fuses it into the verb
items.notes: The last -tari normally takes suru (shita, shitai, shiteru); one -tari alone is common too ('eiga mitari shitai'). Verbs whose -ta is -da give -dari (nondari, asondari). Don't mix it up with -tara.

blocks.label: Give, get, lend, help
blocks.rationale: The giving triad, where direction picks the verb: away from me (ageru), toward me (kureru), I receive (morau) — plus lending (kasu) and helping (tetsudau), the favours that ride on it.
blocks.interference: ageru and kureru both translate 'give' but point opposite ways — anything coming to me or my side is kureru; morau makes the receiver the subject and marks the giver with ni; kashite means 'lend me' (the other person lends), while borrowing from your side is kariru (karite ii?); tetsudau is help with a task, the cry for help is tasukete.

items.use: Giving from me or my side to someone else (X ni ageru), and kore ageru means 'here, you can have this'.

example.english: I'm giving this to a friend.

examplePolite.ja: これは友達にあげます。
examplePolite.english: I'm giving this to a friend.

items.freqNote: あげる #668 (kana); 上げる (raise) #837 separately; includes -te ageru
items.notes: Offering to a superior with ageru can sound condescending.

items.use: Someone giving to me or my in-group, with the giver marked by ga and the recipient (me) usually left unsaid.

examplePolite.ja: これは友達がくれました。

items.freqNote: くれる #565; includes -te kureru
items.notes: Things given to you are never ageta: tomodachi ga kureta.

items.use: Receiving something, with me as the subject and the giver marked by ni or kara (X ni moratta).

example.english: I got this from a friend.

examplePolite.ja: これは友達にもらいました。
examplePolite.english: I got this from a friend.

items.freqNote: もらう #313; 貰う #11381; includes -te morau
items.notes: moratta and kureta describe the same event from two angles.

items.use: Helps someone with a task, with the person or the task marked by o; later forms build on it: nanka tetsudaou ka? offers help and tetsudatte kureru? asks for it.

example.ja: 明日の引っ越し、手伝うよ。

examplePolite.ja: 明日の引っ越し、手伝いますよ。

items.freqNote: 手伝う #508
items.notes: tasukete! is the cry for help; tetsudatte is for a hand with a task.

items.use: Lends something, with the borrower marked by ni; kashite (lend me) is the everyday way to ask to borrow or use a pen, a charger or a shop's bathroom.

example.english: Can I borrow a pen for a sec?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ペン貸してください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could I borrow a pen?

items.freqNote: 貸す #658; 借りる (borrow) #673
items.notes: kashite is learned here as a chunk; the -te request itself comes in F4. Borrowing is kariru (ichidan): karite ii? = can I borrow it?, karita = borrowed.

blocks.label: Favours, passive, causative
blocks.rationale: The giving/receiving triad that marks who benefits from an action, the everyday thanks built on kureru, the passive for things done to you (often unwanted), and the causative in its everyday jobs: -sasete for asking to do something yourself, and -sasete morau / -sasete kureru for being allowed to.
blocks.interference: Same act, three viewpoints: tomodachi ga oshiete kureta / tomodachi ni oshiete moratta / tomodachi ni oshiete ageta. Kureru points toward the speaker, ageru away, and morau takes the receiver's view with the giver on ni. The passive keeps that ni frame, often for something unwanted: tomodachi ni tetsudatte moratta (glad) vs tomodachi ni okorareta (not glad), so a favour takes -te morau, not the passive. The ichidan passive sounds like the I3 potential (taberareru = can eat / gets eaten), while godan keeps them apart (ieru / iwareru); casual potentials often drop the ra (tabereru), passives never do. When you thank someone for an act, keep the kureru: oshiete kurete arigatou, never oshiete arigatou or oshiete agete arigatou. The causative swaps the passive's -are-/-rare- for -ase-/-sase- on the same stem (iwareta = I was told, iwasete = let me say), and -asete/-sasete asks to do it yourself where plain -te asks the other person: kangaete (you think it over) vs kangaesasete (let me think it over). Godan verbs never take the extra sa: yasumasete, not yasumasasete.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form when someone does something for you or your side (oshiete kureta), and is the base of casual requests (-te kureru?).

examplePolite.ja: 友達が教えてくれました。

items.freqNote: rank of kana くれる, mostly the auxiliary use
items.notes: Leaving it off sounds cold: oshiete kureta thanks the person, oshieta only reports. As a request, -te kurenai? is softer than -te kureru?

items.use: Thanks someone for one specific thing they did for you. It goes on any verb's -te form (kite, tetsudatte, oshiete), and the kureru is what makes the act a favour to you.
items.politeJa: 〜てくれてありがとうございます

example.ja: 今日は来てくれてありがとう。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kite kurete arigatou gozaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は来てくれてありがとうございます。

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of kana くれる, the rarer part (ありがとう alone #128), so an upper bound
items.notes: Uses the same -te + feeling frame as okurete gomen (sorry I'm late) and kite yokatta (glad I came). Politely, once the act is over and you're parting, the past is usual: kite kurete arigatou gozaimashita.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for a favour seen from the receiver's side, with the doer marked by ni (tomodachi ni oshiete moratta); it also frames requests (-te moraeru?).

example.ja: 友達に教えてもらった。
example.english: I got a friend to tell me.

examplePolite.ja: 友達に教えてもらいました。
examplePolite.english: I got a friend to tell me.

items.freqNote: rank of kana もらう (main verb 'receive' and the auxiliary combined)
items.notes: moratta suggests you asked for it; kureta credits the giver's kindness. The doer takes ni with morau but ga with kureru.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for a favour done for another person, outward from the speaker (oshiete ageta, katte ageru).

examplePolite.ja: 友達に教えてあげました。

items.freqNote: rank of kana あげる (main verb 'give' and the auxiliary combined)
items.notes: Offered to someone's face (yatte ageru yo) it can sound condescending; avoid it toward superiors.

items.use: Puts you on the receiving end of what someone did, with the doer on ni. The everyday one is iwareta, reporting what someone told you (isha ni yasume tte iwareta); many others are unwelcome (okorareta, ame ni furareta). Godan verbs change -u to -areru (okoru -> okorareru; after a vowel, -u becomes -wareru: iu -> iwareru), ichidan verbs swap -ru for -rareru (taberu -> taberareru), and the irregulars are sareru and korareru.

example.english: A friend got mad at me yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日友達に怒られました。
examplePolite.english: A friend got mad at me yesterday.

items.freqNote: rank of the auxiliary られる, which also counts ichidan potential and honorific -rareru; れる #3142, される #22435; the tokenizer splits most passives off the verb (言われる, 怒られる not found as wholes), a few keep their own entry (呼ばれる #2851)
items.notes: It even works on verbs that take no object, for being put out (ame ni furareta = got caught in the rain), and keeps o for something of yours (saifu o torareta = got my wallet taken). Don't use it for English 'got broken' or 'was left open': Japanese uses the intransitive verb (keitai kowarechatta, mado ga aiteru), and kowasareta says someone broke it. The ichidan passive sounds the same as the full potential (taberareru), so context decides; casual speech often shortens the potential to tabereru, so a full -rareru in casual talk leans passive.

items.use: Asks to be allowed to do something yourself: to have a go (yarasete, let me try), to offer (harawasete, let me pay) or to stall (chotto kangaesasete, let me think). Godan verbs change -u to -asete (yaru -> yarasete; after a vowel, -u becomes -wasete: harau -> harawasete), ichidan verbs swap -ru for -sasete (kangaeru -> kangaesasete), and the irregulars are sasete and kosasete.
items.politeJa: 〜あせてください／〜させてください

examplePolite.ja: 今日は払わせてください。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; the tokenizer folds the causative into the verb (auxiliaries せる #16515, させる #31829); only lexicalised forms rank on their own (待たせる #851, やらせる #7775, 休ませる #27904; short -asu forms やらす #4504, 待たす #7648); 払わせる, 考えさせる, 言わせる not found
alsoIn: 05-acquisition-order contested calls, month 8 (causative productive only in -sasete kudasai / -sasete morau)
items.notes: The stalling set phrase is chotto kangaesasete (polite: sukoshi kangaesasete kudasai). Two more everyday frames to produce: with gomen it apologises for what you put someone through (matasete gomen, shinpai sasete gomen; polite matasete sumimasen), and with the favour verbs it reports permission (kyou wa hayaku kaerasete moratta, I got to go home early today; kaerasete kureta, they let me go home). Casual speech often shortens godan -asete to -ashite (yarashite, iwashite); recognise it, but produce -asete. Making someone do something in general (kodomo ni yasai o tabesaseru) is recognition-only for now.

blocks.label: Asking someone
blocks.rationale: Ways to get the listener to do something: asking for a thing, the bare -te and the softer favour forms, then the 'don't' form.
blocks.interference: -te is blunt; -te kureru? and -te moraeru? are plain asks, and the negatives -te kurenai? and -te moraenai? are softer still. onegai (polite kudasai) asks for a thing, and kudasai also makes -te polite. -naide is the 'don't' of -te.

items.use: The bare te-form is the everyday casual request to friends and family (matte, mite, kiite). Add chotto or ne to soften it.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待って

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってください

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (bare て #458 is mostly connective; ください #350)
alsoIn: vocab-trainer learner-phrases: mou ichido itte kudasai
items.notes: -te kudasai is polite but still direct; with strangers, -te moraemasu ka is safer.

items.use: A softer request for a favour, asked as a negative question. It is one step up from bare -te and fine with friends and family.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待ってくれない？
example.english: Sorry, could you wait a sec?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってくれませんか
examplePolite.english: Sorry, could you wait a moment?

items.freqNote: rank of くれる; くれない alone #78901 undercounts (tokenizer splits)
items.notes: The negative question makes it softer than -te kureru?, and it is not a refusal. Rising, it's a request; flat, it's a complaint: tetsudatte kurenai = they won't help me.

items.use: Asks for a favour framed as something you would receive. It is about as soft as -te kureru?, and its polite form -te moraemasu ka is the safe choice with clerks and strangers.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待ってもらえる？
example.english: Sorry, could you wait a bit?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってもらえますか
examplePolite.english: Sorry, would you mind waiting a moment?

items.freqNote: rank of もらえる (all uses)
items.notes: The negative is softer: -te moraenai? casually, and -te moraemasen ka, the softest of the set, politely.

items.use: Asks someone not to do something. It is built on the -nai form (wasurenai → wasurenaide) and often softened with ne.

examplePolite.ja: これを忘れないでくださいね

items.freqNote: rank of ないで (includes 'without doing')
items.notes: In the middle of a sentence, -naide means 'without doing' (nenaide benkyou shita).

blocks.label: Look and show
blocks.rationale: Seeing and letting someone see: look or watch, show, and look for.
blocks.interference: mite (look) and misete (show me) differ by one syllable and reverse who does the looking; 'look for' is sagasu, never a form of miru.

items.use: Looking at something, watching shows and checking messages (mita?), and mite! points something out.

examplePolite.ja: ちょっとこれを見てください。
examplePolite.english: Please take a look at this.

items.freqNote: 見る #55; includes auxiliary -te miru
items.notes: Seeing a person, as in meeting up, is au, not miru.

items.use: Showing something to someone (X ni miseru), and misete is the standard 'let me see' for photos, phones and shop items.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、それ見せてください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could I see that?

items.freqNote: 見せる #265; includes -te miseru

items.use: Searching for lost things, people, jobs or places, and X sagashiteru n desu kedo is the standard way to open in a shop.

example.english: I'm looking for my keys right now.

examplePolite.ja: 今鍵を探してます。
examplePolite.english: I'm looking for my keys right now.

items.freqNote: 探す #391; 捜す #708 counted separately
items.notes: Success is mitsuketa / mitsukatta (found it), not sagashita.

blocks.label: Knowing and learning
blocks.rationale: Verbs for what you know: understand, know, remember, forget, and study — the ones a learner uses about themselves in every exchange.
blocks.interference: wakaranai = I can't understand or work it out, shiranai = I have no information — but when you just can't answer a question (a stranger asks the way), wakarimasen / wakannai is the soft default and shirimasen sounds curt. 'Remember' is oboeteru, not shitteru; both live in the -teru form. oboeru is fixing a fact in memory and benkyou suru is putting in study time (tango oboeta / nihongo benkyou shiteru).

items.use: Understanding or being able to tell (wakaru?, wakaranai), with the thing understood marked by ga, and wakatta doubles as 'got it / OK'.

examplePolite.ja: この言葉は分かりますか？

items.freqNote: 分かる #213; kana わかる #1492 counted separately, so combined use is higher than either rank
items.notes: wakatteru = 'I know already', which can sound irritated.

items.use: Having a piece of information or knowing a person or place, where the positive is always shitteru and the negative always shiranai (never *shittenai).

examplePolite.ja: この言葉は知ってますか？

items.freqNote: 知る #74 (all inflections; 知ってる not found as a unit); 知らない #669 as its own entry
items.notes: Polite shirimasen can sound like 'not my business'; wakarimasen is the safe polite 'I don't know'.

items.use: Getting something into memory (oboeru) and still having it (oboeteru / oboetenai), so 'do you remember?' is always oboeteru?

example.ja: あの人の名前覚えてる？
example.english: Do you remember that person's name?

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito no namae o oboetemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あの人の名前を覚えてますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you remember that person's name?

items.freqNote: 覚える #255
items.notes: Bare oboeru means 'memorise'; remembering now is oboeteru, and 'oh, now I remember!' is omoidashita, not oboeta.

items.use: Forgetting names, facts and plans and leaving things behind, mostly as wasureta / wasurechatta, plus the reminder wasurenaide ne (don't forget) and a, wasureteta (oh, I'd forgotten).

examplePolite.romaji: ano hito no namae o wasuremashita.
examplePolite.ja: あの人の名前を忘れました。

items.freqNote: 忘れる #201
items.notes: Leaving an item behind is also wasureru: kasa wasureta.

items.use: Says you study something, with o often dropped in casual speech (nihongo benkyou shiteru); benkyou ni naru (that's good to know) is the stock reply to an explanation.

example.ja: 日本語勉強してるんだ。

examplePolite.romaji: nihongo o benkyou shiteru n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 日本語を勉強してるんです。

items.freqNote: 勉強する is not a separate entry; rank of 勉強 #729
items.notes: benkyou ni narimashita thanks someone for teaching you something.

blocks.label: Got it / say again
blocks.rationale: Saying whether you understood, and asking for a repeat when you didn't.
blocks.interference: wakatta and wakannai differ only in the ending (-tta past vs -nnai negative). nante? asks for the words again, while mou ikkai asks for a full replay.

items.use: Says you've understood, or agrees to a request or plan: the casual 'okay, will do'.

examplePolite.ja: 分かりました、後でやります。

items.freqNote: the tokenizer reduces 分かった to its dictionary form; rank of 分かる #213
items.notes: As a question, 'wakatta?' checks that the other person understood.

items.use: Says you don't understand or don't know, so the other person rephrases or moves on.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと分かんない。
example.english: Sorry, I don't really get it.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと分かりません。

items.freqNote: 分かんない #1567; other forms are folded into 分かる #213
items.notes: For 'I don't know' about a fact, wakannai (polite wakarimasen) is the safer choice; shiranai (shirimasen), said flatly, can sound cold, like 'no idea, not my problem'. shiranai also means you've never heard of it.

items.use: Asks someone to repeat what they just said when you missed the words.

example.english: Sorry, what did you just say?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、今何て言いました？
examplePolite.english: Sorry, what did you just say?

items.freqNote: 何て #834; なんて #84 also counts the 'such as' particle use
items.notes: A bare nante? can sound curt; 'e, nante?' is softer.

items.use: Asks for a replay of what was said, or proposes doing something again.

example.ja: ごめん、もう一回お願い。

examplePolite.ja: すみません、もう一度お願いします。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you say that once more?

items.freqNote: もう一回 #1841; もう一度 #567
items.notes: Polite speech prefers mou ichido to mou ikkai.

blocks.label: Surprise
blocks.rationale: Quick reactions to the unexpected, from puzzlement to disbelief, plus bikkuri shita to say something surprised you.
blocks.interference: e? reacts to something you just heard, while are? reacts to something you notice. honto? asks whether it's true, while uso! exclaims that it can't be. bikkuri shita says it surprised you (or made you jump), so you can also use it later when you tell someone about it.

items.use: Instant surprise at what you just heard, or a quick 'sorry, what?' when you missed it.

examplePolite.romaji: e? kekkon suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: えっ？結婚するんですか？

items.freqNote: えっ #83; bare え #137
items.notes: A flat, long ee (ええ, #131) is a polite 'yes'; a rising, drawn-out ee?! is stronger surprise than e?. To a superior, say 'sumimasen, mou ichido...' rather than a bare e? to ask for a repeat.

items.use: Asks 'is that true?' about good news, bad news or anything doubtful. Said flat, honto also agrees: 'it really is'.

examplePolite.romaji: hontou desu ka? kekkon suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 本当ですか？結婚するんですか？

items.freqNote: 本当 #199 counts every use; the casual spelling ほんと is #1785
items.notes: honto ni (B) is the adverb 'really, truly'.

items.use: Exclaims disbelief at surprising news. It literally means 'a lie' but accuses nobody, though it's too blunt to say to a superior.

examplePolite.romaji: e, hontou desu ka? kekkon suru n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、本当ですか？結婚するんですか？

items.freqNote: split across spellings: ウソ #1168, 嘘 #1544, うそ #2305
items.notes: 'uso desho!' is the stronger 'you've got to be kidding'. No polite form: in polite speech say 'e, hontou desu ka?'

items.use: Puzzlement when you notice something is off, missing, or not what you expected.

examplePolite.romaji: are? kagi ga nai n desu kedo...
examplePolite.ja: あれ？鍵がないんですけど…
examplePolite.english: Huh? I can't find my key...

items.freqNote: あれ #98 also counts the pronoun 'that' (J); the clipped あれっ is #18307
items.notes: This isn't the pronoun are 'that thing' (J): here it stands alone, with a rising pitch.

items.english: that surprised me; you startled me
items.use: The everyday way to say something surprised you, whether it's news you heard or someone making you jump. It works in the moment and also when you tell the story later.

example.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, bikkuri shita yo.
example.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、びっくりしたよ。
example.english: I was surprised to hear you're getting married.

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon suru tte kiite, bikkuri shimashita yo.
examplePolite.ja: 結婚するって聞いて、びっくりしましたよ。
examplePolite.english: I was surprised to hear you're getting married.

items.freqNote: びっくりした #1488; びっくり #1350
items.notes: Like yokatta, it stays past even in the moment. After a jump scare you say aa, bikkuri shita! (you scared me!). The non-past bikkuri suru looks ahead: bikkuri suru yo (you'll be surprised). Mark what surprised you with ni: sono nyuusu ni bikkuri shita.

blocks.label: Showing interest
blocks.rationale: Backchannel reactions that show you're following and taking in what's said.
blocks.interference: hee is 'oh, interesting', aa is 'oh, right', naruhodo is 'that explains it', and tashika ni is 'fair point'. Only tashika ni says you've been persuaded.

items.use: Marks realisation or recognition ('aa, sore ka'). Before naruhodo or sokka it shows the penny has dropped.

examplePolite.ja: ああ、あの店ですね。

items.freqNote: ああ #63
items.notes: A bare aa meaning 'yeah' sounds masculine. aa 'like that' is a different word (J).

items.use: Shows interested surprise at something new; draw it out ('heee') for more surprise.

example.ja: へえ、それは知らなかった。

examplePolite.romaji: hee, sou na n desu ka. shirimasen deshita.
examplePolite.ja: へえ、そうなんですか。知りませんでした。
examplePolite.english: Oh, is that so? I didn't know that.

items.notes: On its own it can sound flippant to a superior; follow it with sou na n desu ka.

items.use: Shows that an explanation has clicked and makes sense to you.

example.ja: なるほど、そういうことか。
example.english: Ah, so that's what it is.

examplePolite.romaji: naruhodo, sou iu koto desu ka.
examplePolite.ja: なるほど、そういうことですか。
examplePolite.english: I see, so that's what it is.

items.freqNote: なるほど #379
items.notes: To a superior it can sound like you're judging them; sou na n desu ne is safer.

items.use: Concedes the other person's point, often before you add your own view ('tashika ni... demo').

example.ja: 確かに、ちょっと高いね。
example.english: True, it is a bit pricey.

examplePolite.romaji: tashika ni, chotto takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 確かに、ちょっと高いですね。
examplePolite.english: That's true, it is a bit expensive.

items.freqNote: 確かに #230
items.notes: tashika on its own means 'if I remember right', which is a different use.

blocks.label: Replies with sou
blocks.rationale: Five fixed replies built on sou. The ending decides whether you confirm, agree, take in news or doubt.
blocks.interference: sou confirms a fact, sou da ne agrees with an opinion, sokka and sou na n da take in news (sou na n da sounds more interested), and sou kana doubts. Drill all five after the same lead-in.

items.use: Confirms that what the other person said is right, usually about you or something you know ('so you're from Osaka?' 'sou').

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu, takai n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そうです、高いんですよ。

items.freqNote: そう #31, counting every use including 'that way' (J)
items.notes: Doubled 'sou sou!' is eager agreement; a rising sou? means 'really? you think so?'. sou meaning 'that way' is in J.

items.use: Agrees with an opinion or feeling you share. Drawn out ('sou da nee...', polite 'sou desu nee...'), it buys thinking time before you answer.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ne, takai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうですね、高いですね。
examplePolite.english: Yes, it is pricey, isn't it.

items.freqNote: そうだね #850; polite そうですね #539
items.notes: To confirm a fact about yourself, say sou desu, not sou desu ne.

items.use: Takes in new information or an explanation: 'oh, I see', sometimes with a hint of 'oh well'.

example.english: Oh, I see, so it's expensive.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ka, takai n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうですか、高いんですね。

items.freqNote: そっか #482; そうか only reaches #149930 because the tokenizer usually splits it (そう+か)
items.notes: Say it with a falling pitch. A rising sou desu ka? sounds doubtful, and bare sou ka sounds pensive or masculine.

items.use: Reacts to news with interest ('oh, really?') and invites the other person to say more.

example.romaji: sou na n da, takai n da ne.
example.ja: そうなんだ、高いんだね。

examplePolite.romaji: sou na n desu ka, takai n desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: そうなんですか、高いんですね。
examplePolite.english: Oh, is that so? So it's expensive.

items.freqNote: rank of the polite そうなんですか #1181; the casual そうなんだ is split by the tokenizer
items.notes: The safest default reaction when someone tells you something about themselves. With yo, 'sou na n da yo' confirms your own news: 'yeah, it is'.

items.use: Softly doubts what the other person just said without contradicting them; said slowly to yourself, it means 'I wonder'.

example.romaji: sou kana, sonna ni takakunai yo.
example.ja: そうかな、そんなに高くないよ。
example.english: You think? It's not that expensive.

examplePolite.romaji: sou desu ka ne, sonna ni takakunai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そうですかね、そんなに高くないですよ。
examplePolite.english: You think so? It's not that expensive.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer splits そうかな, and polite そうですかね / そうでしょうか are not found; component かな #90)
items.notes: In polite replies, sou deshou ka is the firmer, more formal objection; sou desu ka ne (drawn out: 'sou desu ka nee...') is the gentle one.

blocks.label: Talking about talk
blocks.rationale: Words for handling what's said: quoting it, raising a related topic, naming the subject, summing it up.
blocks.interference: sou ieba jumps to something new, tsumari restates what was just said; -tte reports someone's words, -ni tsuite names the topic.

items.use: Spoken quote marker after anything said, thought, heard or asked, followed by iu, omou, kiku and the like ('kuru tte itta'). Works the same in desu/masu speech; to is the written/formal quote marker. Sentence-final, it reports hearsay: 'ashita ame da tte' = 'I hear it'll rain'.

examplePolite.ja: 来るって言ってましたよ。

items.freqNote: って #18, also counts topic tte and hearsay tte
items.notes: After n it shrinks to te: 'nan te itta?' (nan + tte) = 'what did he say?'

items.english: oh yeah; come to think of it
items.use: Brings up something that just came to mind, linked to the conversation or not; the natural way to switch topics mid-chat.

example.english: Oh yeah, are you off tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: sou ieba, ashita wa yasumi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: そういえば、明日は休みですか？
examplePolite.english: By the way, are you off tomorrow?

items.freqNote: そういえば #607 (+ そう言えば #8072)
items.notes: For a deliberate change of subject with no reminder, tokorode ('by the way').

items.use: Attaches to a noun to name the topic of talking, thinking, asking or knowing ('nihon ni tsuite kiku'); small talk often uses no koto instead.

example.ja: それについて、なんか聞いてる？
example.english: Have you heard anything about that?

examplePolite.romaji: sore ni tsuite, nanika kiitemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それについて、何か聞いてますか？
examplePolite.english: Have you heard anything about that?

items.freqNote: について #426
items.notes: Before a noun it takes no: 'nihon ni tsuite no hon'.

items.use: Rephrases or sums up what was said; with '...tte koto?' it checks that you understood.

example.ja: つまり、来ないってこと？

examplePolite.romaji: tsumari, konai tte koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: つまり、来ないってことですか？
examplePolite.english: So you mean you're not coming?

items.freqNote: つまり #499

blocks.label: Say, talk, ask
blocks.rationale: Speech-act verbs: say, talk, ask or listen, tell, ask a favour.
blocks.interference: English 'ask' splits into kiku (a question) and tanomu (a favour), and 'tell' into iu (words), hanasu (talk about) and oshieru (give information).

items.use: Reporting words with tte or to (nante itta?), naming things (X tte iu), and sou iu / kou iu for 'that kind of'.

examplePolite.ja: 今なんて言いましたか？

items.freqNote: 言う #28; kana いう #167 counted separately; quotative って-forms split off by the tokenizer
items.notes: Pronounced yuu; itta / itte sound the same as iku's, but casual speech often says yutta / yutte, which keeps them apart.

items.use: Talking with someone (X to hanasu), telling about something, and speaking a language (nihongo hanaseru?).

example.english: I'll tell you about it later.

examplePolite.ja: 後で話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll tell you about it later.

items.notes: Quoting someone's exact words is iu, not hanasu.

items.use: Listening (kiite), hearing news (kiita?) and asking someone a question, with the person asked marked by ni.

examplePolite.ja: 友達に聞いてみました。

items.freqNote: 聞く #67; 聴く #1930 separately
items.notes: Bare tomodachi ni kiita usually means 'I heard it from a friend'; kiite mita makes it 'I asked'.

items.use: Giving someone information or know-how, where oshiete is the everyday 'tell me' for numbers, directions and tips.

examplePolite.ja: 電話番号を教えてください。
examplePolite.english: Could you give me your phone number?

items.freqNote: 教える #196
items.notes: Not just 'teach': michi oshiete = 'tell me the way'.

items.use: Asking someone to do something (X ni tanomu) and ordering food or a delivery (nani tanomu?).

example.english: I asked a friend to do it.

examplePolite.ja: 友達に頼みました。
examplePolite.english: I asked a friend to do it.

items.notes: A direct tanomu (yo)! = 'I'm counting on you' leans masculine; to ask a favour yourself say onegai / onegai shimasu — 'X, tanomimasu' is how a boss hands out a task.

blocks.label: Naming and framing
blocks.rationale: Three ways to talk about a whole idea: an activity you like or find hard (-no), a thing by its name (-tte iu), and a conclusion you want to deny (-wake ja nai).
blocks.interference: -no names the action (iku no ga suki) while wake ja nai denies a conclusion (iku wake ja nai); -tte iu labels a name and becomes to iu in careful speech.

items.use: After a plain verb, turns the action into a noun so you can say you like it, are good at it or find it hard (ryouri suru no ga suki, iku no wa muri).

examplePolite.romaji: ryouri suru no ga suki desu.
examplePolite.ja: 料理するのが好きです。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; の #1 is dominated by the possessive particle
items.notes: 'I like to cook' needs it: *ryouri suru ga suki is wrong. With shumi wa ... and dekiru, use koto instead: shumi wa ryouri suru koto, oyogu koto ga dekiru.

items.use: After a name or clause, labels it (sakura tte iu mise = a shop called Sakura) or asks what something is called (nante iu no?).

example.ja: さくらっていう店知ってる？
example.english: Do you know a place called Sakura?

examplePolite.romaji: sakura tte iu omise shittemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: さくらっていうお店知ってますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know a place called Sakura?

items.freqNote: rank of っていう across all uses (naming, quoting, tte iu ka); って言う #1659; careful-speech という #104, also all uses
items.notes: Careful speech uses to iu (sakura to iu omise). Polite 'what's it called?': nan to iimasu ka? Also a hedge: tte iu ka = or rather.

items.use: After a plain clause, denies a conclusion the listener might draw (kirai na wake ja nai), and often trails off into kedo.

example.romaji: kirai na wake ja nai kedo...
example.ja: 嫌いなわけじゃないけど…
example.english: It's not that I don't like it, but...

examplePolite.romaji: kirai na wake ja nai desu kedo...
examplePolite.ja: 嫌いなわけじゃないですけど…
examplePolite.english: It's not that I don't like it, but...

items.freqNote: rank of fused わけじゃない; わけ alone #272, わけない #449
items.notes: Trap: without ja it flips: iku wake nai = no way I'm going; iku wake ja nai = it's not that I'm going. Na-adjectives take na (hima na wake ja nai); nouns take na casually, to iu in careful speech. Often opens with betsu ni; more formal: -wake ja arimasen.

blocks.label: Think, feel, mind
blocks.rationale: Verbs for what's going on in your head: an opinion (omou), thinking it over (kangaeru), something on your mind (ki ni naru), a hunch (ki ga suru), minding it (ki ni suru) and taking care (ki o tsukeru).
blocks.interference: omou gives a view (... to omou) while kangaeru means working something through (mada kangaeteru); ki ga suru (a hunch, takes a clause) and ki ni naru (it nags at me, takes ga) share ki but differ in particle and verb; ki ni naru (it bothers me) and ki ni suru (I let it bother me) are an intransitive/transitive pair, heard mostly as ki ni naru and ki ni shinaide; ki o tsukete (take care) is the one with o, said at goodbyes.

items.use: Attaches with to to any clause to state an opinion or guess softly (ii to omou), and -ou to omotteru states a plan.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ame ga furu to omoimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日雨が降ると思います。
examplePolite.english: I think it will rain tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 思う #33
items.notes: Someone else's view uses omotteru (Tanaka-san mo sou omotteru); nouns and na-adjectives keep da before to: ii hito da to omou, kirei da to omou (never *ii hito to omou).

items.use: Actively thinking something through or coming up with ideas, and the polite way to put off a decision (chotto kangaete mimasu / kangaete okimasu).

examplePolite.ja: それはまだ考えてます。

items.freqNote: 考える #112
items.notes: Hearing chotto kangaete okimasu usually means a polite no; 'I think that ...' is to omou, not to kangaeru.

items.use: Something keeps pulling your attention, as curiosity, interest or worry, with the thing marked by ga (X ga ki ni naru).

example.romaji: ashita no tenki, ki ni naru.
example.english: I'm a bit worried about tomorrow's weather.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no tenki ga ki ni narimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日の天気が気になります。
examplePolite.english: I'm a little concerned about tomorrow's weather.

items.freqNote: 気になる #368 as a lexicalized entry
items.notes: Its active partner: ki ni shinaide = don't worry about it.

items.use: Attaches to any clause to mark it as a hunch rather than a claim (... ki ga suru), sounding more intuitive than to omou.

example.romaji: ashita ame furu ki ga suru.
example.english: I have a feeling it'll rain tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita ame ga furu ki ga shimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 明日雨が降る気がします。
examplePolite.english: I have a feeling it will rain tomorrow.

items.freqNote: 気がする #554 as a lexicalized entry
items.notes: No to: a clause attaches directly (furu ki ga suru); a na-adjective takes na and a noun takes mitai na (hen na ki ga suru, uso mitai na ki ga suru).

items.use: Says someone minds or worries about something, with the thing marked by o; mostly heard as ki ni shinaide (don't worry about it) after an apology or thanks, and ki ni shinai (I don't mind).

example.english: It's fine, don't worry about it.

examplePolite.romaji: ii desu yo, ki ni shinaide kudasai.
examplePolite.ja: いいですよ、気にしないでください。
examplePolite.english: It's fine, don't worry about it.

items.freqNote: 気にする #725 as a lexicalized entry
items.notes: Also mada ki ni shiteru no? = are you still worried about that?

items.use: Means paying attention so nothing goes wrong; ki o tsukete (take care, get home safe) is a standard goodbye, and ki o tsukemasu (I'll be careful) answers a warning or closes your own apology (sumimasen, kondo kara ki o tsukemasu).

examplePolite.romaji: ki o tsukete kaette kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 気をつけて帰ってくださいね。

items.freqNote: 気をつける #1226; 気をつけて #1735 and 気を付ける #2218 counted separately
items.notes: The danger takes ni: kuruma ni ki o tsukete = watch out for cars.

blocks.label: How / this way
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/do manner words plus dou yatte, dou iu and dou shita: how something went, how it is done, 'like that', what exactly is going on, and what's wrong.
blocks.interference: dou asks for an opinion or report (dou datta?), dou yatte asks for the method (dou yatte iku?), dou iu koto? asks what's going on or what someone is getting at (once it's explained: aa, sou iu koto ka), and dou shita no? asks what has happened to you. dou iu asks what something is, donna (J7) what it is like: dou iu hito? = who is he to you, donna hito? = what's he like, and donna koto? = like what?; for what a word means, use dou iu imi? (G). The bare reply sou (sou da ne) is drilled in G, so the so- card here is sou iu.

items.use: Asks for an opinion, a report or a plan in one word (dou?, dou datta?, dou suru?, dou omou?), and after a noun it suggests (ashita dou?).

examplePolite.ja: 映画はどうでしたか？

items.freqNote: extra-polite いかが #840
items.notes: Shop staff use the extra-polite ikaga desu ka when offering something.

items.english: that kind of; like that (what you said)
items.use: Refers back to something just said or mentioned (sou iu koto = so that's it, sou iu hito = that kind of person); the same sou follows verbs of thinking and doing (sou omou = I think so, sou yatte = like that).

example.english: Oh, so that's what you mean.

examplePolite.ja: そういうことですか。
examplePolite.english: Oh, so that's what you mean.

items.freqNote: そういう #129; そうやって #919; bare そう #31 is mostly the reply (G)
items.notes: The a- version aa iu / aa yatte (something you both saw) is mostly for recognition; sou works almost everywhere you might say aa.

items.use: Demonstrates a way of doing something while you show it (kou yatte, kou suru to), and kou iu means 'this kind of'.

example.romaji: kou yatte tsukau n da yo.
example.ja: こうやって使うんだよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kou yatte tsukau n desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: こうやって使うんですよ。

items.freqNote: こういう #281; こうやって #807
items.notes: kou? with a gesture means 'like this?', the easiest way to check you're doing it right.

items.use: Asks for the method or route (dou yatte iku?, dou yatte tsukuru?), where bare dou would ask for an opinion.

examplePolite.romaji: dou yatte tsukau n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どうやって使うんですか？

items.notes: Alone, dou yatte? works as a quick 'How?'

items.use: The check-in when someone looks upset, hurt or late (dou shita no?); after a noun it asks what became of the thing (kagi dou shita? = what did you do with the key?).

example.romaji: dou shita no? genki nai ne.
example.ja: どうしたの？元気ないね。

examplePolite.romaji: dou shita n desu ka? genki nai desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: どうしたんですか？元気ないですね。

items.notes: Staff and doctors say dou shimashita ka? to ask what the problem is. Don't mix it up with dou suru? (what will you do?).

items.english: what exactly (+ noun); dou iu koto? = how so? what's going on?
items.use: Goes before a noun to ask what exactly something is: dou iu koto? (how so? what's going on?), dou iu hito? (who is he, exactly? how do you know him?), dou iu kankei? (how are you two connected?). It is the question partner of sou iu. To ask what a word means, use dou iu imi? (G).

example.romaji: e, dou iu koto? ashita konai no?
example.ja: え、どういうこと？明日来ないの？
example.english: Wait, what's going on? You're not coming tomorrow?

examplePolite.romaji: e, dou iu koto desu ka? ashita konai n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: え、どういうことですか？明日来ないんですか？
examplePolite.english: Wait, what's going on? You're not coming tomorrow?

items.notes: dou iu koto? with a light rising tone is the everyday 'how so?'; said flat and hard it becomes 'what is the meaning of this?!', like dou iu wake? (see F-wake-da). With clerks and strangers, dou iu imi desu ka? (G) is the safe way to ask for clarification. In nihongo de dou iu? (how do you say it in Japanese?), iu is the verb 'say', not this word.

blocks.label: What kind
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do 'kind' row for describing something or asking what it is like.
blocks.interference: donna (what kind) vs dono (which one); sonna is the neutral 'that kind you mentioned', anna often sounds critical.

items.use: Describes something you are showing or experiencing (konna kanji, konna no hajimete), and konna ni means 'this much, so'.

examplePolite.romaji: konna kanji de ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: こんな感じでいいですか？

items.notes: konna ni + adjective is an exclamation: konna ni oishii n da! (I didn't know it was this good!)

items.use: Describes what the other person has or just said, and builds push-back (sonna koto nai = that's not true); alone, sonna! means 'no way!'

examplePolite.romaji: sonna kanji de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: そんな感じでいいですよ。

items.notes: sonna ni + negative means 'not that much' (sonna ni takakunai); it has its own entry, sonna ni.

items.use: Goes before a noun to ask someone to describe it (donna hito?, donna kanji?); any particle goes after that noun (donna kanji ga ii?).

example.english: What sort of thing do you want?

examplePolite.romaji: donna kanji ga ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: どんな感じがいいですか？
examplePolite.english: What sort of thing would you like?

items.notes: donna hito? asks for a description; dono hito? asks you to pick one.

items.use: Describes something you both saw or know, mostly in anna hito or anna koto, and is often disapproving.

example.english: I'd like it like that one.

examplePolite.ja: あんな感じがいいです。
examplePolite.english: I'd like it like that one.

items.notes: anna hito often sounds critical, like 'someone like that'.

blocks.label: Amazing & awful
blocks.rationale: Strong reactions at both ends of the scale: amazing, best, worst, terrible, and yabai, which can mean either.
blocks.interference: saikou and saiaku both start with sai- and mean opposite things, so learn saikou first and add saiaku once it is solid. sugoi and yabai share a sentence: same feeling, but yabai is casual only.

items.use: The all-purpose impressed reaction ('sugoi!') to people, skills, views and news; it also marks sheer intensity, good or bad (sugoi ame = torrential rain), and as sugoku it becomes 'really, very' (B).

examplePolite.ja: この歌、すごいですね

items.freqNote: すごい #114; masculine-rough variant すげえ #1510 (noted, not carded)
items.notes: The rough male sugee is heard all the time in dramas; recognise it, but say sugoi. Casually, bare sugoi also works as 'really' (sugoi oishii = really tasty); with desu, use sugoku or totemo.

items.use: The top-end enthusiastic verdict on a day, meal, person or experience ('saikou!'); it takes da or datta like a noun.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は最高でした

items.use: The top-end complaint about a day, event, person or situation; said alone, 'saiaku!' is the standard 'ugh, terrible' reaction to bad luck.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は最悪でした

items.notes: sai-kou and sai-aku only differ after sai-, so hear the whole word before you react.

items.use: Says something is terrible (weather, a cold, traffic) or that someone is mean or unfair; 'hidoi!' is the reaction to being treated badly, and 'sore wa hidoi' is sympathy for someone's story.

examplePolite.ja: それはひどいですね

items.notes: Said to someone's face, 'hidoi!' means 'that's mean!'

items.use: Casual intensity word with two senses, 'uh-oh, I'm in trouble' (the original) and 'insanely good' (younger speakers); tone and context decide which.
items.politeJa: すごいです / まずいです

examplePolite.ja: この歌、すごいですね

items.freqNote: spelling split: ヤバい #1166, やばい #2058, やべえ #4269
items.notes: The 'uh-oh' sense: 'yabai, okureru!' = Oh no, I'm going to be late! Don't use it with clerks or strangers: politely, say sugoi desu for the good sense and mazui desu for the uh-oh sense (mazui desu ne, okuremasu).

blocks.label: Soon, suddenly, gradually
blocks.rationale: How soon something happens, from right away to 'it's about time', plus whether a change comes out of the blue or bit by bit.
blocks.interference: sugu = right after, mou sugu = the event is close, sorosoro = it's time (mostly to leave), kyuu ni = without warning, usually in past tense. dandan is the opposite of kyuu ni: the same change spread out, usually with -te kita (dandan samuku natte kita vs kyuu ni samuku natta).

items.use: Makes an action immediate or close at hand (sugu iku, sugu kaeru). It also builds ima sugu and mou sugu.

examplePolite.ja: すぐ行きます。

items.notes: ima sugu means 'right this minute'. sugu can also mean 'easily' (sugu okoru = gets angry easily) and 'very near' (sugu soko = right over there, eki kara sugu = right by the station).

items.use: Says that a time or event is about to arrive, before a verb (mou sugu tsuku) or a noun (mou sugu natsu = summer's nearly here).

examplePolite.ja: もうすぐ着きます。

items.freqNote: もうすぐ #691
items.notes: It is about time only. 'Almost' as in nearly all is hotondo, and 'a little more' is mou sukoshi.

items.use: Signals that it's time to move on, most often to leave (sorosoro kaeru). It softens wrapping things up.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ帰りますね。

items.freqNote: そろそろ #413
items.notes: The polite way to excuse yourself is sorosoro shitsurei shimasu.

items.use: Marks an abrupt, unexpected change or action. kyuu ni dou shita no? means 'what's got into you?'

example.english: It's suddenly turned cold, hasn't it?

examplePolite.ja: 急に寒くなりましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's suddenly turned cold, hasn't it?

items.freqNote: 急に #345; synonyms 突然 #573, いきなり #723
items.notes: kyuu ni gomen ne = sorry for the short notice; kyuu na youji ga dekite = something came up (the standard excuse). totsuzen (stronger) and ikinari (casual, abrupt) are near-synonyms.

items.use: Says a state changes bit by bit. It almost always pairs with -ku naru / -ni naru, plus -te kita for change up to now (dandan wakatte kita = it's slowly starting to make sense) or -te iku for change from now on (dandan samuku natte iku). Learn natte kita (has been getting) as a chunk here; the -te kuru pattern itself comes later (I-te-kuru).

example.ja: だんだん寒くなってきたね。
example.english: It's been gradually getting colder, hasn't it?

examplePolite.ja: だんだん寒くなってきましたね。
examplePolite.english: It's been gradually getting colder, hasn't it?

items.notes: dandan is for a change in degree (getting colder, getting used to it), not for doing something in small portions. For that, use sukoshi zutsu (sukoshi zutsu tabete, sukoshi zutsu oboeru). For 'slowly' as a speed (speak slowly), use yukkuri.

blocks.label: If / even if
blocks.rationale: The four 'if' endings plus 'even if', all on one 'jikan aru' sentence so only the ending changes.
blocks.interference: English gives all five as 'if/when': -tara is the default, -nara picks up what was just said, -te mo flips to 'even if', -ba means 'that's all it takes', -to is automatic and never takes a request or plan after it.

items.use: Conditional built on the -ta form: 'if' for hypotheticals, 'when / once' for things sure to happen, and 'when I did X, I found Y' in stories. The safe default when unsure which 'if' fits.

example.english: If you've got time, come by.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga attara, kite kudasai ne.
examplePolite.ja: 時間があったら、来てくださいね。
examplePolite.english: If you have time, please come by.

items.freqNote: たら #2818, misleadingly low: tokenizer fuses most -tara into the verb token (cf. だったら #207, よかったら #938)
items.notes: Polite speech keeps plain -tara; -mashitara sounds very formal.

items.use: Takes up something just said or known and builds on it: 'if it's X / if you're going to X'. Attaches to nouns and plain forms ('sushi nara, ii mise shitteru').

example.ja: 時間あるなら、手伝ってよ。
example.english: If you've got time, help me out.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga aru nara, chotto tetsudatte moraemasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 時間があるなら、ちょっと手伝ってもらえますか？
examplePolite.english: If you've got time, could you give me a hand?

items.freqNote: なら #77
items.notes: English speakers overuse nara for every 'if'; save it for picking up what was said. Timing trap: with nara the main action can come first ('nihon ni iku nara, kore yonde' = read this before you go), while 'nihon ni ittara, ...' = once you're there.

items.use: Te-form + mo: the result holds anyway ('ame ga futte mo iku'). Adjectives take -kute mo, nouns and na-adjectives de mo; casual alternative -tatte.

example.ja: 時間あっても、行かない。
example.english: Even if I have time, I'm not going.

examplePolite.ja: 時間があっても、行きません。
examplePolite.english: Even if I have time, I won't go.

items.freqNote: ても #13684, misleadingly low: tokenizer splits -te + mo; casual たって #1142
items.notes: Listen for what follows: 'tabete mo ii?' = 'can I eat it?', while 'tabete mo, ...' = 'even if I eat'. Don't treat -te mo as a kind of -tara; it flips the meaning ('even if' vs 'if').

items.use: Conditional on the e-stem (areba, ikeba, yasukereba): 'if X, then Y', often with the sense that X is all it takes. Also inside -ba ii, -nakereba and dou sureba.

example.english: If I have time, I'll go.

examplePolite.ja: 時間があれば、行きます。
examplePolite.english: If I have time, I'll go.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; ば alone unusable (#183446); rank of できれば, cf. なければ #1873, よければ #2273
items.notes: Casually -nakereba shrinks to -nakya; -kerya / -rya (yokerya, arya) sound rough and male: recognise, don't produce. After an action verb, -ba can't lead into a request or invitation; use -tara ('tsuitara, denwa shite').

items.use: Plain form + to: Y always or automatically follows X; used for directions, how things work and habits ('migi ni magaru to, eki ga aru'). The main clause can't be a request, invitation or plan.

example.ja: 時間あると、いつも寝ちゃう。
example.english: Whenever I have time, I end up sleeping.

examplePolite.romaji: jikan ga aru to, itsumo nechaimasu.
examplePolite.ja: 時間があると、いつも寝ちゃいます。
examplePolite.english: Whenever I have time, I end up sleeping.

items.freqNote: と #7, counts every と (and, with, quote), not just the conditional
items.notes: '...to, kite' (a request) is wrong; use -tara for that.

blocks.label: Later and next time
blocks.rationale: These push something to a later point: later today, the next occasion, next in line, or again.
blocks.interference: English 'next time' is usually kondo. tsugi is the next in order, ato de stays within the same occasion, and mata just means 'again'.

items.use: Says something happens again (mata kita), and closes goodbyes and invitations (mata ne, mata kite ne).

examplePolite.romaji: mata watashi ga harau n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: また私が払うんですか？

items.freqNote: また #91, includes the 'also' connector sense
items.notes: mata ne and mata ashita are the everyday goodbyes. The 'also' sense belongs to connectors. Men say ore here in casual talk (mata ore ga harau no?).

items.use: Puts something off until later, usually the same day (ato de ne). After a -ta verb, -ta ato de means 'after doing'.

examplePolite.ja: 後で払いますね。

items.freqNote: 後で #1484; kana あとで #3950
items.notes: Business speech uses nochi hodo. ato de is fine in ordinary polite talk. ato + an amount means 'X more, X left' (ato go-fun = five more minutes).

items.use: Points to the next occasion or some future one. It is how people float plans and soft invitations (kondo nomi ni ikou).

examplePolite.ja: 今度払いますね。

items.notes: mata kondo ('another time') is often a polite no. kondo no + a day means 'this coming' (kondo no doyoubi). After an earlier try, kondo wa can mean 'this time' (kondo wa umaku itta).

items.use: Points to the next item in a sequence or line (tsugi no eki, tsugi wa?). tsugi ni marks the next step.

examplePolite.romaji: tsugi wa doko ni ikimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 次はどこに行きますか？

items.notes: tsugi wa also means 'next time' for a definite next occurrence (tsugi wa ki o tsukete = be careful next time). kondo is vaguer and is the word for invitations.

blocks.label: Last, this, next month
blocks.rationale: The sen-, kon- and rai- of the week words applied to months, with no exceptions.
blocks.interference: sengetsu, kongetsu and raigetsu differ only in the first syllable, exactly like senshuu, konshuu and raishuu. Like the week words, they take no ni: raigetsu hikkosu, not raigetsu ni hikkosu.

items.use: Last month, for recaps. It uses the same sen- as senshuu, so it pairs with past tense.

examplePolite.ja: 先月引っ越したんです。

items.freqNote: 先月(せんげつ) #2840

items.use: This month, for budgets, schedules and deadlines. It uses the same kon- as konshuu.

examplePolite.ja: 今月引っ越すんです。

items.freqNote: 今月(こんげつ) #2267

items.use: Next month, for plans and deadlines. It uses the same rai- as raishuu.

examplePolite.ja: 来月引っ越すんです。

items.freqNote: 来月(らいげつ) #2256

blocks.label: Last, this, next year
blocks.rationale: The same grid for years, where two of the three words are irregular.
blocks.interference: Only rainen fits the sen-/kon-/rai- pattern: this year is kotoshi and last year is kyonen. kyonen has a short kyo- (kyo-ne-n), unlike the long kyou of 'today', so don't stretch it. Like the week and month words, all three take no ni.

items.use: Last year, the usual anchor for recaps. Like kinou, it pairs with past tense.

examplePolite.ja: 去年結婚したんです。

items.freqNote: 去年(きょねん) #1422
items.notes: It breaks the sen- pattern. Say a short kyo- (kyo-ne-n, three beats), not the long kyou of 'today'. sakunen (昨年, #5231) is the formal version heard in business talk and the news: recognise it, but say kyonen even in desu/masu.

items.use: This year, for yearly plans and recaps, and the New Year line kotoshi mo yoroshiku.

examplePolite.ja: 今年結婚するんです。

items.freqNote: 今年(ことし) #1145
items.notes: It breaks the kon- pattern: kotoshi. The kon- reading turns up in work talk as konnendo (今年度, this fiscal year).

items.use: Next year, for plans and hopes. It is the one year word that fits the rai- pattern of raishuu and raigetsu.

examplePolite.ja: 来年結婚するんです。

items.freqNote: 来年(らいねん) #2055

blocks.label: this/that: ways & sides
blocks.rationale: The ko/so/a/do direction row for which way, whose side and which of two, each with a polite -chira form.
blocks.interference: dotchi is for two choices, dore for three or more; kotchi and sotchi can also mean 'me' and 'you', so listen for people, not places. The -chira forms are what you say to customers and strangers; with coworkers kotchi/dotchi + desu is normal.

items.use: Points to a direction, a side or one of two choices (kotchi ga ii), and casually also means 'me, my side' (kotchi wa daijoubu).

examplePolite.ja: こちらがいいです。

items.freqNote: polite こちら #200
items.notes: kochira also introduces people: kochira wa tanaka-san desu.

items.use: Asks which of two, or which direction, and takes ga (dotchi ga ii?).

example.english: Which of the two do you want?

examplePolite.ja: どちらがいいですか？

items.freqNote: polite どちら #1013
items.notes: dotchi demo ii means 'either is fine'.

items.use: The direction or choice on the listener's side, and casually a way to say 'you' without anata (sotchi wa dou?).

examplePolite.ja: そちらがいいですよ。

items.freqNote: polite そちら #1162
items.notes: sotchi wa? means 'and you?', a casual way around anata.

items.use: The direction or thing away from both of you, used mostly for pointing out the way (atchi da yo).

example.english: That one over there looks better.

examplePolite.ja: あちらがいいですね。
examplePolite.english: That one over there looks better.

items.freqNote: polite あちら #1685
items.notes: Learn atchi da yo, 'it's that way', first.

blocks.label: In, on, near, other
blocks.rationale: Relational nouns that attach to another noun with no to say where something is (in, on, in front, near) or that it is a different one.
blocks.interference: naka/soto, ue/shita, mae/ushiro and chikaku come after the noun (hako no naka, eki no mae) but hoka comes before (hoka no hito); ue/shita also mean older/younger, and mae also means before/ago in time.

items.use: Places things in or out of something (kaban no naka, soto de), and X no naka de ichiban means 'the most out of X'.

example.romaji: naka ja nakute, soto ni aru yo.
example.ja: 中じゃなくて、外にあるよ。

examplePolite.romaji: naka ja nakute, soto ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 中じゃなくて、外にありますよ。

items.freqNote: 中 read なか #133; 外 soto #437
items.notes: naka also means 'relationship' (naka ga ii = get along well).

items.use: Places things above or below (tsukue no ue), and gives relative age or rank (futatsu ue = two years older).

example.romaji: ue ja nakute, shita ni aru yo.
example.ja: 上じゃなくて、下にあるよ。
example.english: It's not on top, it's underneath.

examplePolite.romaji: ue ja nakute, shita ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 上じゃなくて、下にありますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's not on top, it's underneath.

items.freqNote: 上 read うえ #321; 下 shita #622
items.notes: shita also means 'tongue' and 'did' (past of suru); context sorts it.

items.use: Comes before no or ni: hoka no means 'another, other' and hoka ni means 'besides, anything else'.

examplePolite.ja: 他のはありませんか？

items.freqNote: plus ほか #1673, 他にも #1824
items.notes: hoka ni wa? is the quick 'anything else?' follow-up.

items.use: Places people and things in front or behind (eki no mae, ushiro no seki); X no mae de is the standard way to set a meeting point.

example.romaji: mae ja nakute, ushiro ni aru yo.
example.ja: 前じゃなくて、後ろにあるよ。
example.english: It's not on the front, it's on the back.

examplePolite.romaji: mae ja nakute, ushiro ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 前じゃなくて、後ろにありますよ。
examplePolite.english: It's not on the front, it's on the back.

items.freqNote: 前 #80, all senses combined (time sense shared with A-mae); 後ろ ushiro #1090
items.notes: eki no mae de matteru ne = I'll wait in front of the station. In time, the opposite of mae is ato (ato de = later), not ushiro.

items.use: Says something is close by: after a noun + no it means 'near X' (eki no chikaku), and on its own it means 'nearby' (chikaku ni aru, chikaku no mise).

example.romaji: eki no chikaku ni aru yo.

examplePolite.romaji: eki no chikaku ni arimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 駅の近くにありますよ。

items.freqNote: 近く #464; adjective 近い chikai #751
items.notes: For 'a nearby shop' say chikaku no mise, not chikai mise; chikai + noun mostly comes as ichiban chikai (the nearest). The adjective chikai talks about the distance itself (eki kara chikai = close to the station).

blocks.label: Person, thing, matter, place
blocks.rationale: The four general nouns that let you talk around any word you don't know.
blocks.interference: mono is a thing you can touch (taberu mono), koto is an act or topic (suki na koto), tokoro is a place or a trait (yasashii tokoro).

items.use: Any person or people, usually with a description in front (ii hito, ano hito), and hito ni yoru means 'it depends on the person'.

examplePolite.ja: 好きな人、いますか？

items.notes: People take iru, not aru: hito ga iru.

items.use: A concrete thing, usually with a description in front, so you can name what you lack the word for (taberu mono, hoshii mono).

example.romaji: suki na mono tanonde ii yo.
example.ja: 好きなもの頼んでいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: suki na mono tanonde ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 好きなもの頼んでいいですよ。

items.notes: mono da at the end means 'that's just how it is' (sou iu mono da).

items.use: An abstract thing such as an act, event or topic (suki na koto, sonna koto), X no koto means 'about X', and it is the base of patterns like -ta koto ga aru.

example.romaji: suki na koto shite ii yo.
example.ja: 好きなことしていいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: suki na koto shite ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 好きなことしていいですよ。

items.notes: tanaka-san no koto ga suki means 'I like Tanaka-san'; X no koto turns a person into a topic (about X, X as a person).

items.use: A place (ii tokoro) or a trait of someone or something (yasashii tokoro = their kind side); X no tokoro, casually X no toko, means X's place (tanaka-san no toko ni iku = go to Tanaka-san's).

example.romaji: suki na tokoro de ii yo.
example.ja: 好きなところでいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: suki na tokoro de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 好きなところでいいですよ。

items.freqNote: ところ #187 pools the aspect pattern (A -tokoro) and tokoro de; 所 #574; casual とこ #280
items.notes: You can't go ni a person: tomodachi no tokoro ni iku, not tomodachi ni iku. The aspect pattern -tokoro (tabeteru tokoro) is a separate card in A.

blocks.label: Checking with you
blocks.rationale: Tags that pull the listener into agreement, plus tte koto? to check you've understood what they said.
blocks.interference: desho? means 'surely you agree' (often 'told you'), ja nai? offers your view as a rising question, and jan states it with a falling tone, not as a question. tte koto? restates the other person's words to check you understood.

items.use: A rising tag that expects agreement, meaning 'see, I told you' or 'you know what I mean'. Everyone uses it in casual speech.

examplePolite.ja: これいいでしょう？

items.freqNote: tokenizer files でしょ under でしょう #147 (bare でしょ #43859); includes polite 'probably'
items.notes: With a falling tone, polite deshou means 'probably' (ame deshou). In casual speech, guess with tabun, kamo or to omou. A bare final darou and the tag daro? lean masculine, while nan darou / dou darou (I wonder) are used by everyone. With people above you, a rising deshou? can sound pushy; desu yo ne? (kore ii desu yo ne?) is the safer check.

items.use: Offers your view softly as a rising question (ii ja nai? = that's nice, no?). It attaches directly to nouns and adjectives (tanaka-san ja nai?, kirei ja nai?, ii ja nai?). After verbs, use n ja nai? (ame furu n ja nai?).

example.romaji: are, ano hito tanaka-san ja nai?
example.ja: あれ、あの人田中さんじゃない？
example.english: Wait, isn't that Tanaka over there?

examplePolite.romaji: are, ano hito tanaka-san ja nai desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: あれ、あの人田中さんじゃないですか？
examplePolite.english: Oh, isn't that Tanaka-san over there?

items.freqNote: rank of じゃない, which merges plain negation; じゃないか #202
items.notes: Tone decides the meaning: rising ame ja nai? = isn't it rain?, while flat ame ja nai = it isn't rain. After an i-adjective it is always this tag, never negation, because the negative is -kunai.

items.use: Contracted ja nai said with a falling tone. It presents something as obvious or newly noticed (ii jan = hey, that's nice) and isn't a real question.

examplePolite.romaji: kore ii ja nai desu ka
examplePolite.ja: これいいじゃないですか

items.freqNote: #363 じゃん (Kansai やん #1690)
items.notes: It spread to Tokyo from Yokohama and the surrounding region and is now heard nationwide; Kansai speakers say yan. With verbs it means 'I told you': datte itta jan (I told you so!). In polite speech, asserting ...ja nai desu ka about things the listener can't know sounds presumptuous.

items.use: Restates what the other person said to check you understood, which is vital for a learner. It attaches to the plain form.

example.english: So you mean tomorrow's no good?

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa muri tte koto desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は無理ってことですか？
examplePolite.english: So you mean tomorrow's no good?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (ってこと and ということ not found; こと #26 too generic)
items.notes: sou iu koto? (is that what you mean?) works as a reply on its own. to iu koto desu ka is the more formal polite option, for meetings and email.

blocks.label: How sure
blocks.rationale: A ladder of certainty from 'maybe' through 'should be' to 'no way', all on one base sentence about someone arriving.
blocks.interference: From least to most sure: kamo (could go either way), to omou (my opinion), n ja nai (I'd guess), hazu (should, by reasoning); wake nai is just as sure in the other direction (no way). hazu is about what you expect: not your own plans, which take tsumori, and never advice, which takes -ta hou ga ii. hazu ga nai also means 'can't be', but calmly, by reasoning; wake nai is the everyday, emphatic one. wake nai and wake ja nai both deny, but one ja softens it: kirai na wake nai = no way I'd hate it, kirai na wake ja nai (kedo) = it's not that I hate it (but...).

items.use: Marks something as possible but uncertain. It attaches to any plain clause, with no da after nouns (ame kamo).

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くかもしれません

items.freqNote: #240 かも (かもしれない #219, polite かもしれません #665)
items.notes: kamo desu is common among younger coworkers but sounds a bit loose; with superiors or customers, use kamo shiremasen.

items.use: Presents a statement as your own opinion or guess so it doesn't sound blunt. It attaches to the plain form, with da after nouns (ame da to omou).

example.english: I think they'll be here soon.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くと思います
examplePolite.english: I think they'll be arriving soon.

items.freqNote: rank of 思う (all uses)
items.notes: Use it for your own thoughts only; for someone else, say to omotteru. The casual variant is tte omou. For 'I don't think...', negate the clause: konai to omou (I don't think they'll come), not kuru to omowanai.

items.use: Gives a soft but fairly confident guess or opinion, either as a rising question or as a flat statement. After nouns, use na n ja nai.

example.ja: そろそろ着くんじゃない？
example.english: They'll probably be here soon, no?

examplePolite.romaji: sorosoro tsuku n ja nai desu ka
examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くんじゃないですか
examplePolite.english: I'd say they'll be here soon.

items.freqNote: んじゃない not found (split); rank of じゃない (んじゃ #32265)
items.notes: A sharp, falling ...n ja nai! is a scolding 'don't!' (sawaru n ja nai!). Flat, it can also deny an explanation: asobi ni iku n ja nai = it's not that I'm going to play.

items.use: States what you expect on good grounds, such as a schedule, what someone said, or how things normally work. After nouns it is no hazu; after na-adjectives, na hazu.

example.english: They should be here any minute.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ着くはずです
examplePolite.english: They should be arriving any minute.

items.notes: hazu ga nai means 'can't possibly'; hazu datta means 'was supposed to (but didn't)'. It is never advice: 'you should rest' is yasunda hou ga ii.

items.use: Flatly rules something out as impossible or absurd ('no way', 'as if'). On its own it makes the stock retort sonna wake nai (jan)! = no way / that can't be. It goes on any plain clause, often with jan or desho (wakaru wake nai jan = how would I know?), and nouns and na-adjectives take na before it (uso na wake nai, hima na wake nai).

example.english: No way they'll be here yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada tsuku wake nai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: まだ着くわけないですよ
examplePolite.english: There's no way they'll be here yet.

items.freqNote: わけない #449 (token also covers the adjective 訳ない 'easy', whose kanji spelling is #8290); わけがない #2398; cf. はずない #2095, はずがない #2504
items.notes: One ja softens it rather than flipping it: kirai na wake ja nai (kedo) = it's not that I hate it (but...). The same word is also an adjective meaning 'easy, no trouble': sonna no wake nai yo = that's nothing, one 'no' away from sonna wake nai yo = no way. Even in polite speech it flatly contradicts, so don't aim it at a superior's idea (say sore wa chotto... instead). The careful polite form is wake ga arimasen.

blocks.label: More enders
blocks.rationale: Four endings built on items you already have: -te plus ne for a friendly ask, n da plus yo for an insistent reason, darou, the plain form of deshou, for wondering aloud, and -tara plus ii na for hoping.
blocks.interference: darou is the plain deshou, but in casual speech only its wondering uses (nan darou, daijoubu darou ka) are neutral, so say kamo for 'probably' and desho? for 'right?'. n da yo pushes a reason across where n da just explains, and -te ne assumes a yes where -te kurenai? asks. ikitai na wants to do it yourself; iketara ii na hopes you'll get the chance, and haretara ii na hopes for something out of your hands. Swap na for yo and it becomes advice (kiitara ii yo = you should ask).

items.use: Adds ne to a casual -te request so it sounds warm rather than bossy. It is the everyday way to ask or remind friends, family and kids (mata renraku shite ne, ki o tsukete ne). It assumes they'll go along, so it's a friendly instruction, not a question.

example.ja: ごめん、ちょっと待ってね
example.english: Sorry, hang on a sec, OK?

examplePolite.ja: すみません、ちょっと待ってくださいね

items.freqNote: no usable rank — てね #24031 undercounts (tokenizer splits)
items.notes: -naide ne is the 'don't' version (wasurenaide ne). -te kudasai ne sounds like giving instructions, which is fine from staff or between coworkers but bossy to a superior, so ask them with -te moraemasu ka. Mid-story -te ne (kinou eki ni itte ne, ...) is just 'and then' plus ne, not a request.

items.use: Gives the listener an explanation they don't have yet, with yo pushing it across: why something happened, news, or a correction. Everyone uses it. After a question word it turns into a rough, masculine rebuke (nani shiteru n da yo! = what the hell are you doing?), so recognise that one; the neutral version is nani shiteru no!?

example.english: I've got a headache, that's why.

examplePolite.romaji: atama ga itai n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 頭が痛いんですよ
examplePolite.english: I have a headache, you see.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of んだ (んだよ not found)
items.notes: no yo (atama itai no yo) is the feminine version, now mostly heard from older women and in dramas; young women just say n da yo or no. Giving a superior an excuse with n desu yo sounds defensive; plain n desu is safer.

items.use: The plain form of deshou. Wondering aloud is neutral and everyone says it, whether with a question word (nan darou, dou darou, doko itta n darou) or with ka (daijoubu darou ka). As a falling 'probably' (ashita wa ame darou) or the rising tag daro? (right?), it sounds masculine and blunt, so most casual speakers say kamo (or tabun) for 'probably' and desho? for 'right?' instead.

examplePolite.ja: 会議はいつでしょうか
examplePolite.english: When is the meeting, I wonder?

items.freqNote: #102 だろう (だろ #119; でしょう #147, which also counts casual でしょ)
items.notes: dou darou on its own is a handy non-answer ('hmm, hard to say'). Polite deshou is neutral for everyone, whether as 'probably' (ame deshou) or as deshou ka (I wonder). In fast speech the wondering form is often just daro, said falling (itsu daro); that is neutral. Only the rising daro? (right?) is the masculine tag.

items.english: I hope / I wish / it'd be nice if
items.use: Hopes for something you can't simply do yourself, like weather, results or someone else's choice: add ii na to a -tara clause (haretara ii na = I hope it's sunny). With a potential verb it hopes you'll get the chance (iketara ii na = I hope I can go; mata aetara ii ne = hope we can meet again), and about something that isn't so it means 'I wish' (okane ga attara ii na = I wish I had money). ii na is half to yourself; -tara ii ne and polite -tara ii desu ne share the hope with the listener, and -nakattara ii na hopes something won't happen.

example.ja: 一緒に行けたらいいな
example.english: I hope we can go together.

examplePolite.romaji: issho ni iketara ii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行けたらいいですね
examplePolite.english: It'd be great if we could go together.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits and folds たら into the verb (standalone たら #2818); いいな #173635 undercounts; いい #24, な #16 (merged with prohibitive/attributive na), なあ #387; cf. といい #3058
items.notes: -ba ii na and -to ii na mean the same; to say you want to do it, use -tai, and for 'what should I do?' use dou shitara ii? (I-tara-ii).

blocks.label: Accepting and declining
blocks.rationale: Answers to a request, suggestion or invitation: yes, an eager yes, and the soft no.
blocks.interference: ii yo grants a request and ii ne welcomes an idea. Bare 'ii desu' in reply to an offer means 'no thanks', and chotto... is the polite trailing no.

items.use: Grants a request or permission, or tells someone not to worry ('ii yo, ii yo').

examplePolite.ja: いいですよ、明日行きます。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer mostly splits いいよ and finds it as a unit only at #3841; いい #24 counts every use)
items.notes: In reply to an offer, bare 'ii desu' (often with a hand wave) usually means 'no thanks'; in reply to 'kore de ii desu ka?' it means 'yes, that's fine'.

items.use: Welcomes a suggestion, or praises something someone shows or tells you.

examplePolite.ja: いいですね、明日行きましょう。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer mostly splits いいね and finds it as a unit only at #5365; いい #24 counts every use)
items.notes: ii na (with na) is envy, 'lucky you / I wish', not approval.

items.use: Declines politely: you trail off after chotto instead of saying no, and the listener fills in the refusal.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、明日はちょっと…

items.freqNote: ちょっと #46 counts every use; the refusal is a subset
items.notes: Don't finish the sentence; trailing off is the refusal. When you hear it, take it as a no and don't ask why.

blocks.label: Fun, tasty, cute
blocks.rationale: The positive comments you make about food, things, activities and shows, plus boring as the let-down.
