blocks.interference: tanoshii (fun to do) and omoshiroi (interesting or entertaining in itself) are the classic mix-up, and the shared job sentence keeps the difference to one word. kawaii (ka-wa-i-i) is easily misheard as kowai (ko-wa-i, scary, in a later block).

items.use: Says food or drink tastes good, at nearly every meal; often a one-word reaction ('oishii!') or the past oishikatta as thanks to the cook.

examplePolite.ja: これ、おいしいですね

items.freqNote: おいしい #302 (美味しい #5867)
items.notes: umai is a blunter casual 'tasty' (more common from men, but not male-only) and also means 'good at'; oishii is safe for everyone and the safe choice with desu.

items.use: A reaction to anything cute or charming (animals, babies, clothes, design, people), used much more widely and freely than English 'cute'.

examplePolite.ja: その服、かわいいですね

items.notes: Don't confuse it with kowai (scary): ka-wa-i-i has four beats, ko-wa-i has three. kawaisou is a different word meaning 'poor thing, what a shame', not 'looks cute'.

items.use: Says an activity or time is fun for the people taking part, most often in the past after an event (tanoshikatta).

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa tanoshii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は楽しいですね

items.freqNote: 楽しい #283
items.notes: It doesn't mean 'happy': that is ureshii (glad about something).

items.use: Says something is interesting or entertaining (shows, ideas, people, places) and also 'funny' (a joke, a person); it is the default praise for content.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa omoshiroi desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は面白いですね

items.freqNote: 面白い #558 (おもしろい #3445)
items.notes: tanoshii is about the fun of doing something; omoshiroi is about the thing itself being interesting or entertaining. For a game, show or book, omoshiroi is the normal praise ('it's good').

items.use: Says something is boring or dull (a show, a job, a person, a day); the opposite of omoshiroi, and in fast speech often tsumannai.

example.ja: この仕事、つまんないね

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa tsumaranai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事はつまらないですね

items.freqNote: つまらない #2645; contracted つまんない #2662 is roughly equal
items.notes: The -nai is part of the word, not a negative. Its own negative is tsumaranakunai. Casual speech mostly says tsumannai; use the full tsumaranai with desu.

blocks.label: New, pretty, kind, skilled
blocks.rationale: What you notice and praise about people and their things: new, pretty or clean, kind, good at something.
blocks.interference: kirei (pretty, clean; said kiree) is close by ear to kirai (hate, earlier block): per 11-list-adjectives keep kirei at least 12 items after kirai, and listen for the pitch, since KI-ree falls after the first beat while ki-RAI rises and stays up. kirei is beautiful or clean while kawaii (earlier block) is cute: a sunset is kirei, a puppy kawaii. yasashii here is only 'kind'; for 'easy' say kantan (earlier block).

items.use: Says something is new: things you've bought, a job, a shop, a phone, news; it goes straight before a noun (atarashii shigoto).

examplePolite.ja: その服、新しいですか？

items.freqNote: 新しい #301
items.notes: Its opposite furui (old) means not new and never describes a person's age: furui tomodachi is a long-time friend. For age, say toshiue (older than me).

items.use: Says something looks lovely or is clean and tidy: views, places, people, rooms, handwriting; kirei ni makes it an adverb (kirei ni shite = tidy it up).

examplePolite.ja: 海がきれいですね

items.notes: Said kiree; a na-adjective despite the -i: kirei ja nai, kirei datta (never kireikunai).

items.use: Describes a kind or gentle person or act; after arigatou, yasashii ne compliments someone for a kindness they just did.

example.english: Thanks, that's so kind of you.

examplePolite.ja: ありがとうございます、優しいですね
examplePolite.english: Thank you, that's so kind of you.

items.freqNote: 優しい #419; 易しい 'easy' #45300 (kantan covers 'easy')
alsoIn: vocab-trainer core-vocab: i-adjectives (carded there as 'easy', the other yasashii)
items.notes: A separate yasashii means 'easy'; use kantan for that and keep this card for 'kind'. yasashii desu ne suits peers and people you know well; to a stranger, boss or teacher who helps you, say arigatou gozaimasu, tasukarimashita instead.

items.use: Compliments someone else's skill: X ga jouzu (you're good at X), or jouzu da ne after watching them; jouzu ni = well, skilfully. About yourself, use it only in the negative or as a goal (mada jouzu ja nai, jouzu ni naritai): claiming it sounds like boasting.

examplePolite.ja: 料理が上手ですね

items.notes: Reply to nihongo jouzu! with ie ie, mada mada desu (casual: iya, mada mada da yo); for your own strengths say tokui. To a boss or teacher, jouzu desu ne sounds like grading them: praise the result instead (sugoi desu ne).

blocks.label: All / a lot
blocks.rationale: Words for how much there is: the whole lot, or plenty of it.
blocks.interference: takusan and ippai both mean 'a lot', but ippai is chattier and also means 'full'. zenbu means 'all of it', not 'a lot'.

items.use: Means 'all / everything' for things and amounts. zenbu de means 'in total' (zenbu de ikura?).

examplePolite.ja: 全部食べましたよ

items.notes: For people use minna, not zenbu. subete (#732) is the formal, written-leaning variant. Trap: zenbu + negative usually means 'not all of it': zenbu wa tabenakatta = I didn't eat all of it (some is left). For 'none at all' say nani mo tabenakatta or zenzen tabenakatta.

items.use: The neutral 'a lot / many' for amounts and counts. It goes straight before the verb with no particle (takusan aru).

examplePolite.ja: まだたくさんありますよ

items.freqNote: たくさん #418; kanji 沢山 #15969

items.use: Chatty 'loads'. It also means 'full' (onaka ippai) and 'at my limit' (ippai ippai).

examplePolite.ja: まだいっぱいありますよ

items.freqNote: いっぱい #512; 一杯 #2892 includes the 'one cupful' sense
items.notes: 'Onaka ippai' means 'I'm full'. Ippai is a bit more colloquial than takusan. Ear trap: flat ippai = lots / full; ippai with the pitch high on the first i and falling after it = one cup, a drink (ippai nomi ni ikou = let's go for a drink). Before a noun both ippai and takusan take no (takusan no hito).

blocks.label: Making plans
blocks.rationale: Arranging to see someone: wait, meet, decide, get in touch.
blocks.interference: 'See a friend' is au with ni, not miru; kimeta (I decided) vs kimatta (it's been settled) is the pair to watch inside kimeru.

items.use: Waiting for someone or something (X o matsu), and matte / chotto matte is the all-purpose 'hold on'.

example.english: I'll wait for you at the station.

examplePolite.ja: 駅で待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll be waiting at the station.

items.freqNote: 待つ #71
items.notes: matteru = 'I'll be waiting' as well as 'I'm waiting'.

items.use: Meeting or seeing a person, planned or by chance, with the person marked by ni (or to for a mutual meet-up).

example.english: What time should we meet tomorrow?

examplePolite.ja: 明日何時に会いましょうか？
examplePolite.english: What time shall we meet tomorrow?

items.freqNote: 会う #110; 合う (fit, match) #563 separately
items.notes: Homophone au 合う = fit / match (saizu ga au).

items.use: Deciding on something (X ni kimeru = go with X) and asking or saying whether a decision is made (kimeta?, mada kimetenai).

example.ja: 週末の予定もう決めた？
example.english: Have you made plans for the weekend yet?

examplePolite.romaji: shuumatsu no yotei wa mou kimemashita ka?
examplePolite.ja: 週末の予定はもう決めましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you decided your weekend plans yet?

items.freqNote: 決める #261; intransitive 決まる #335 separately
items.notes: kimatta = 'it's been decided' (no one named); kimeta = 'I/we decided'.

items.use: Getting in touch by any channel — text, call or message — and the standard way to close a plan (mata renraku suru ne), with renraku shite = let me know.

examplePolite.ja: また連絡しますね。

items.freqNote: 連絡する not found as a unit; rank of the noun 連絡
items.notes: The person contacted takes ni: senpai ni renraku suru.

blocks.label: Meeting up
blocks.rationale: The verbs of the day itself: hanging out, getting there, running late.
blocks.interference: tsuku is arriving, not coming (ima iku, mou sugu tsuku, tsuita); asobu is hanging out, never playing a sport (tenisu suru); okureta (was late) and okutta (sent) differ by one sound.

items.use: Means spending free time for fun, kids playing or adults hanging out (tomodachi to asobu); asobou is the casual invite and asobi ni kite means 'come over'.

examplePolite.ja: 今度遊びましょう。

items.notes: Playing a sport or game is suru (tenisu suru, geemu suru); piano or guitar is hiku.

items.use: Says someone gets to a place, marked by ni (eki ni tsuita), and carries the meet-up messages: mou sugu tsuku, tsuita yo, tsuitara renraku shite.

example.english: I just got to the station.

examplePolite.ja: 今駅に着きました。
examplePolite.english: I've just arrived at the station.

items.freqNote: 着く #957; kana-written つく #355 can't be split by sense and is mostly the 付く/点く senses (come on, stick); 付く #1570 is a separate entry
items.notes: Homophone tsuku 'come on, stick' (付く/点く): denki ga tsuita = the light came on.

items.use: Says someone or something is late for a set time or behind schedule, with the event marked by ni (kaigi ni okureta); okurete gomen is the apology on arrival and densha okureteru (the train's delayed) the standard excuse.

example.ja: ごめん、10分ぐらい遅れる。
example.english: Sorry, I'll be about ten minutes late.

examplePolite.ja: すみません、10分ぐらい遅れます。
examplePolite.english: Sorry, I'll be about ten minutes late.

items.freqNote: 遅れる #955
items.notes: A friend complaining you're late says osoi!; okureta is the explanation.

blocks.label: If-openers
blocks.rationale: Sentence-starting words that set up a condition or follow from one, all built around -tara.
blocks.interference: dattara overlaps with jaa (And then block): dattara explicitly builds on what was just said; moshi never stands alone, it still needs the conditional ending.

items.use: Opens a sentence to flag a hypothetical, so the -tara / -ba / -nara / -te mo at the end is expected.

example.ja: もし雨だったら、やめよう。
example.english: If it rains, let's call it off.

examplePolite.ja: もし雨だったら、やめましょう。
examplePolite.english: If it rains, let's call it off.

items.notes: Moshi alone doesn't make an 'if'; the ending still has to be -tara, -ba, -nara or -te mo.

items.use: Starts a reply that builds a plan on what the other person just said.

example.ja: だったら、明日にしよう。
example.english: In that case, let's make it tomorrow.

examplePolite.ja: でしたら、明日にしましょう。
examplePolite.english: In that case, let's make it tomorrow.

items.freqNote: だったら #207 (also counts noun + dattara mid-sentence); polite でしたら #3192; near-synonym それなら #1552

items.use: Softens an offer or invitation so it's easy to say no; goes at the start of the sentence.

example.ja: よかったら、一緒に行く？
example.english: If you're up for it, want to come along?

examplePolite.ja: よかったら、一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come along?

items.freqNote: よかったら #938; よければ #2273
items.notes: Same word in desu/masu speech; yokereba is a touch more formal, yoroshikereba is keigo.

blocks.label: Asking about words
blocks.rationale: The learner's extraction tools: get a word explained, a meaning cleared up, or the Japanese supplied.
blocks.interference: -tte nani? asks what something is, dou iu imi? asks what it means or what someone meant, and nihongo de nante iu? goes from English or a gesture to the Japanese.

items.use: Put any unknown word in front ('X tte nani?') to get it explained. It also asks what a thing is.

examplePolite.ja: それって何ですか？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (って #18 counts every quotative use)
items.notes: nani becomes nan before desu: 'X tte nan desu ka'.

items.use: Asks what a word means, or what someone meant by what they said.

example.ja: それってどういう意味？
example.english: What do you mean by that?

examplePolite.romaji: sore tte dou iu imi desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それってどういう意味ですか？
examplePolite.english: What do you mean by that?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; どういう #177, 意味 #287)
items.notes: Said sharply, it means 'what's that supposed to mean?'

items.use: Point at something or say the English word, then ask this to get a native speaker to give you the Japanese.
items.kana: にほんごでなんていう
items.politeJa: 日本語で何て言いますか

example.romaji: sore tte nihongo de nante iu?
example.ja: それって日本語で何て言う？
example.english: How do you say that in Japanese?

examplePolite.romaji: sore tte nihongo de nante iimasu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それって日本語で何て言いますか？
examplePolite.english: How do you say that in Japanese?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (multi-word frame; 日本語 #3651)
items.notes: Say eigo instead of nihongo to ask for the English.

blocks.label: Earlier and lately
blocks.rationale: These point back into the past, from a moment ago to long ago, and all fit the same 'sore ... kiita' frame.
blocks.interference: kono aida = one recent occasion; saikin = the recent stretch up to now; mae ni = some earlier time; mukashi = long ago, often for old habits.

items.use: Refers back to something earlier today, anywhere from seconds to a few hours ago.

example.english: I heard that a minute ago.

examplePolite.ja: それはさっき聞きました。
examplePolite.english: I heard that a minute ago.

items.freqNote: さっき #253; formal 先ほど(さきほど) #1337
items.notes: Staff and business speech say sakihodo. sakki is fine with desu/masu.

items.use: Points to one recent past occasion, days or weeks ago (kono aida itta mise = the place we went the other day).

example.english: I heard that the other day.

examplePolite.ja: それはこの間聞きました。
examplePolite.english: I heard that the other day.

items.freqNote: この間 #883; casual こないだ #1644; synonym この前 #800; formal 先日 #1182
items.notes: Casually it is often squeezed to konaida (sore konaida kiita). kono mae means the same, and senjitsu is the formal version. kono aida wa arigatou thanks someone again for last time, and Japanese speakers expect it.

items.use: Covers the recent stretch up to now, for trends, current life and recent news (saikin isogashii).

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa saikin yoku kikimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは最近よく聞きますね。

items.notes: saikin dou? is the stock 'how have you been?'.

items.use: Refers to an earlier time: mae ni (before, once before), mae wa (used to), and a time span + mae for 'ago' (ni-nen mae).

examplePolite.ja: それは前に聞きました。

items.freqNote: 前 #80, all senses including spatial 'front'
items.notes: The same word means 'in front' (see mae / ushiro). -mae ni after a verb has its own card.

items.english: long ago; in the old days
items.use: Frames the distant past and old habits (mukashi wa yoku itta = I used to go a lot). mukashi kara means 'for ages'.

example.english: I used to listen to that a lot.

examplePolite.ja: それは昔よく聞きました。
examplePolite.english: I used to listen to that a lot.

items.notes: mukashi mukashi opens folk tales ('once upon a time').

blocks.label: So far, from now
blocks.rationale: Phrases that place a statement relative to now: up to now, from here on, as things stand, and for a while.
blocks.interference: ima made and ima no tokoro can both mean 'so far'. ima made looks back, and ima made wa with past tense hints that something has changed, while ima no tokoro reports a state that still holds. kore kara looks forward.

items.use: Looks back over the time up to now, often with past tense or experience (ima made ichido mo nai), and in ima made nani shiteta no? (what have you been doing all this time?). kore made is a more formal synonym.

example.romaji: ima made wa daijoubu datta n da kedo.
example.ja: 今までは大丈夫だったんだけど。
example.english: It was fine until now, though.

examplePolite.romaji: ima made wa daijoubu datta n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: 今までは大丈夫だったんですけど。
examplePolite.english: It was fine until now, though.

items.freqNote: 今まで(いままで) #370; formal-leaning これまで #952
items.notes: ima made arigatou is the standard thanks when someone leaves or something ends.

items.use: Points forward from this moment, to something about to start (kore kara dekakeru) or to everything from here on. ima kara means the same for the immediate moment.

examplePolite.ja: これからどうしますか？

items.freqNote: これから #2065 (likely undercounted: the tokenizer can split これ + から); near-synonym 今から(いまから) #972
items.notes: kore kara mo yoroshiku ('I'm counting on you going forward') is a common closing line.

items.use: Hedges a status or plan as true for now but open to change (ima no tokoro yotei nai).

examplePolite.ja: 今のところ大丈夫です。

items.freqNote: 今のところ(いまのところ) #2474
items.notes: toriaezu is 'for now' for a stopgap action, while ima no tokoro describes how things stand.

items.use: Gives a vague stretch of time, short or long, without numbers (shibaraku matte, shibaraku aenai).

example.english: I'll be busy for a while.

examplePolite.ja: しばらく忙しいんです。
examplePolite.english: I'll be busy for a while.

items.freqNote: しばらく #602
items.notes: For 'long time no see', friends say hisashiburi and the polite form is ohisashiburi desu (お久しぶり, #1495). shibaraku desu is an older, formal version: recognise it, but don't produce it.

blocks.label: How you're doing
blocks.rationale: The small-talk status words for checking in and making plans: well, busy, free.
blocks.interference: isogashii and hima are opposites that fill the same casual invitation slot (ashita no yoru, ___?), so learn isogashii first and then swap in hima. Politely, ask oisogashii desu ka? or aitemasu ka?, not hima desu ka?

items.use: The check-in word ('genki?' = how are you doing?) for someone you haven't seen in a while; it also describes good health, good spirits and lively people.

example.english: Long time no see. How have you been?

examplePolite.ja: お久しぶりです。お元気でしたか？
examplePolite.english: It's been a long time. How have you been?

items.notes: When you ask about someone else politely, add o- (ogenki desu ka?); about yourself it stays genki desu.

items.use: Says a person is busy; it is the standard small-talk status (saikin isogashii) and the polite excuse for turning something down.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no yoru wa oisogashii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 明日の夜はお忙しいですか？

items.freqNote: 忙しい #447
items.notes: Describes people, days and workplaces (kyou wa isogashii, isogashii jiki), but not a crowded street: that is hito ga ooi or konderu. Asking about someone else politely, add o-: oisogashii desu ka? The opener oisogashii tokoro sumimasen = sorry to bother you when you're busy.

items.use: Says someone has free time ('hima?' is the standard opener before an invitation) or is bored with nothing to do (hima da naa).

examplePolite.romaji: ashita no yoru nara hima desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 明日の夜なら暇ですよ
examplePolite.english: If it's tomorrow night, I'm free.

items.notes: Asking a coworker, clerk or stranger 'hima desu ka?' can sound like 'got nothing to do?'. To ask politely, say ashita no yoru, aitemasu ka? or jikan arimasu ka?; hima desu is fine about yourself.

blocks.label: Choosing
blocks.rationale: Noun + particle frames for picking among options (deciding, settling, suggesting loosely) plus the frame for when only one option is left.
blocks.interference: koohii ni suru (I'll have coffee), koohii de ii (coffee will do), koohii demo (coffee or something) change only the particle; -demo after a noun is not 'but': it softens here, but can also mean 'even'.

items.english: X will do, X is fine
items.use: After a noun, settles on it as good enough (mizu de ii, kore de ii?) when ordering, checking or accepting something.

examplePolite.ja: コーヒーでいいです。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits で+いい (いい #24)
items.notes: Can sound like 'it'll have to do'; koohii ga ii is the keen choice. To accept a host's offer, say koohii o onegai shimasu; kore de ii desu ka? (is this OK?) is always safe.

items.use: After a noun, picks it from the options (kore ni suru, raishuu ni suru), the standard way to order or settle a choice.

example.ja: じゃあ、コーヒーにする。

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、コーヒーにします。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits に+する (fused ことにする 'decide to' #886)
items.notes: With a verb it becomes koto ni suru: iku koto ni shita = I decided to go.

items.use: After a noun, offers it as one loose example so a suggestion sounds soft (ocha demo, eiga demo), mostly in invitations.

example.english: Want to grab a coffee or something?

examplePolite.ja: コーヒーでも飲みませんか？
examplePolite.english: Shall we grab a coffee or something?

items.freqNote: rank of でも, shared with 'but' and 'even'; an upper bound
items.notes: Three readings after a noun: a loose example in offers and invitations (ocha demo), 'even' (kodomo demo wakaru, sensei demo shiranai), and 'any-' after question words (nandemo ii). Only at the start of a sentence does demo mean 'but'.

items.use: After a plain verb, says it's the only option left (yaru shika nai, matsu shika nai), for resolve or resignation.

example.english: I guess I just have to do it.

examplePolite.ja: もうやるしかないです。
examplePolite.english: I guess I just have to do it.

items.freqNote: rank of fused しかない; also counts plain 'only X' after nouns
items.notes: After a noun it's plain 'only': kore shika nai = this is all there is. More formal: -shika arimasen.

blocks.label: Getting attention
blocks.rationale: Openers that call someone over, point something out, or stop things.
blocks.interference: chotto matte asks someone to wait, while chotto ii? asks for a moment of their time. nee calls a friend; hora points at something.

items.use: Gets a friend's attention before a question, suggestion or piece of news; doubled 'nee nee' is eager.

examplePolite.ja: あの、明日お時間ありますか？
examplePolite.english: Um, do you have time tomorrow?

items.notes: nee opens a sentence; the ending ne closes one.

items.use: Points something out ('hora, mite'), says 'see, I told you', or hands something over.

examplePolite.romaji: hora, mite kudasai. niji desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: ほら、見てください。虹ですよ。

items.notes: It can sound pushy to a superior.

items.use: Asks someone to wait or stop, or holds the floor while you think or check something.
items.politeJa: ちょっと待ってください

example.romaji: chotto matte, hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ちょっと待って、話があるんだけど。
example.english: Wait a sec, there's something I need to tell you.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto matte kudasai, ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっと待ってください、お話があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Just a moment, there's something I'd like to talk to you about.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; 待つ #71 counts every form of matsu; ちょっと #46)
items.notes: matte! on its own is the urgent 'wait!'.

items.use: Opens a request, question or interruption by asking for a moment of someone's time, whether a friend's or a coworker's.

example.romaji: chotto ii? hanashi ga aru n da kedo.
example.ja: ちょっといい？話があるんだけど。
example.english: Got a sec? There's something I need to tell you.

examplePolite.romaji: chotto ii desu ka? ohanashi ga aru n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: ちょっといいですか？お話があるんですけど。
examplePolite.english: Do you have a moment? There's something I'd like to talk to you about.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; ちょっと #46, いい #24)
items.notes: The usual answers are 'un, nani?' or 'ii yo'. To a boss, say chotto yoroshii desu ka.

blocks.label: Buy, use, make
blocks.rationale: Everyday verbs for handling things: buying, using and making them.
blocks.interference: tsukatta (used) and tsukutta (made) differ by one vowel, so they share the kore dare ga ...? frame and are told apart by ear; katte is also the te-form of katsu (win) and of kau 'keep a pet', and the word katte 'selfish / as you like', so context decides.

items.use: Buying anything (X o kau), and nani katta? / doko de katta? is everyday small talk.

examplePolite.romaji: sore, doko de katta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: それ、どこで買ったんですか？

items.notes: Negative is kawanai; homophone kau 飼う = keep a pet.

items.use: Using objects, apps, words, money or time, and tsukatte ii? asks to borrow or use something.

examplePolite.ja: これ、誰が使いましたか？

items.notes: tsukatta (used) and tsukutta (made) differ only in the middle vowel.

items.use: Making, cooking or creating anything — food, plans, friends, even time (jikan o tsukuru).

examplePolite.romaji: kore, dare ga tsukutta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: これ、誰が作ったんですか？

blocks.label: Easy & hard
blocks.rationale: The difficulty scale for tasks and situations, from easy through hard and tough to impossible.
blocks.interference: muzukashii (hard to do or understand), taihen (hard to go through, lots of work) and muri (can't be done) blur together. The shared 'kono shigoto' sentence isolates the nuance, and kantan anchors the easy end.

items.use: Says a task, recipe, explanation or test is easy or simple; kantan ni means 'simply, briefly'.

example.english: This job is easy, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa kantan desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は簡単ですね
examplePolite.english: This job is easy, isn't it?

items.notes: A na-word: before ne or yo it takes da (kantan da ne), and its past is kantan datta, never kantankatta.

items.use: Says something is hard to do or understand (tasks, questions, languages, decisions); chotto muzukashii is also a soft way to say no.

example.english: This job is difficult, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa muzukashii desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は難しいですね
examplePolite.english: This job is difficult, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 難しい #468
items.notes: 'Sore wa chotto muzukashii desu' usually means a polite no, not just 'difficult'.

items.use: Says a situation is tough, a lot of work or a real problem; 'taihen da ne' is the stock sympathy reply to anyone's hard time, and 'taihen!' alone means 'oh no, trouble!'.

example.english: This job is tough, isn't it?

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa taihen desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は大変ですね
examplePolite.english: This job is tough, isn't it?

items.freqNote: 大変 #224; includes the formal 'very' sense
items.notes: In formal speech taihen also means 'very' (taihen moushiwake arimasen).

items.use: Says something is impossible or too much for you; 'muri!' or 'kyou wa muri' is the everyday casual refusal, and muri shinaide means 'don't overdo it'.

example.english: No way we can do this job.

examplePolite.romaji: kono shigoto wa muri desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この仕事は無理ですね
examplePolite.english: No way we can do this job.

items.freqNote: 無理 #217; includes muri suru / muri shinaide
items.notes: Blunt to a superior; chotto muzukashii desu refuses more politely. Everyday casual refusal: ashita? gomen, muri.

blocks.label: Fillers
blocks.rationale: Sounds and words that hold your turn while you think, so a pause doesn't hand it over.
blocks.interference: All five fit the same slot. etto is pure thinking time, ano also softens a request or opens one, maa hedges, nanka makes things vaguer, and nante iu ka hunts for a word.

items.use: Fills the pause while you think of an answer or a word, so you don't go silent.

example.ja: えっと、明日は無理かも。
example.english: Um, let me see... tomorrow might not work.

examplePolite.romaji: etto, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: えっと、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Um, let me see... tomorrow may not be possible.

items.freqNote: えっと #695; えーっと #1373; えーと #5199; ええと #11996, so etto beats the textbook eeto
items.notes: eeto is the slower textbook version; speech mostly uses etto.

items.use: Hesitates before something awkward, or politely gets attention before a question or request ('ano, sumimasen').

examplePolite.romaji: ano, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: あの、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Um... tomorrow may not be possible.

items.freqNote: あの #66 also counts the demonstrative 'that'; the filler-only form あのー is #1320
items.notes: Before a noun it's the J word 'that': ano hito.

items.use: Hedges or half-concedes ('maa, ii ka', oh well, fine), softening an answer you don't want to commit to.

examplePolite.romaji: maa, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: まあ、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Well, tomorrow may not be possible.

items.notes: 'maa maa' means 'so-so' or 'now, now'. Opening a polite answer with maa can sound offhand to a superior. A standalone 'maa!' (oh my!) is a dated feminine exclamation you'll hear in dramas.

items.use: A casual filler that makes what follows vaguer or softer ('nanka, tsukareta', I'm kind of tired).

example.ja: なんか、明日は無理かも。

examplePolite.romaji: nanka, ashita wa muri kamo shiremasen.
examplePolite.ja: なんか、明日は無理かもしれません。
examplePolite.english: Somehow... tomorrow may not be possible.

items.freqNote: the filler なんか is misparsed (#144167); 何か #72 also counts 'something'
items.notes: Overuse sounds young. nanka is also the casual 'something' ('nanka nomu?', want something to drink?) and 'stuff like' ('kore nanka dou?'); only the floating, sentence-opening use is the filler.

items.use: Buys time while you search for the right word mid-sentence.
items.politeJa: 何て言うんでしょうか

example.romaji: nante iu ka, chotto kawatta hito da ne.
example.ja: 何て言うか、ちょっと変わった人だね。
example.english: How should I put it... he's a bit of an odd one.

examplePolite.romaji: nante iu n deshou ka, chotto kawatta hito desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 何て言うんでしょうか、ちょっと変わった人ですね。
examplePolite.english: How should I put it... he's a bit unusual.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (split by the tokenizer; the related っていうか is #948)
items.notes: tte iu ka is different: it means 'or rather', correcting yourself.

blocks.label: First and last
blocks.rationale: Positions in a sequence, going ahead of others, and first-ever experiences. These are the words for explaining steps, taking turns and telling stories.
blocks.interference: saisho and saigo differ only in the ending (sho = start, go = end). hajimete means first-ever, not first in order, and mazu opens a plan. saki ni puts you ahead of someone or something else: mazu tabeyou = let's eat first (step one of a plan), saki ni tabete ii? = can I start eating before you?

items.use: Opens a series of steps or names the top priority (mazu wa ...). Later steps follow with tsugi ni and saigo ni.

examplePolite.ja: まずこれを食べましょう。

items.notes: It can also mean 'almost certainly' (mazu daijoubu, mazu muri). Don't confuse it with mazui (bad, uh-oh): mazu kore = this first; mazui na = uh-oh.

items.use: Names the start of something. saisho ni = first, before anything else; saisho wa = at first, in contrast to later.

example.ja: これ、最初は嫌いだった。
example.english: I didn't like this at first.

examplePolite.ja: これ、最初は嫌いでした。
examplePolite.english: I didn't like this at first.

items.notes: hajime (ni / wa) is a softer synonym.

items.use: Names the end of a sequence or the final one: saigo ni = lastly, saigo no = the last (saigo no hi).

examplePolite.ja: 最後にこれを食べましょう。

items.notes: 'Finally' after a long wait is yatto, not saigo ni.

items.use: Marks a first-ever experience (hajimete kita = my first time here). It is the root of hajimemashite.

example.english: This is my first time eating this.

examplePolite.ja: これ、初めて食べました。
examplePolite.english: This is my first time eating this.

items.freqNote: 初めて #237; kana はじめて #12742; #2670 is 始めて ('starting'), a different word
items.notes: It does not mean first in an order. For 'first, do X' use mazu or saisho ni. nihon wa hajimete? / nihon wa hajimete desu ka? (first time in Japan?) is a stock small-talk question.

items.use: Puts one person or action ahead of another (saki ni itte = go on ahead; saki ni shukudai yaru = I'll do my homework first) or says something is done in advance (saki ni harau = pay up front). Casual speech often drops the ni.

example.english: Mind if I go ahead and start eating?

examplePolite.romaji: saki ni tabete mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 先に食べてもいいですか？
examplePolite.english: Is it all right if I go ahead and start eating?

items.notes: Don't mix it up with sakki (A6, a moment ago): only the double k differs. saki ni kaetta = went home before the others; sakki kaetta = went home a moment ago. 'Before him' is kare yori saki ni, since kare no mae ni usually means 'in front of him'. saki ni itte yo (先に言ってよ) = you should've said so sooner! It sounds the same as saki ni itte (先に行って, go on ahead), so context decides. osaki ni douzo = after you; osaki ni shitsurei shimasu = the set line for leaving work before others.

blocks.label: Price & speed
blocks.rationale: The two everyday scales for errands and plans: what something costs and how early, late, fast or slow it is.
blocks.interference: Antonym pairs get swapped, so learn takai before yasui and hayai before osoi, then mix them; per 11-list-adjectives note 9(d), keep yasui at least 15 items after takai in drill order even though they share a block. takai also means tall or high, and its opposite there is hikui, not yasui.

items.use: Expensive (the daily shopping sense), and also high or tall for buildings, people, voices and levels; the opposite is yasui for price and hikui for height.

examplePolite.ja: このお店、高いですね

items.notes: se ga takai = tall (of a person).

items.use: Says something is cheap or good value (prices, shops, deals); it is the opposite of takai only in the price sense.

examplePolite.ja: このお店、安いですね

items.freqNote: 安い #1315; やすい #1141 is mostly the -yasui suffix (easy to ...), which is not carded
items.notes: It is a different word from the suffix -yasui (easy to ...): tabeyasui = easy to eat.

items.use: Early in time ('mou? hayai!') and fast in speed or progress; it is one word by ear but has two kanji in writing (早い early, 速い fast).

examplePolite.ja: 今日は早いですね

items.freqNote: 早い #396; 速い #2346 (two kanji, one word by ear)
items.notes: The adverb hayaku (quickly, early) is its own item in C.

items.use: Late in time or slow in speed; 'mou osoi' means it's too late now, and 'osoi!' is the complaint to someone who kept you waiting.

examplePolite.ja: 今日は遅いですね

items.notes: 'Late for something' uses the verb okureru (densha ni okureta), not osoi.

blocks.label: Fast, slow, properly, well
blocks.rationale: Everyday manner adverbs that go straight before a verb to say how it's done: speed, care, and whether it works.
blocks.interference: hayaku shite ne (hurry up) and yukkuri de ii yo (no rush) are the opposite pair. yukkuri shite ne on its own means relax, make yourself at home, not 'do it slowly', and the opposite of hayaku in its 'early' sense is osoku. chanto means doing it the right way; umaku means it came out well.

items.use: The adverb form of hayai: before any verb it means fast or early (hayaku kaeru, hayaku okiru), and 'hayaku!' on its own means hurry up.

examplePolite.ja: 早くしてくださいね。

items.freqNote: 早く #144; 速く ('fast') #6275 is counted separately
items.notes: Spoken hayaku covers both 早く (early) and 速く (fast); the sound is the same. To a clerk or coworker, hayaku shite kudasai sounds impatient, so soften it: sumimasen, chotto isoide iru n desu ga... (sorry, I'm in a bit of a hurry).

items.use: A manner adverb for slow, unhurried action: yukkuri de ii (yo) means no rush, take your time, and mou sukoshi yukkuri asks someone to slow down. yukkuri shite ne / yukkuri shitette ne is different: a host's 'relax, make yourself at home'.

examplePolite.ja: ゆっくりでいいですよ。

items.freqNote: ゆっくり #515; set phrase ごゆっくり #1875 counted separately
items.notes: Survival line: mou sukoshi yukkuri hanashite kudasai (please speak a little more slowly), or simply yukkuri onegaishimasu. goyukkuri douzo (enjoy, take your time) is the shop and host set phrase.

items.use: Says something is done the right, responsible way (chanto tabete, chanto kiite), and 'chanto shita hito' is a proper, reliable person.

examplePolite.ja: ちゃんと食べてくださいね。
examplePolite.english: Please make sure you eat properly.

items.notes: kichinto is a stiffer synonym. chanto is fine in polite speech too.

items.use: Says something works out or is done skilfully. It is used mostly in 'umaku iku' (go well) and in negatives that describe trouble (umaku ienai = can't put it well).

examplePolite.ja: 試験、うまくいきましたか？

items.freqNote: rank of うまくいく #761 (うまく行く #10741 and 上手くいく #16573 counted separately); the bare うまく token is only #45903, probably because the tokenizer lemmatises the adverb to うまい #246 (unverified)
items.notes: Learner lifeline: umaku ienai kedo... (I can't put it well, but...).

blocks.label: May and must
blocks.rationale: The permission and obligation ladder on one verb: may, mustn't, must, needn't.
blocks.interference: -nakute mo ii (needn't) gets mistaken for 'mustn't' (-cha dame); anchor both to one verb: kaeranakute mo ii (you don't have to go) vs kaetcha dame (you can't go).

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to ask for or give permission (suwatte mo ii?, tabete ii yo); casual speech often drops mo.

examplePolite.romaji: mou kaette mo ii desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: もう帰ってもいいですか？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits て+も+いい (fused てもいい only #56914); いい #24
items.notes: A refusal usually comes as chotto... rather than a flat dame.

items.use: Contracted -te wa dame, used to forbid or warn against something (sawatcha dame); verbs with -nde take -ja (nonja dame).
items.politeJa: 〜ちゃダメです／〜じゃダメです

examplePolite.ja: まだ帰っちゃダメですよ。

items.freqNote: rank of the contraction ちゃ; ダメ #596, いけない #277 (all uses)
items.notes: -cha dame desu is the friendly version; careful speech uses -te wa dame desu, firm rules -te wa ikemasen, and requests to strangers -naide kudasai.

items.use: Attaches to the -nai stem (ikanakya) for what you've got to do; casual speech usually stops there and leaves off ikenai.

examplePolite.ja: そろそろ帰らなきゃいけませんね。

items.freqNote: tokenizer often splits the contraction, so this undercounts; なきゃいけない #4891, なくちゃ #9360, なければならない #6186
items.notes: -nakucha and -nai to mean the same and are heard too; -nakya is the most common.

items.use: Attaches to the -nai stem to say something isn't necessary (konakute mo ii, ki ni shinakute ii); casual speech drops mo.

example.ja: まだ帰らなくてもいいよ。
example.english: You don't have to go home yet.

examplePolite.romaji: mada kaeranakute mo ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: まだ帰らなくてもいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: You don't have to go home yet.

items.freqNote: rank of fused なくてもいい; split tokens not counted, so likely an undercount
items.notes: It's the opposite of -nakya: 'don't have to', never 'mustn't'.

blocks.label: Wrong, stuck, angry
blocks.rationale: Reactions when something's off: it's different or wrong, I'm in a bind, I made a mistake, someone's angry about it.
blocks.interference: chigau is a state (that's wrong / different) and machigaeru an act (I got it wrong): bangou chigau yo vs bangou machigaeta. okoru is also an act (getting angry), so 'she's angry' is okotteru and 'I got told off' is the passive okorareta; it sounds the same as okoru 'happen'.

items.use: The everyday one-word 'no, that's not it' for correcting someone (far more common than iie in conversation) and the verb for being different (X to chigau); a flat chigau! can sound blunt, so soften with chotto chigau kamo.

examplePolite.ja: 電話番号が違いますよ。

items.freqNote: 違う #94
items.notes: A verb, not an adjective: polite chigaimasu, never *chigai desu.

items.english: be in a bind; be stuck
items.use: Saying a situation causes you trouble, which is the indirect way to object or ask for help (komatta na, komaru n desu kedo).

example.english: That'd be a bit of a problem.

examplePolite.ja: それはちょっと困ります。
examplePolite.english: That would be a bit of a problem for me.

items.notes: komatta = 'I'm stuck (now)'; the past describes the current state.

items.use: Getting something wrong yourself — a number, a word, the way — and the learner's main repair verb (machigaeta, gomen).

example.english: I got the phone number wrong.

examplePolite.ja: 電話番号を間違えました。
examplePolite.english: I got the phone number wrong.

items.freqNote: 間違える #956; intransitive 間違う #711 and noun 間違い #1085 counted separately
items.notes: machigatteru = 'is wrong' (a state); machigaeta = 'I made the mistake'.

items.use: Says someone gets angry: the person you're angry at takes ni (tomodachi ni okotta), and the person you tell off takes o (kodomo o okoru); 'is angry' right now is okotteru, and the passive okorareta means 'got told off'.

examplePolite.ja: まだ怒ってるんですか？

items.freqNote: 怒る #381; homophone 起こる (happen) #936 listed separately
items.notes: okoranaide = don't be mad; sugu okoru = gets angry easily. Homophone 起こる 'happen' is a separate verb.

blocks.label: How sure
blocks.rationale: The certainty dial runs from a soft guess to full commitment, and 'of course' takes the point for granted.
blocks.interference: tabun, kitto and zettai share one frame (___ daijoubu da yo), so only the strength changes. kitto is mostly for confident guesses about others or the future, and rarely for your own firm plans.

items.use: The default hedge: it commits softly to any claim and is often closed with deshou, kamo or to omou.

examplePolite.ja: 多分大丈夫ですよ。

items.freqNote: 多分 #1323 and kana たぶん #1598 are counted separately, so real use is well above either rank
items.notes: osoraku is the stiffer, more formal 'probably'; tabun is fine in desu/masu speech.

items.use: A confident guess about something you can't check, such as someone else's feelings, an outcome or the future.

examplePolite.ja: きっと大丈夫ですよ。

items.notes: To commit to your own plan, say zettai iku (or kanarazu iku); kitto iku sounds like a heartfelt promise rather than a plan. kitto kite ne (be sure to come) is fine.

items.use: The strongest commitment either way, as in zettai iku (definitely going) and zettai dame (absolutely not). It is constant in promises and refusals.

examplePolite.ja: 絶対大丈夫ですよ。

items.notes: zettai ni is the same word; casual speech usually drops the ni. For polite commitments, kanarazu (without fail) is safer, but it doesn't do 'never' the way zettai ikanai does.

items.use: Says something goes without saying, either before a statement or alone as a warm 'of course!' reply.

examplePolite.ja: もちろん行きますよ。

items.freqNote: もちろん #264 (kanji 勿論 #46156)
items.notes: As a reply to a request, mochiron! means 'sure, happy to'.

blocks.label: Together, alone, as is, without asking
blocks.rationale: Set phrases that give the circumstances of an action (with others, by yourself, leaving things as they are, or without asking anyone), and all fit before a verb like iku.
blocks.interference: issho ni and hitori de share the casual question frame (___ iku?). hitori de is about company and katte ni is about permission: hitori de itchatta (went alone) vs katte ni itchatta (went off without asking). For things that happen by themselves it's katte ni (doa ga katte ni shimatta), not hitori de, which is for people. kono mama is the current situation, often 'if things go on like this'; sono mama is that thing as it stands, or carrying straight on without a further step.

items.use: Says an action is shared, with 'X to issho ni' meaning with X. It is the core of every invitation (issho ni ikou, issho ni iku?).

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come along?

items.notes: issho without ni means 'the same': issho da ne = same here. Polite invitations use -masen ka (issho ni ikimasen ka); casual can be iku? or ikanai?

items.use: Says you do something on your own, either without company or without help (hitori de dekiru).

examplePolite.ja: 一人で行きますか？

items.freqNote: 一人で #913; kana ひとりで #7320 and 独りで #9339 counted separately
items.notes: Two people is futari de.

items.use: Keeps the current situation unchanged, as in 'kono mama de ii' (fine like this) and 'kono mama ja dame' (can't go on like this).

examplePolite.romaji: kono mama de ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: このままでいいですよ。

items.notes: kono mama ja... warns where things are heading if nothing changes.

items.english: as is; just like that; straight on
items.use: Leaves something as it is (sono mama de ii = leave it as is, no need to change anything), or carries straight on without a further step (sono mama kaetta = went straight home; sono mama mattete = just wait there).

examplePolite.ja: そのまま帰りました。

items.notes: To a clerk offering a bag or wrapping, sono mama de ii desu means 'it's fine as it is'. Said to a person, sono mama de ii also reassures: you're fine as you are. sono mama omachi kudasai (please hold) is the fixed phone and shop line.

items.english: without asking; as one pleases; by itself (automatically)
items.use: Goes before a verb to say something was done without asking or permission (katte ni kimeta, katte ni tabeta), or that it happened by itself with nobody doing it (doa ga katte ni shimatta). Mostly it's a complaint, but with -te ii it gives free rein (katte ni tabete ii yo = help yourself), and turned on yourself it's an apology (katte ni tsukatte gomen / sumimasen = sorry for using it without asking).

example.english: Don't go deciding things without asking me!

examplePolite.ja: 勝手に決めないでください。
examplePolite.english: Please don't decide things without asking.

items.freqNote: 勝手に #438; bare 勝手 #756
items.notes: katte ni shite! on its own is a huffy 'suit yourself'. By ear it matches katte from kau (buy), pitch included, so only the ni tells them apart: katte kita (went and bought it) vs katte ni kita (came without being asked). katte from katsu (win) has a different pitch.

blocks.label: Let's, suggestions & plans
blocks.rationale: The volitional -ou family for inviting and offering, the softer -nai? invitation and -tara? advice, then tsumori and -ou to omou for your own plans.
blocks.interference: -ou proposes outright, -ou ka asks for agreement or offers help, and -nai? leaves room to say no; -tara? advises the listener rather than inviting them. tsumori is a settled plan, while -ou to omou is a decision you're still making.

items.use: The volitional form proposes doing something together (ikou, tabeyou, shiyou). Godan verbs change the final u to ou (iku → ikou, kaeru → kaerou); ichidan verbs swap ru for you (taberu → tabeyou).

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きましょう

items.freqNote: tokenizer folds the volitional into the verb; rank of いこう (ikou) alone
items.notes: The irregulars are suru → shiyou and kuru → koyou.

items.use: Asks whether to do something together, or offers to do it for the listener (mado akeyou ka? = shall I open the window?).

example.english: Want me to come with you?

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きましょうか？

items.freqNote: casual 行こうか not found (volitional folded into verb); rank of polite ましょうか
items.notes: With a falling tone it can be self-directed: jaa, kaerou ka (well, guess I'll head home).

items.use: Invites the listener with a rising negative question (issho ni ikanai?), which leaves room to decline. It is softer than -ou.

examplePolite.ja: 一緒に行きませんか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like to come along?

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (ない #43 merges all negation; ませんか #111176 tokenizer-split)
items.notes: The rising tone is what makes it an invitation; flat ikanai just means 'I'm not going.'

items.use: Suggests, with a rising tone, something the listener could do for their own good (yasundara?, kiite mitara?). The fuller form is -tara dou?. -ba? (sureba?) is curter and can sound dismissive (katte ni sureba? = suit yourself).

example.english: Why don't you take a break?

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと休んだらどうですか
examplePolite.english: Why don't you take a little break?

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; rank of たら alone
items.notes: With superiors -tara dou desu ka can sound pushy; -ta hou ga ii kamo is gentler.

items.use: States a plan you've already decided on. It attaches to the plain form (iku tsumori, ikanai tsumori).

example.ja: 今日は早く寝るつもり
example.english: I'm planning to go to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hayaku neru tsumori desu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は早く寝るつもりです
examplePolite.english: I plan to go to bed early tonight.

items.freqNote: #208 つもり
items.notes: After a past verb it means 'I thought I had': itta tsumori = I thought I'd said it. Asking others about their tsumori can sound like a challenge (dou iu tsumori? = what do you think you're doing?), so ask about plans with ...suru no? / ...n desu ka. For loose plans, -ou to omotteru is softer.

items.use: Shares a plan you're deciding on now or are still considering. It is softer than tsumori.

example.romaji: kyou wa hayaku neyou to omou
example.ja: 今日は早く寝ようと思う
example.english: I think I'll go to bed early tonight.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hayaku neyou to omoimasu
examplePolite.ja: 今日は早く寝ようと思います
examplePolite.english: I think I'll go to bed early tonight.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (volitional folded into verb; 思う #33 covers all uses)
items.notes: Polite speech keeps the plain volitional (neyou to omoimasu, never *nemashou to omoimasu); -ou to omotteru = I've been thinking of it.

blocks.label: Expected or not
blocks.rationale: Reactions to how things match expectations: confirmed, admirably confirmed, flatly refused, or tentatively suspected.
blocks.interference: yappari (turned out as I thought) and sasuga (praise: just what you'd expect of them) share '___ kenta da ne', but yappari kenta da ne can be a sigh (late again) while sasuga kenta da ne is praise. masaka (surely not!) and moshikashite (could it be?) share '___ wasureta no?'.

items.use: Confirms that something turned out as you thought, restates a settled opinion (yappari natsu wa biiru da ne = summer means beer, after all), or marks a change of mind (yappari yameru = actually, I'll skip it).

example.english: Typical Kenta, just as I thought.

examplePolite.ja: やっぱり健太さんですね。
examplePolite.english: Typical Kenta, just as I thought.

items.freqNote: やっぱり #150; clipped やっぱ #576; formal やはり #979
items.notes: Casual speech clips it to yappa. yahari is the formal, written-leaning form (meetings, news); in desu/masu speech yappari is normal.

items.english: impressive; as expected (of you); that's X for you
items.use: Praise that someone lives up to their reputation, either alone ('sasuga!') or as 'sasuga X da ne'. With ni, it means 'understandably, as you'd expect': sasuga ni tsukareta (I'm tired, understandably), sasuga ni sore wa muri (that's really too much).

examplePolite.ja: さすが健太さんですね。
examplePolite.english: Just what you'd expect from Kenta.

items.freqNote: さすが #463; さすがに #1098 counted separately
items.notes: Bare sasuga is praise; for bad news you expected, use yappari. sasuga ni is the separate 'understandably, even so' sense. Said flatly, sasuga da ne can be sarcastic.

items.use: Expresses disbelief, either alone as 'no way!' or to open a guess you hope is wrong (masaka ... ja nai yo ne).

examplePolite.ja: まさか忘れたんですか？

items.notes: masaka! alone is a full reaction: no way!

items.use: Floats a guess or a tentative question, usually ending in no?, kana or kamo.

example.english: Did you forget, by any chance?

examplePolite.ja: もしかして忘れたんですか？
examplePolite.english: Did you forget, by any chance?

items.freqNote: もしかして #431; variant もしかしたら #988 counted separately
items.notes: moshikashitara is the 'if by any chance' variant (moshikashitara kuru kamo). Polite-safe opener for a sensitive guess: moshikashite, tanaka san desu ka? (Are you Mr. Tanaka, by any chance?)

blocks.label: Glad, let down, worried
blocks.rationale: Your own emotional reactions to news, to what's coming and to being noticed: glad, disappointed, looking forward, scared, worried, embarrassed.
blocks.interference: kowai (scared) and shinpai (worried) share the exam-results sentence so only the feeling changes, and ureshii and zannen are paired replies to news. kowai also sounds like kawaii (cute, earlier block): three beats against four. tanoshimi (looking forward to it) is not tanoshii (fun, earlier block): say ryokou, tanoshimi before the trip and ryokou, tanoshikatta after it. hazukashii (embarrassed, shy) and ureshii are the two ways to take a compliment, bashful against pleased. hazukashii is one beat away from muzukashii (difficult, earlier block): ha-zu-ka-shii vs mu-zu-ka-shii, so add it once muzukashii is solid, then drill chotto hazukashii against chotto muzukashii and listen for ha- vs mu-.

items.use: Says you are glad about something specific (a gift, news, a compliment), either as 'ureshii!' or as -te ureshii; it describes your own feeling, not a general state of happiness.

examplePolite.ja: それはうれしいです

items.notes: 'Happy in life' is shiawase; ureshii is for one good thing that happened. About someone else, say ureshisou (looks happy).

items.use: The reaction to disappointing news, a cancellation or a missed chance ('zannen!', 'sore wa zannen'), and the base of -te zannen (it's a shame that ...: aenakute zannen = shame we couldn't meet).

examplePolite.ja: それは残念ですね

items.notes: Use it for let-downs; for real hardship the sympathy line is taihen da ne. It is not an apology: for 'I'm sorry' use gomen or sumimasen.

items.use: Says something is scary or that you are scared (films, heights, people, the future); about a strict person it means 'intimidating'.

example.english: I'm scared to see my exam results.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no kekka ga kowai desu
examplePolite.ja: 試験の結果が怖いです
examplePolite.english: I'm scared to see my exam results.

items.notes: The same word covers 'scary' (the thing) and 'scared' (you); context decides.

items.use: Says you are worried about someone or something (X ga shinpai), and shinpai shinaide means 'don't worry'; it is na-class even though it ends in -ai.

example.english: I'm worried about my exam results.

examplePolite.romaji: shiken no kekka ga shinpai desu
examplePolite.ja: 試験の結果が心配です
examplePolite.english: I'm worried about my exam results.

items.freqNote: 心配 #210; includes the verb shinpai suru
items.notes: Also a verb, shinpai suru; the form you'll use most is shinpai shinaide (don't worry).

items.use: Says you're looking forward to something coming up, as a one-word reply to any plan (tanoshimi!) or X ga tanoshimi; it is a noun, so it takes da / desu, and tanoshimi ni shiteru is the fuller 'I'm looking forward to it'.

examplePolite.ja: 旅行、楽しみですね
examplePolite.english: I'm looking forward to the trip.

items.freqNote: 楽しみ #869
items.notes: Politely, tanoshimi ni shitemasu is the set phrase for 'I'm looking forward to it'.

items.use: Says you feel embarrassed or shy, or that something is embarrassing: after a mistake, at a compliment or when being watched ('hazukashii!', hazukashii kara yamete = stop, it's embarrassing).

example.ja: ちょっと恥ずかしいな

examplePolite.ja: ちょっと恥ずかしいです

items.freqNote: 恥ずかしい #672
items.notes: About someone else or what they did, it is a criticism ('embarrassing, shameful'). For how someone else feels, say hazukashisou (looks embarrassed).

blocks.label: When, before, after, while
blocks.rationale: Clauses that time one action against another: when, before, after and at the same time.
blocks.interference: Each takes a different verb form: -mae ni is always non-past (deru mae ni); -toki takes a plain verb in either tense, and the tense shows the order (deru toki = as I leave, deta toki = once I'd left); -te kara takes the -te form (dete kara); -nagara takes the masu-stem, with one person doing both actions (arukinagara).

items.use: Makes a 'when X' clause after a plain verb, an adjective, or noun + no (kodomo no toki). The verb's tense shows whether X has happened yet.

example.english: I'll call you when I leave.

examplePolite.ja: 出るとき電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you when I leave.

items.freqNote: 時(とき) #293, includes the noun 'time'; kana とき #633
items.notes: The verb before toki stays plain even in polite speech. Tense sets the order: iku toki katta = bought it on the way there; itta toki katta = bought it there. For 'once X happens, then Y', use -tara: tsuitara denwa suru.

items.use: Means 'before X' after a dictionary-form verb or noun + no (neru mae ni, shigoto no mae ni). The verb stays non-past even when talking about the past.

example.romaji: deru mae ni denwa suru ne.
example.english: I'll call you before I leave.

examplePolite.romaji: deru mae ni denwa shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 出る前に電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you before I leave.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits 前に (#183446 is the tail floor); 前 #80 covers every sense incl. spatial 'front'. No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: Always use the dictionary form: deru mae ni, never deta mae ni.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form to put one action after another (tabete kara deru) or to mark a starting point, 'since' (nihon ni kite kara).

example.english: I'll call you after I leave.

examplePolite.ja: 出てから電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you after I leave.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits; から #14 counts every kara (mostly 'because / from'). No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: -ta ato de (deta ato de) is the other 'after' and means much the same here.

items.use: Joins two actions one person does at once, using the masu-stem (arukinagara hanasu). The main action comes last.

example.romaji: eki made arukinagara denwa suru ne.
example.ja: 駅まで歩きながら電話するね。
example.english: I'll call you on my walk to the station.

examplePolite.romaji: eki made arukinagara denwa shimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 駅まで歩きながら電話しますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll call you on my walk to the station.

items.notes: It only works with one person. 'While you were out' needs -aida or -toki.

blocks.label: Start, stop, keep at it
blocks.rationale: Phases of an activity — something starting (hajimaru) or you starting it (hajimeru), its ending, quitting it — plus ganbaru, the effort of keeping at it.
blocks.interference: owatta = it finished (shigoto owatta, done for the day) while yameta = someone stopped or quit (shigoto yameta, quit the job); hajimaru (it starts, ga) vs hajimeru (you start it, o): eiga ga hajimaru / shigoto o hajimeru.

items.use: Starting an activity, hobby, job or meeting (X o hajimeru), and hajimeyou means 'let's start'.

examplePolite.ja: 最近ヨガを始めました。

items.freqNote: 始める #330; intransitive 始まる #435 separately
items.notes: Transitive; the thing itself starting is hajimaru (jugyou ga hajimaru).

items.use: Says an event, class, show or season starts, with it marked by ga; starting something yourself is hajimeru with o.

examplePolite.ja: 何時から始まりますか？

items.freqNote: 始まる #435
items.notes: mou hajimatteru = it's already started.

items.use: An activity coming to an end (shigoto owatta?), and owatta! also announces that your own task is done.

example.english: Are you done with work yet?

examplePolite.ja: もう仕事は終わりましたか？

items.freqNote: 終わる #190
items.notes: Slang owatta... = 'I'm doomed' (shiken owatta = I bombed the exam); that sense is slang, not 'it finished'.

items.use: Stopping an action, giving up a habit or plan, and quitting a job or school (X o yameru), with yamete! meaning 'stop it!'

example.english: Did you already quit your job?

examplePolite.ja: もう仕事を辞めましたか？
examplePolite.english: Have you already quit your job?

items.freqNote: やめる #117 (kana); 辞める (quit a job) #604 separately
items.notes: Written 辞める for quitting a job, やめる for stopping an action; one word by ear.

items.use: Putting in effort or holding out (ganbaru, ganbatta), and ganbarimasu is a standard polite promise to do your best.

examplePolite.ja: 次は頑張ります。
examplePolite.english: I'll do my best next time.

items.freqNote: 頑張る #235; lexicalized 頑張って #736 and 頑張れ #1637 counted separately
items.notes: The bare encouragement ganbatte is drilled as a formula among the social phrases.

blocks.label: Becoming
blocks.rationale: Change-of-state frames on naru and suru: something becomes X, someone makes it X, a skill or habit gradually comes about.
blocks.interference: kami mijikaku natta (it got short) vs kami mijikaku shita (I made it short) differ only in naru vs suru; -you ni naru attaches to verbs, -ku naru to adjectives.

items.use: Marks a change of state: i-adjectives take -ku naru (samuku naru), na-adjectives and nouns take ni naru (genki ni naru, isha ni naru).

examplePolite.ja: 髪、短くなりましたね。

items.freqNote: rank of なる (all uses; change-of-state dominant)
items.notes: ii -> yoku naru: yoku natta = it got better.

items.use: Makes something X on purpose: i-adjectives take -ku suru (yasuku suru, hayaku shite), na-adjectives take ni suru (shizuka ni shite), often as a -te request.

example.english: I got my hair cut short.

examplePolite.ja: 髪、短くしました。
examplePolite.english: I got my hair cut short.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; する #15 counts all doing
items.notes: Common as a request: hayaku shite (hurry up), shizuka ni shite (keep it down). Na-adjective ni suru isn't the choosing ni suru: kirei ni suru = tidy it up, koohii ni suru = I'll have coffee.

items.use: After a plain verb, often a potential, marks a gradual change in ability or habit (hanaseru you ni natta, hayaku okiru you ni natta).

example.ja: ちょっと話せるようになった。
example.english: I can speak a little now.

examplePolite.ja: 少し話せるようになりました。
examplePolite.english: I can speak a little now.

items.freqNote: rank of fused ようになる
items.notes: It implies change over time; for losing an ability say -naku natta (taberarenaku natta).

blocks.label: Seems / I heard
blocks.rationale: Endings that show where your information comes from: what you see, what you infer, and what you heard. All four share one base sentence.
blocks.interference: -sou is how something looks right now. mitai is the everyday 'seems', from what you see or from what you've heard; rashii and tte clearly mark it as secondhand. Polite hearsay oishii sou desu is easy to confuse with oishisou desu (looks tasty).

items.use: Says how something looks right now, before you know for sure (oishisou). On verb stems it means something is about to happen (furisou = looks like rain).

example.ja: このケーキおいしそう

examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、おいしそうですね
examplePolite.english: This cake looks delicious, doesn't it?

items.freqNote: tokenizer glues -sou to stems; rank of おいしそう alone (なさそう #2362; bare そう #31 is mostly 'so')
items.notes: It attaches to the stem (oishii → oishisou); the irregulars are ii → yosasou and nai → nasasou. It is not for what's plainly visible: a red car is akai, not *akasou. kawaisou means 'poor thing', not 'looks cute'.

items.use: Says something seems so, either from what you see yourself (dare mo inai mitai) or from what you've heard (oishii mitai da yo). It is the everyday catch-all; rashii is a bit more detached. It also means 'like a' (kodomo mitai, kodomo mitai na hito).

example.ja: このケーキおいしいみたい
example.english: This cake seems to be good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki, oishii mitai desu yo
examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、おいしいみたいですよ
examplePolite.english: This cake's supposed to be good.

items.freqNote: #99 みたい (みたいな #951)
items.notes: No da before it: ame mitai, not *ame da mitai.

items.use: Ends a sentence to pass on what someone said or what you heard (ashita ame da tte). It attaches to the plain form and keeps da after nouns.

example.ja: このケーキおいしいって
example.english: They say this cake is good.

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki, oishii sou desu yo
examplePolite.ja: このケーキ、おいしいそうですよ
examplePolite.english: I hear this cake is good.

items.freqNote: rank of って, which merges quotative and topic uses
items.notes: Polite oishii sou desu (I hear it's good) and oishisou desu (it looks good) differ only in the i. Also very common: oishii tte kikimashita (I heard it's good).

items.use: Passes on secondhand information you believe but didn't witness, with a little more distance than mitai or tte. No da after nouns (ame rashii).

example.ja: このケーキおいしいらしい

examplePolite.romaji: kono keeki wa oishii rashii desu
examplePolite.ja: このケーキはおいしいらしいです

items.freqNote: #218 らしい
items.notes: Directly after a noun it can instead mean 'typical of' (otokorashii = manly).

blocks.label: Speaker-marking enders
blocks.rationale: Variants of yo and ne that you'll hear constantly from friends and in dramas, each marking the speaker as young, male, rough, feminine or from Kansai. Mid-sentence sa is fine in moderation and yo na is normal if you're a man; zo and the rising wa are mostly for recognising, not copying.
blocks.interference: zo and wa both take the place of yo: zo pushes, falling wa just announces your own move or reaction, and rising wa is the feminine one. sa fills pauses inside a sentence the way mid-sentence ne does, and yo na is simply a masculine yo ne.

items.use: Dropped after a phrase to hold the listener's attention while you talk (ano sa = hey, listen; kinou sa, ...). Both genders use it, younger speakers especially. At the end of a sentence it sounds offhand and leans masculine (nantoka naru sa = eh, it'll work out).

example.romaji: kinou sa, tanaka-san ni atta n da
example.ja: 昨日さ、田中さんに会ったんだ
example.english: So yesterday, I ran into Tanaka-san.

examplePolite.romaji: kinou desu ne, tanaka-san ni atta n desu yo
examplePolite.ja: 昨日ですね、田中さんに会ったんですよ
examplePolite.english: So yesterday, I ran into Tanaka-san.

items.freqNote: #88 さ, which may also count the noun suffix -sa split off words like 優しさ/大切さ (not found whole), so treat as an upper bound; さあ 'well' #263 is separate
items.notes: It replaces da, never follows it (sou sa, not *sou da sa). Tacked onto every phrase it sounds sloppy; mid-sentence ne does the same job more softly.

items.use: The masculine counterpart of yo ne. It checks or agrees with something you both believe (sou da yo na = yeah, exactly). Men say it all the time with friends; women mostly say yo ne.

examplePolite.romaji: ashita wa yasumi desu yo ne?
examplePolite.ja: 明日は休みですよね？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — よな #12379 undercounts (tokenizer splits)
items.notes: Said to yourself, it's a rueful 'yeah, I guess' (muri da yo na...). Polite speech has only desu yo ne, so the gender difference disappears.

items.english: I'll..., then (falling, announcing) / soft assertion (rising, fem)
items.use: Two endings that sound alike. Said falling, it announces your own decision or reaction (jaa, iku wa; muri da wa); it is Kansai, gender-neutral and now common among young people everywhere. Said rising, it is the soft feminine assertion of older women and drama characters, dated in real Tokyo speech.

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、行きますね

items.freqNote: #75 わ, which merges rising (feminine) and falling (Kansai / neutral) wa (わよ #489, わね #647)
items.notes: Polite speech drops it (jaa, ikimasu ne; muri desu ne), though Kansai speakers keep it (ikimasu wa). It is unrelated to the topic particle wa (kore wa). Record and drill only the falling wa; the rising one is the feminine wa.

items.use: A forceful masculine yo for warnings, rallying a group and announcements (abunai zo!, iku zo!). You hear it constantly from fathers, coaches, bosses and drama heroes; recognise it, but say yo.

examplePolite.ja: じゃあ、行きますよ

items.notes: Pepping yourself up (yoshi, ganbaru zo) is the mildest use, and women say that too. ze (ikou ze, yatta ze) is its swaggering cousin, always aimed at a buddy and never said to yourself; most men only say it jokingly.

blocks.label: Not at all / not much
blocks.rationale: The negative-degree scale: each sets how strong a 'no' is before a negative verb or adjective, from zenzen 'not at all' to sonna ni 'not that much'. nakanaka adds 'just won't', for things that are slow or hard to make happen.
blocks.interference: zenzen means 'not at all', hotondo 'hardly' and anmari 'not very'. sonna ni ('not that …') measures against a degree already in the air, either what someone said or what you'd expect, so it often answers a worry or a claim; anmari just rates the thing as low. nakanaka is about time and effort, not amount: nakanaka konai = it's taking ages, zenzen konai = it isn't coming at all. Without a negative, hotondo flips to 'almost all', sonna ni to 'so much' and nakanaka to 'pretty, more than expected' (nakanaka ii is close to kekkou ii but sounds like a verdict).

items.use: Means 'not at all' before a negative verb or adjective. With a few words like daijoubu, ii, heiki and chigau it means 'totally' (zenzen daijoubu, zenzen chigau).

example.english: I don't get it at all.

examplePolite.ja: 意味が全然わかりません
examplePolite.english: I have no idea what it means.

items.notes: 'Zenzen ii' or 'zenzen daijoubu (desu)' means 'totally fine' and is the stock reply to an apology ('no worries at all'). It's heard all the time, in desu/masu speech too, though sticklers object. zenzen + other positive adjectives (zenzen oishii) is slangy, so don't produce it. imi wakannai on its own is also a casual 'that makes no sense'.

items.use: Means 'not very / not much' before a negative. It is the soft, hedged no, gentler than zenzen.

example.ja: 意味あんまりわかんない

examplePolite.ja: 意味があまりわかりません
examplePolite.english: I don't really get what it means.

items.freqNote: あんまり #603; the neutral/polite form あまり #871
items.notes: 'Anmari…' said alone, trailing off, is a polite 'not really'. Without a negative it means 'too much': anmari da yo! = that's going too far; amari ni takakute kaenakatta = it was so expensive I couldn't buy it. For 'not that …' (sonna ni warukunai), see sonna ni.

items.use: Before a negative it means 'hardly / barely' (hotondo nai). With a positive it means 'almost all' (hotondo owatta).

example.ja: 意味ほとんどわかんない

examplePolite.ja: 意味がほとんどわかりません
examplePolite.english: I barely understand what it means.

items.notes: Its meaning flips with the verb: hotondo shitteru = know almost all, hotondo shiranai = know hardly any. As a noun: hotondo no hito = most people; hotondo ga = most of them.

items.use: Goes before a negative to say 'not as much as you'd think' (sonna ni warukunai = not that bad). Without a negative it means 'so much' (sonna ni tabeta no? = you ate that much?). Said alone, 'e, sonna ni?' reacts to an amount: 'what, that much?', usually surprise, sometimes doubt.

examplePolite.ja: そんなに悪くないですよ

items.notes: konna ni ('this much', about what's here) and anna ni ('that much', about something you both remember) work the same way: konna ni takusan iranai = I don't need this many; anna ni ganbatta noni = after all that effort. anmari can't do the 'not as much as you imply' job.

items.use: With a negative it means something just won't happen despite trying or waiting, or is taking ages (nakanaka konai, nakanaka oboerarenai, nakanaka umaku ikanai). Before an adjective it means 'pretty, more than expected' (nakanaka ii, nakanaka muzukashii).

example.ja: バス、なかなか来ないね
example.english: The bus is taking forever, huh.

examplePolite.ja: バス、なかなか来ませんね
examplePolite.english: The bus is taking a while, isn't it.

items.freqNote: kana spelling; rank covers both senses (中々 is #54755)
items.notes: Used as praise, it sounds like you're grading the thing. To a boss, or to the person who cooked, say hontou ni or sugoku instead.

blocks.label: Something, someone
blocks.rationale: Question word + ka = some-, used to ask whether rather than what.
blocks.interference: nanika atta? asks whether anything happened (answer un / uun); nani ga atta? asks what happened (answer with the thing).

items.use: Asks whether there is something (nanika atta?) or offers something unspecified (nanika nomu?); in fast speech it becomes nanka.

examplePolite.ja: 何かあったんですか？

items.notes: Casually most people say nanka: nanka atta no? The same nanka is also a filler (G).

items.use: An unspecified person: dareka kita? asks whether anyone came, while dare ga kita? asks who came.

examplePolite.ja: さっき誰か来ましたか？

items.use: An unspecified place, often with the particle after it dropped (dokoka iku?); doko iku? would ask where.

examplePolite.ja: どこか行くんですか？

items.notes: Casually dokoka is said dokka (どっか #788); use dokoka in polite speech.

items.use: An unspecified time, mostly for future wishes and loose plans (itsuka ikitai, itsuka mata).

examplePolite.ja: いつか行きたいですね。

items.freqNote: ５日 read いつか #3202 and 五日 #43449 counted separately
items.notes: itsuka also means 'the fifth (day)'; context separates them.

blocks.label: Comfort and cheer
blocks.rationale: What you say back to someone's news: relief, a shrug, encouragement, denying a put-down, and congratulations.
blocks.interference: yokatta looks like a past tense but is relief you feel right now; it says you're glad, while omedetou congratulates the person (people often say both). shouganai accepts a bad outcome, while sonna koto nai rejects a negative claim.

items.use: Relief or gladness at an outcome ('yokatta, ma ni atta'). About someone else's news, it means 'I'm glad for you'.

example.english: Phew, I made it in time!

examplePolite.ja: それはよかったですね！
examplePolite.english: Oh, I'm so glad to hear that!

items.freqNote: the tokenizer reduces よかった to its dictionary form よい #120 (いい #24 holds the present tense)
items.notes: It's the past of ii; *iikatta doesn't exist.

items.use: Accepts a setback you can't change and moves on; it also means 'oh well, if I must' when you give in.

example.ja: しょうがない、また明日行こう。
example.english: Oh well, let's go again tomorrow.

examplePolite.romaji: shouganai desu ne, mata ashita ikimashou.
examplePolite.ja: しょうがないですね、また明日行きましょう。
examplePolite.english: It can't be helped. Let's go again tomorrow.

items.freqNote: しょうがない #999; 仕方ない #1770; しかたない #1845
items.notes: shikatanai (or shikata ga nai) means the same and sounds slightly more formal; shaanai is the slangy version.

items.use: Encourages someone before or during any effort, from an exam to a long shift. The usual reply is 'un, ganbaru'.

examplePolite.ja: 明日の試験、頑張ってください。

items.freqNote: 頑張って #736; 頑張る #235; 頑張れ #1637
items.notes: Said to a boss, it can sound a little presumptuous. To someone already struggling, muri shinaide (don't overdo it) is kinder.

items.use: Brushes off a compliment ('your Japanese is so good!'), or reassures someone who's putting themselves down.

examplePolite.romaji: e, sonna koto nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: え、そんなことないですよ。

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement (the tokenizer splits the phrase)
items.notes: In polite speech you also hear 'sonna koto arimasen'.

items.use: Congratulates someone on good news, a birthday or the new year. The occasion goes in front: tanjoubi omedetou.
items.politeJa: おめでとうございます

example.ja: 結婚するんだ！おめでとう！

examplePolite.romaji: kekkon suru n desu ka. omedetou gozaimasu!
examplePolite.ja: 結婚するんですか。おめでとうございます！

items.freqNote: おめでとう #774; polite おめでとうございます #1249
items.notes: For the new year, say akemashite omedetou (gozaimasu). It often comes with yokatta: yokatta ne, omedetou!

blocks.label: Depends / without / instead / for / so that
blocks.rationale: Linkers that do the job of an English preposition or 'so that': depends on X, without doing X, instead of X, in order to / for X, so that (not) X.
blocks.interference: -naide (without) vs -nakute (because not). -naide and -kawari ni both come out as 'instead of': -naide follows verbs only and also means 'without' (kasa motanaide deta, where kawari ni can't go), while kawari ni also follows nouns (koohii no kawari ni ocha) and can mean 'in return' (oshiete kureru kawari ni ogoru; sentence-initial sono kawari = 'but in return'). -tame ni (purpose, an action you choose) vs -you ni (so that): after potentials and verbs you don't control only you ni sounds right (hanaseru you ni, maniau you ni, not hanaseru tame ni); after -nai, you ni is the everyday choice (wasurenai you ni) and -nai tame ni sounds stiff. Listen around it: noun + no you ni is 'like' (yume no you ni), itta you ni is 'like I said', and you ni naru / you ni iu mean 'come to' / 'tell someone to'; they all sound the same.

items.use: Noun + ni yoru: the answer depends on X; the all-purpose hedge when yes or no would be too strong ('hito ni yoru', 'toki ni yoru').

example.romaji: sore wa hito ni yoru ne.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa hito ni yorimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは人によりますね。

items.freqNote: による #1018; によって #939; near-synonym 次第 #1911
items.notes: Mid-sentence it becomes ni yotte: 'hito ni yotte chigau' = varies by person. 'X ni yoru to' = 'according to X' ('yohou ni yoru to, ame da tte').

items.use: -nai form + de: you do the main action without doing X, or instead of X ('nenaide benkyou shita').

example.ja: 朝ごはん食べないで来た。

examplePolite.ja: 朝ごはんを食べないで来ました。

items.freqNote: ないで #3426 (also counts the request 'don't'; tokenizer often fuses with the verb)
items.notes: For a negative reason use -nakute ('wakaranakute komatta'), not -naide. At the end of a sentence it's a request: 'ikanaide' = 'don't go'.

items.use: Puts one thing in place of another: noun + no kawari ni = 'instead of X' (koohii no kawari ni ocha), plain verb + kawari ni = 'instead of doing' or 'in return for doing' (oshiete kureru kawari ni, ogoru yo = teach me and I'll buy you dinner). At the start of a sentence sono kawari (no ni) sets a condition, 'but in return' (ii yo. sono kawari, ashita tetsudatte ne), or balances a downside, 'to make up for it' (takai kedo, sono kawari oishii).

example.romaji: watashi no kawari ni itte kureru?
example.ja: 私の代わりに行ってくれる？
example.english: Can you go in my place?

examplePolite.romaji: watashi no kawari ni itte kuremasen ka?
examplePolite.ja: 私の代わりに行ってくれませんか？
examplePolite.english: Could you go in my place?

items.freqNote: 代わりに #1457 (exact form); bare noun 代わり #870 and その代わり #2876 are separate entries; homophone 変わる #226
items.notes: Same sound as kawaru 'change' (H-kawaru) and its noun kawari (kawari nai? = how've you been?), but this kawari comes from the other kawaru, 'take someone's place' (kawarou ka? = want me to take over?). Said alone, kawari ni = 'instead' (kawari ni yattoku yo = I'll do it instead); kawari alone = a replacement (kawari ga inai). okawari = seconds / a refill. Even in polite speech the verb before it stays plain: iku kawari ni denwa shimashita, not ikimasu kawari ni.

items.use: Plain verb + tame ni = in order to; noun + no tame ni = for X's sake ('kenkou no tame ni'). The 'because of' reading is news/written; in chat use de or kara.

example.romaji: ryokou suru tame ni, chokin shiteru.
example.ja: 旅行するために、貯金してる。

examplePolite.romaji: ryokou suru tame ni, chokin shitemasu.
examplePolite.ja: 旅行するために、貯金してます。
examplePolite.english: I'm saving up so I can travel.

items.freqNote: ために #124 (purpose and cause together); ため #203
items.notes: Tame ni needs an action you choose to do; with potentials, -nai forms and verbs you don't control (maniau, wakaru), use -you ni instead ('mieru you ni', 'maniau you ni', 'wasurenai you ni').

items.english: so that; so as not to
items.use: Plain verb + you ni gives a purpose you can't directly control: after potentials (hanaseru you ni), non-volitional verbs like kikoeru and maniau, or when the purpose is someone else's state (minna ga wakaru you ni), where tame ni doesn't fit; after -nai forms it's the everyday choice (wasurenai you ni). The polite form goes on the main verb.

example.ja: 忘れないように書いとくね。
example.english: I'll write it down so I don't forget.

examplePolite.romaji: wasurenai you ni kaite okimasu ne.
examplePolite.ja: 忘れないように書いておきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll write it down so I don't forget.

items.freqNote: ように #158, which also counts the simile 'like' and 'as' (itta you ni); ようになる #462 and ようにする #903 are separate entries
items.notes: At the end of a sentence it's a reminder or wish: 'kaze hikanai you ni ne' = 'don't catch a cold, OK?'; polite: 'kaze o hikanai you ni ki o tsukete kudasai ne'. As a set wish it keeps -masu even with friends: 'umaku ikimasu you ni' = 'here's hoping it goes well'. A different you ni: 'mae mo itta you ni' = 'like I said before'.

blocks.label: Honestly, actually
blocks.rationale: Openers that flag how real or how frank the next thing said is.
