blocks.interference: jitsu wa (reveals something new) and shoujiki (gives a frank opinion) share one frame. maji de is slang for 'seriously', so swap in hontou ni outside friends.

items.use: Opens a confession, a piece of news or a favour, and signals that something real or unexpected is coming.

example.romaji: jitsu wa anmari suki ja nai.
example.ja: 実はあんまり好きじゃない。
example.english: Actually, I don't really like it.

examplePolite.romaji: jitsu wa amari suki ja nai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 実はあまり好きじゃないです。
examplePolite.english: Actually, I don't really like it.

items.notes: Often stretched as jitsu wa ne... to buy a moment before the news.

items.use: Goes at the start of a sentence to mark a frank opinion, often a negative one; shoujiki ni iu to means 'to be honest'.

example.ja: 正直、あんまり好きじゃない。
example.english: Honestly, I'm not a big fan.

examplePolite.romaji: shoujiki, amari suki ja nai desu.
examplePolite.ja: 正直、あまり好きじゃないです。
examplePolite.english: Honestly, I'm not a big fan.

items.freqNote: rank includes adjectival 'honest' uses of 正直
items.notes: As a na-adjective it means 'honest' (shoujiki na hito).

items.use: A casual intensifier ('really, seriously') among friends. Said alone with a rising tone, it means 'seriously?'.

examplePolite.romaji: kore, hontou ni oishii desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: これ、本当においしいですね。

items.freqNote: マジで is not a token; rank of マジ
items.notes: Never with superiors or strangers; use hontou ni instead (often clipped to honto ni in speech). maji? alone works too; maji ka is rough and male-coded.

blocks.label: Size, length & amount
blocks.rationale: How big or long something is and how much of it there is: the size and quantity scales, plus nagai for length and for time.
blocks.interference: ookii (big) and ooi (many) both start with oo-: hito ga ooi means 'crowded', while ookii hito is 'a big person'. Within each pair, learn the first word before adding its opposite. nagai is length and duration (kami ga nagai, nagai aida = a long time), not overall size, and it shares ookii's 'kono X, chotto ___' sentence. For a long way (distance) say tooi (far), not nagai: eki made tooi.

items.use: The size of things and people, loudness (ookii koe = a loud voice) and how big a matter is; before nouns, ookina is just as common.

example.ja: この靴、ちょっと大きい
example.english: These shoes are a bit big.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa chotto ookii desu
examplePolite.ja: この靴はちょっと大きいです
examplePolite.english: These shoes are a little big.

items.freqNote: 大きい #536; the prenominal 大きな #538 is counted separately
items.notes: For 'a lot of', use ooi or takusan, not ookii.

items.use: The size of things, quiet voices (chiisai koe) and childhood (chiisai koro = when I was little); before nouns it is also chiisana.

example.ja: この靴、ちょっと小さい
example.english: These shoes are a bit small.

examplePolite.romaji: kono kutsu wa chotto chiisai desu
examplePolite.ja: この靴はちょっと小さいです
examplePolite.english: These shoes are a little small.

items.freqNote: 小さい #879; prenominal 小さな #1079
items.notes: chiisana goes only before a noun (chiisana mise); at the end of a sentence it is always chiisai.

items.use: Says there are many or a lot of something, or that something happens often (machigai ga ooi); it works after the noun (hito ga ooi) and not normally in front of it.

example.english: There are a lot of people today.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hito ga ooi desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日は人が多いですね
examplePolite.english: There are a lot of people today.

items.notes: Not 'ooi hito' for 'many people'; say takusan no hito instead.

items.use: Says there are few or not much of something; the opposite of ooi, with the same after-the-noun pattern (hito ga sukunai).

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa hito ga sukunai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日は人が少ないですね

items.notes: Not sukoshi (a little, B): sukunai describes an amount, sukoshi gives one.

items.use: Describes length (hair, lines, roads) and, just as often, duration: a long film, meeting or wait. nagai aida means 'for a long time'.

example.ja: この映画、ちょっと長いね
example.english: This film's a bit long, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kono eiga wa chotto nagai desu ne
examplePolite.ja: この映画はちょっと長いですね
examplePolite.english: This film is a little long, isn't it?

items.notes: nagaku natte gomen = sorry this got long (a message or a talk); the opposite is mijikai (short).

blocks.label: Busy right now
blocks.rationale: Ways to say whether you're free right now: whether there's time, whether you're in the middle of something, or whether you're about to act.
blocks.interference: -chuu attaches to nouns (denwa-chuu) and -tokoro to verbs. With -tokoro the verb form picks the stage: suru tokoro = about to, shiteru tokoro = in the middle of, shita tokoro = just did.

items.use: Time as something you have or lack (jikan aru? = got a minute?, jikan nai = no time). It also counts hours (ni-jikan).

examplePolite.ja: 今お時間いいですか？

items.freqNote: 時間(じかん) #181
items.notes: Asking about someone else's time, say ojikan (ojikan ii desu ka?). Your own time is always jikan.

items.use: Attaches to an activity noun to say you're busy with it right now (shigoto-chuu, kaigi-chuu, denwa-chuu).

examplePolite.ja: すみません、今電話中です。

items.freqNote: 中(ちゅう) #417; じゅう reading #9118; なか reading #133 is 'inside'
items.notes: Read -juu, the same kanji means 'throughout': ichinichi-juu = all day.

items.english: about to / in the middle of / just did
items.use: Pins down the exact stage of an action, depending on the verb form before it: taberu tokoro (about to eat), tabeteru tokoro (eating right now), tabeta tokoro (just ate).

example.ja: 今電話するところだった。
example.english: I was just about to call you.

examplePolite.ja: 今電話するところでした。
examplePolite.english: I was just about to call you.

items.freqNote: ところ #187, includes 'place'; casual とこ #280
items.notes: Casual speech often clips it to toko (ima deru toko). For 'on the way', say tochuu (ima mukatteru tochuu), not itteru tokoro. tabeta tokoro = just finished eating; tabeta bakari = only recently ate (could be hours or weeks).

blocks.label: Too, easy, hard
blocks.rationale: Suffixes on the verb stem that grade how something goes: too much, easy, hard, and the way to do it.
blocks.interference: -yasui and -nikui are opposites on the same stem (kakiyasui / kakinikui), and -yasui here is not 'cheap'; -sugiru makes a verb, -kata makes a noun.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem or adjective stem for overdoing or excess (tabesugita, takasugiru, shizukasugi), and the bare -sugi is common in reactions.

example.ja: 昨日ちょっと飲みすぎた。
example.english: I drank a bit too much last night.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日ちょっと飲みすぎました。
examplePolite.english: I drank a bit too much last night.

items.freqNote: rank of 過ぎる (also 'pass by'); kana すぎる #838, noun すぎ #2478 (tabesugi)
items.notes: Casual reactions use bare -sugi to mean 'so X', not 'too X': oishisugi = so good, kawaisugi = so cute (youth slang; keep it among friends).

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem for 'easy to' (wakariyasui, tsukaiyasui) or 'prone to' (tsukareyasui), and conjugates like an i-adjective.

example.english: This pen is easy to write with.

examplePolite.ja: このペン、書きやすいです。
examplePolite.english: This pen is easy to write with.

items.freqNote: rank of kana やすい, the suffix (安い 'cheap' #1315 is separate); 分かりやすい #3193
items.notes: Not 'cheap': after a verb stem yasui means easy.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem for 'hard to' (kikinikui, tabenikui), a soft way to say something is awkward or inconvenient.

example.english: This pen is hard to write with.

examplePolite.ja: このペン、書きにくいです。
examplePolite.english: This pen is hard to write with.

items.freqNote: rank of kana にくい, the suffix (憎い 'hateful' #3878 separate); 分かりにくい #12919
items.notes: iinikui n da kedo (this is hard to say, but...) is a common lead-in to awkward news.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem to make a noun meaning the way to do it (tsukaikata, yarikata, iikata), which covers 'how do you...?' without new grammar.

example.english: Do you know how to use this?

examplePolite.ja: これの使い方分かりますか？
examplePolite.english: Do you know how to use this?

items.freqNote: rank of 言い方, the top -kata compound; やり方 #1241, 使い方 #3636 (方 'kata' #292 mixes 'person')
items.notes: The object takes no: kanji no kakikata (*kanji o kakikata). Suru nouns take no shikata: benkyou no shikata.

blocks.label: Take, put, cost, call, enough
blocks.rationale: Wide-reach light verbs whose meaning comes from the object: toru (take, pass, get), dasu (put out, take out, hand in, pay) and its opposite ireru (put in, include, make tea), kakaru (time or money it takes), kakeru (cause trouble, call, spend, put on), plus tariru for whether what you have is enough.
blocks.interference: 'It takes an hour' is kakaru, not toru; kakaru (it takes, ga) and kakeru (spend, call, o) are an intransitive/transitive pair: jikan ga kakaru vs jikan o kakeru. dasu is likewise the transitive partner of deru, and ireru of hairu: uchi o deta (I left home) vs gomi o dashita (I put the trash out), heya ni haitta (I went in) vs kaban ni ireta (I put it in the bag). kakaru says how much something takes and tariru whether you have that much (kekkou kakaru kedo, okane tariru?).

items.use: Picking up or passing things (sore totte), plus light-verb uses for taking a break, a photo, a seat or a licence (yasumi o toru, shashin toru).

examplePolite.ja: すみません、それ取ってください。
examplePolite.english: Excuse me, could you pass me that?

items.freqNote: 取る #228; homophone 撮る (take a photo) #649 separately
items.notes: totte (take) vs tootte (pass through) differ only in vowel length.

items.use: How much time or money something takes (jikan ga kakaru, dore kurai kakaru?), and also incoming calls and locks being on.

examplePolite.ja: どれくらいかかりますか？

items.freqNote: かかる #385 (kana); 掛かる #5316 separately
items.notes: Intransitive partner of kakeru: jikan ga kakaru (it takes) / jikan o kakeru (spend).

items.use: Causing trouble (meiwaku o kakeru), phoning (denwa o kakeru), spending time, locking, and putting on glasses or sauce.

examplePolite.ja: 迷惑をかけてすみません。

items.freqNote: かける #244 (kana, all senses); 掛ける #2742 separately
items.notes: For phoning, casual talk more often says denwa suru: ato de denwa suru ne.

items.english: put out; take out; hand in; pay
items.use: Puts or takes something out, with it marked by o (gomi dasu, saifu dasu, shukudai dasu), covers paying (kyou wa watashi ga dasu yo = I'll get this today), and builds set phrases like genki dashite (cheer up) and koe dasu (speak up).

example.english: Did you put the trash out this morning?

examplePolite.ja: 今朝ゴミを出しましたか？
examplePolite.english: Did you put the trash out this morning?

items.notes: After a verb stem it means 'start to': ame ga furidashita = it started raining.

items.english: put in; include; make (tea); turn on
items.use: Puts something into something else, with the thing marked by o and the place by ni (kaban ni ireru); it also covers making tea or coffee, letting someone into a group or plan (watashi mo irete), and switching something on.

example.ja: コーヒーに砂糖入れる？
example.english: Do you take sugar in your coffee?

examplePolite.ja: コーヒーにお砂糖入れますか？
examplePolite.english: Would you like sugar in your coffee?

items.freqNote: 入れる #222; 淹れる (making tea/coffee) #19863 listed separately
items.notes: Ichidan (irete, ireta), unlike its godan partner hairu (haitte, haitta).

items.use: Says whether there's enough money, time, food or people, with the thing marked by ga; you mostly hear it as tarinai (not enough) and in the question tariru? (kore de tariru?).

examplePolite.ja: 時間が全然足りません。

items.freqNote: 足りる #764; 足りない #3974 separately (tokenizer mostly splits it into 足り + ない)
items.notes: Also means 'short of' or 'missing': hitori tarinai = we're one person short. 'That's enough!' / 'no more, thanks' is mou ii, not tariru.

blocks.label: About / exactly
blocks.rationale: Hedging an amount or pinning it down exactly.
blocks.interference: gurai goes after the number and daitai goes before it, and they can stack (daitai ichijikan gurai). choudo is the opposite pole: exactly.

items.use: Goes after a number or word to mean 'about' (gofun gurai) or 'to that extent' (sore gurai, onaji gurai).

examplePolite.ja: 1時間ぐらいかかりますよ

items.freqNote: ぐらい #342; the same particle spelled くらい is #299 (adjective 暗い is listed separately, #1480)
items.notes: kurai and gurai are interchangeable. 'Onaji gurai' means 'about the same'. sore gurai also means 'that much at least': sore gurai wakaru yo = I know that much.

items.use: Goes before a number or claim to mean 'roughly / mostly' (daitai wakatta). It hedges any amount or statement.

example.ja: 大体1時間ぐらいかかるよ

examplePolite.ja: 大体1時間ぐらいかかりますよ

items.freqNote: 大体 #1240; kana-spelled だいたい separately #3197
items.notes: Opening a complaint, it means 'in the first place' (daitai, nande…).

items.use: Means 'exactly / just right' for amounts, sizes and timing (choudo ii, choudo ima).

example.ja: ちょうど1時間かかった

examplePolite.ja: ちょうど1時間かかりました

items.notes: 'Choudo ii' (just right) and 'choudo yokatta' (perfect timing) are the most common chunks.

blocks.label: Nothing, nobody
blocks.rationale: Question word + mo + a negative verb = nothing, no one, nowhere.
blocks.interference: With a negative verb all three mean no-thing, no one, nowhere; when a particle is needed it goes before mo (dare ni mo, doko ni mo).

items.use: With a negative verb means 'nothing, not anything' (nanimo nai, nanimo tabenakatta).

examplePolite.ja: 何もありませんよ。

items.freqNote: 何にも (nan ni mo) #1238
items.notes: The emphatic casual form is nan ni mo (nan ni mo nai).

items.use: With a negative verb means 'no one' (daremo inai), and splits around a particle (dare ni mo iwanai = won't tell anyone).

examplePolite.ja: 誰もいませんよ。

items.freqNote: 誰にも (dare ni mo) #743
items.notes: daremo ga + a positive verb means 'everyone' but sounds formal (daremo ga shitteru); casually say minna shitteru.

items.use: With a negative verb means 'nowhere, not anywhere' (doko ni mo ikanai), keeping ni or de inside.

examplePolite.ja: どこにもありませんよ。

items.freqNote: どこも not found; rank of どこにも
items.notes: dokomo with a positive verb means 'everywhere' (dokomo onaji); casually ni is often dropped with a negative too (dokomo itte nai = haven't been anywhere).

blocks.label: Softeners
blocks.rationale: Words that take the edge off: downplaying, hedging an action, and softening a request.
blocks.interference: betsu ni denies something the listener might assume ('it's not that...'), while toku ni just says nothing stands out; a bare 'betsu ni.' sounds curt and toku ni doesn't. ichiou (just in case) is not toriaezu (for now).

items.english: not particularly; not really; it's not that...
items.use: Denies something the listener might assume ('it's not that...'), usually with a negative (betsu ni okotte nai, betsu ni mondai nai). betsu ni ii yo / betsu ni ii kedo means 'I don't mind' but can sound grudging, and a bare 'betsu ni.' is a curt 'whatever'.

examplePolite.romaji: betsu ni okotte nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 別に怒ってないですよ。

items.notes: A bare 'betsu ni.' as a reply sounds cold; say toku ni nai instead. Exceptions to the negative rule: betsu ni ii (I don't mind) and the bare curt reply.

items.use: Singles one thing out (toku ni kore ga suki), and with a negative it is the neutral, polite-safe 'nothing in particular'.

examplePolite.romaji: toku ni mondai nai desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 特に問題ないですよ。

items.notes: toku ni nai (desu) is the safe answer to 'any questions?'.

items.use: Hedges an action done to be safe (ichiou kakunin suru) or a claim that is only technically true (ichiou dekita).

example.english: I'll take an umbrella just in case.

examplePolite.ja: 一応傘持っていきます。
examplePolite.english: I'll take an umbrella just in case.

items.notes: It also works as modesty: ichiou eigo hanaseru = I speak English, sort of.

items.use: Goes at the front of a request or preference and softens it by making it conditional.

example.ja: できれば明日がいいな。

examplePolite.romaji: dekireba ashita ga ii n desu kedo.
examplePolite.ja: できれば明日がいいんですけど。

items.notes: Literally 'if it can be done': dekiru + -ba.

blocks.label: Same & different
blocks.rationale: Comparing and sorting: the same, another one, weird, normal, all sorts.
blocks.interference: onaji takes a noun directly (onaji iro) but betsu needs no (betsu no iro), and the shared sentence makes that the only difference. futsuu and hen are opposites on the same 'sore, ___ da yo' sentence.

items.use: Says things are the same (X to onaji) for comparisons on any topic; it goes straight before a noun with no na or no (onaji iro).

examplePolite.ja: 同じ色がいいです

items.notes: watashi mo onaji (same here) is the easy everyday reply.

items.use: Means another or a separate one: betsu no X (a different X) and betsubetsu (separately), for choices, payments, plans and people.

examplePolite.romaji: betsu no iro ga ii desu
examplePolite.ja: 別の色がいいです

items.freqNote: 別 #500; includes the adverb betsu ni (C)
items.notes: Paying separately is betsubetsu de (onegaishimasu). betsu ni (not really) is its own item in C.

items.use: Says something is strange or off (a taste, a sound, a person, a situation); hen na X goes in front of any noun.

examplePolite.ja: それは変ですよ

items.notes: About a person (hen na hito) it is a real criticism; about a taste or a noise it is neutral.

items.use: Says something is normal, usual or average and serves as the baseline in comparisons (futsuu wa = usually); futsuu ni means 'normally' and, in casual speech, 'honestly, genuinely' (futsuu ni oishii = it's actually really good).

examplePolite.ja: それは普通ですよ

items.freqNote: 普通 #344; includes adverbial futsuu ni
items.notes: As an answer to 'how was it?', futsuu means 'just OK, nothing special'. It is lukewarm, not praise.

items.use: Means many different things without listing them: iroiro na X (all sorts of X), iroiro atta (a lot happened), iroiro arigatou (thanks for everything).

example.ja: 今日はいろいろあった

examplePolite.ja: 今日はいろいろありました

items.notes: As a reply, iroiro desu ne means 'it varies, it depends'.

blocks.label: Go and do
blocks.rationale: Errand and direction frames on iku and kuru, which say where the trip goes around an action.
blocks.interference: katte kuru (go buy and come back), katte iku (buy on the way, then go), kai ni iku (go out to buy): the same verb on three trips; -te + iku/kuru vs stem + ni. In casual speech katteku (on my way) and katte kuru (go and come back) differ only by the final -ru; listen for it.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for going to do something and coming back (katte kuru, itte kimasu), or for a change that has set in (samuku natte kita).

examplePolite.ja: 飲み物買ってきますね。

items.freqNote: rank of kana くる, mostly the auxiliary (来る #52 is 'come')
items.notes: itte kimasu (I'm off) is this pattern frozen as a set phrase.

items.use: Attaches to the -te form for doing something on the way out or taking it along (motte iku, tabete iku), or for a change that will keep going (fuete iku).

example.english: I'll pick up drinks on my way.

examplePolite.ja: 飲み物買っていきますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll pick up drinks on my way.

items.freqNote: rank of kana いく, mostly the auxiliary (行く #40 is 'go'); contracted てく #7358
items.notes: Casual speech shortens it to -teku: motteku, katteku.

items.use: Attaches to a verb stem for the purpose of a trip (tabe ni iku, ai ni kita) and works with other movement verbs (tori ni kaeru).

example.english: I'm heading out to buy drinks.

examplePolite.ja: 飲み物買いに行きますね。
examplePolite.english: I'm going out to buy drinks.

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits に+行く (行く #40 counts all going)
items.notes: Suru nouns drop suru: kaimono ni iku, benkyou ni kita.

blocks.label: Until, by, while still
blocks.rationale: Clauses that mark the edges of a time window: until, by, and while the window is still open.
blocks.interference: 'Until' is -made (the action lasts up to X) and 'by' is -made ni (it happens once before X). -uchi ni means acting while a state still holds.

items.use: Means 'until' after a dictionary-form verb or a time word (kuru made matsu, ashita made). It pairs with kara for ranges and also means 'as far as' a place.

example.english: I'll wait until you get back.

examplePolite.ja: 帰るまで待ってますね。
examplePolite.english: I'll wait until you get back.

items.freqNote: まで #64, all senses including spatial 'as far as'
items.notes: The action fills the whole span. For a deadline, use -made ni.

items.use: Sets a deadline: the action happens once, some time before X (ashita made ni okuru).

example.romaji: kaeru made ni wa owaru yo.
example.ja: 帰るまでには終わるよ。
example.english: It'll be done by the time you're back.

examplePolite.romaji: kaeru made ni wa owarimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 帰るまでには終わりますよ。
examplePolite.english: It'll be done by the time you're back.

items.freqNote: tokenizer splits (までに not listed); まで #64 covers every made. No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: Quick test: if English says 'until', use made; if it says 'by', use made ni.

items.use: Says to act while a condition still holds (atsui uchi ni, wakai uchi ni). With a negative, -nai uchi ni means 'before X happens'.

examplePolite.ja: 熱いうちに食べてください。
examplePolite.english: Please eat it while it's hot.

items.freqNote: うち #113 is mostly 'home / we'. No usable rank — judgement
items.notes: Don't hear it as uchi ni ('to home'). Here it follows a verb, an adjective, or noun + no. ima no uchi ni = while you still can. -teru uchi ni = while doing X, before you knew it (hanashiteru uchi ni kuraku natta).

blocks.label: Getting through, giving up, not wasting a chance
blocks.rationale: Words for handling a situation: start somewhere, push past the details, manage somehow, say how it ended, take an outcome as settled in advance, and don't waste a chance or an effort.
blocks.interference: toriaezu (for now, as a first step) and tonikaku (anyway, whatever else) share '___ yatte miyou'. nantoka is about managing despite trouble; kekkyoku is about the final outcome. douse also comes out as 'anyway', but tonikaku pushes on while douse takes the outcome as settled in advance, usually the bad one (douse muri da, it won't work anyway); kekkyoku reports how it really ended (kekkyoku muri datta). sekkaku can't fill the '___ yatte miyou' slot on its own. It needs da kara: sekkaku da kara yatte miyou (since we have the chance), never 'sekkaku yatte miyou'. douse nara (if it's happening anyway) gives 'might as well': douse matsu nara, kafe de matou (if we have to wait anyway, let's wait in a café). It starts from 'this is happening regardless', where sekkaku starts from 'this is a rare chance'. sekkaku ... noni (after all that trouble) often leads into kekkyoku: sekkaku tsukutta noni, kekkyoku tabenakatta (I went to the trouble of making it, and in the end they didn't eat it).

items.use: Marks a first step or a temporary choice made before deciding the rest (toriaezu biiru, toriaezu yatte miru).

example.ja: とりあえずやってみよう。
example.english: Let's just try it for now.

examplePolite.ja: とりあえずやってみましょう。

items.freqNote: とりあえず #864; 取りあえず #5786 counted separately
items.notes: toriaezu biiru (beer to start) is the classic first order at an izakaya.

items.use: Cuts past details or doubts to the main point or action (tonikaku ikou, tonikaku tsukareta).

example.ja: とにかくやってみよう。
example.english: Never mind the details, let's just try it.

examplePolite.ja: とにかくやってみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Never mind the details, let's just try it.

items.notes: It also pivots a story to its point: tonikaku, sugokatta (anyway, it was amazing).

items.use: Says something gets handled despite difficulty, as in nantoka naru (it'll work out), nantoka dekita and nantoka shite (do something!).

examplePolite.ja: 何とかなりますよ。

items.freqNote: 何とか #1078; kana なんとか #2646 counted separately
items.notes: It also stands in for a forgotten name: nantoka san (Mr. So-and-so).

items.use: Sums up how things finally turned out, often against the plan, which makes it key for telling stories.

example.english: In the end, it didn't work out.

examplePolite.ja: 結局ダメでした。
examplePolite.english: In the end, it didn't work out.

items.notes: kekkyoku reports the final outcome; yappari says it matched what you expected.

items.english: since we have the chance; after all that trouble
items.use: Marks a chance or an effort as too good to waste, so it only fits something rare or effortful, never a plain 'since'. sekkaku da kara (since we have the chance) and sekkaku kita n da kara (since we came all this way) suggest making the most of it, sekkaku ... noni (after all that trouble) complains that it went to waste, and sekkaku no + noun means 'rare, long-awaited' (sekkaku no yasumi, my rare day off).

example.ja: せっかくだから、やってみよう。
example.english: Since we've got the chance, let's give it a go.

examplePolite.ja: せっかくですから、やってみましょう。
examplePolite.english: Since we have the chance, let's give it a try.

items.freqNote: せっかく #465 (kanji 折角 #47246)
items.notes: A polite way to turn down an offer: sekkaku desu kedo, kyou wa chotto... (that's kind of you, but today's a bit...).

items.english: anyway (it's settled regardless); might as well (douse nara)
items.use: Treats an outcome as settled whatever you do. Often it's resigned (douse muri da, douse wasureru yo), and aimed at someone it sounds sulky or bitter (douse kikanai n desho). It's also a neutral 'anyway' when you give a reason: douse hima da shi, tetsudau yo (I'm free anyway, so I'll help). It never moves a story on the way English 'anyway' does; that's tonikaku.

example.english: It's not going to work anyway.

examplePolite.ja: どうせ無理ですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's not going to work anyway.

items.freqNote: どうせ #580; どうせなら #5798 counted separately
items.notes: douse nara (if it's happening anyway) is the upbeat 'might as well': douse nara ii no kaou yo (if we're buying one anyway, let's get a good one).

blocks.label: Comparing
blocks.rationale: The frames that rank things: most, more, than, than expected, and not as.
blocks.interference: The thing before yori loses and the thing before no hou ga wins. In a comparison hodo needs a negative and means 'not as … as', which an English ear can mishear as a positive comparison.

items.use: Makes any adjective superlative ('the most'). kono naka de ('out of these') sets the range.

example.english: Today's the coldest day of the year, huh.

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa kotoshi ichiban samui desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日は今年一番寒いですね
examplePolite.english: Today's the coldest day of the year, isn't it.

items.notes: 'Ichiban suki' (my favourite) is the chunk you will use most.

items.use: Goes after the winning item to say 'X is more …' (kotchi no hou ga ii). It is the standard answer to 'dotchi?'.

example.romaji: kyou no hou ga samui ne

examplePolite.romaji: kyou no hou ga samui desu ne
examplePolite.ja: 今日の方が寒いですね

items.freqNote: rank of 方 (ほう) across all uses, including -ta hou ga ii advice; kana ほう also #639
items.notes: The full frame is A yori B no hou ga …, but in speech either half usually stands alone. no goes only after a noun (kotchi no hou ga ii). Adjectives and verbs take hou ga directly (yasui hou ga ii, iku hou ga hayai); never yasui no hou ga.

items.use: Goes after the item being beaten to mean 'than' (kinou yori samui). In speech it usually stands alone; the full frame adds no hou ga to the winner.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日より寒いですね
examplePolite.english: It's colder than yesterday, isn't it.

items.freqNote: rank includes the formal 'from' sense and adverbial yori
items.notes: Trap: the thing before yori is the one that loses (has less of the quality). Kinou yori samui = today is colder.

items.use: Says that something was more (or less) than you expected, and works with any adjective (omotta yori takai, omotta yori hayakatta).

examplePolite.ja: 思ったより寒いですね

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer splits 思ったより and 思ってたより (both not found); components より #132, 思う #33
items.notes: Two pool items used as one chunk. Casual speech often uses omotteta yori (思ってたより) with the same meaning. The let-down version is omotta hodo … nai.

items.use: With a negative it means 'not as … as' (kinou hodo samukunai). It also marks extreme extent (shinu hodo, 'to death'). After an amount in polite or service speech it simply means 'about' (juppun hodo kakarimasu = it takes about ten minutes), with no negative and no comparison.

example.english: It's not as cold as yesterday.

examplePolite.ja: 昨日ほど寒くないですね
examplePolite.english: It's not as cold as yesterday, is it.

items.freqNote: ほど #288; kanji 程 #9747
items.notes: Trap: in a comparison, hodo always means NOT as … as, never 'as … as'. -ba … hodo means 'the more … the more'.

blocks.label: Anything, anyone
blocks.rationale: Question word + demo = any- at all, for the free-choice answers.
blocks.interference: nandemo ii (anything's fine) vs nanimo iranai (I don't want anything): demo usually goes with a positive verb and mo with a negative (nandemo nai 'it's nothing' is the set exception); it is nan-, not nani-, before demo.

items.use: Free choice: anything at all is fine (nandemo ii yo), with a positive verb, unlike nanimo.

examplePolite.ja: 何でもいいですよ。

items.freqNote: 何でも #728; なんでも #3802
items.notes: nandemo nai ('it's nothing') is a set phrase in G.

items.use: Any time at all, the easy yes to a scheduling question (itsudemo ii yo, itsudemo kite).

examplePolite.ja: いつでもいいですよ。

items.use: Any place at all (dokodemo ii yo, dokodemo aru).

examplePolite.ja: どこでもいいですよ。

items.freqNote: likely undercounted (tokenizer probably splits どこ+でも); judgement: moderately common

items.use: Any person at all (daredemo ii yo, daredemo dekiru = anyone can do it).

examplePolite.ja: 誰でもいいですよ。

items.freqNote: likely undercounted (tokenizer probably splits 誰+でも); judgement: moderately common

blocks.label: Advice
blocks.rationale: The standard ways to give advice, warn against something, and ask what to do.
blocks.interference: Positive advice takes the past -ta (yasunda hou ga ii), negative takes plain -nai (muri shinai hou ga ii), never -nakatta; -tara ii is the softer one and is how you ask: dou shitara ii?

items.use: Attaches to the past form to give firm advice (yasunda hou ga ii), with present meaning despite the past form.

example.romaji: kyou wa yasunda hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 今日は休んだ方がいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa yasunda hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は休んだ方がいいですよ。

items.freqNote: rank of ほうがいい (方がいい #1346); shared with -nai hou ga ii and comparative 'X no hou ga ii'
items.notes: Can sound strong; soften with kamo (yasunda hou ga ii kamo).

items.use: Attaches to the plain -nai form to advise against something (ikanai hou ga ii, muri shinai hou ga ii).

example.romaji: kyou wa muri shinai hou ga ii yo.
example.ja: 今日は無理しない方がいいよ。

examplePolite.romaji: kyou wa muri shinai hou ga ii desu yo.
examplePolite.ja: 今日は無理しない方がいいですよ。
examplePolite.english: It's better not to push yourself today.

items.freqNote: rank of ほうがいい, shared with -ta hou ga ii
items.notes: Never *-nakatta hou ga ii: positive takes -ta, negative takes -nai.

items.use: Attaches to the -tara form to ask for advice (dou shitara ii?) or to suggest something gently (kiitara ii yo).

examplePolite.ja: どうしたらいいですか？

items.freqNote: no usable rank — judgement; tokenizer folds たら into the verb (standalone たら #2818)
items.notes: -ba ii (dou sureba ii?) means the same and sounds slightly more careful. Casual suggestions often stop at -tara? or -tara dou?: kiitara? = why don't you ask?

notes: Out of scope by design: topic nouns, numbers, counters, clock times, dates, day-of-week and month names, keigo beyond desu/masu.

Relative time words (asa, yoru, raishuu, kotoshi...) and several endings (darou, n da yo, -te ne, plus the mostly-heard sa / wa / zo / yo na) were cut by the selection panel and restored afterwards through the same write and three-lens review steps.

A second review of all 621 cuts (per-category reviewer + usage and redundancy checks) re-added 33 clear gaps plus 10 strong maybes and boku (learner request): e.g. atsui, samui, itai, kirei, otsukare, oyasumi, hisashiburi, tetsudau, okureru, -you ni, the passive. Cut verdicts are stored on each entry in cuts.

The remaining 16 maybes were then added at the learner's request (nakanaka, douse, nigate, hazukashii, nagai, abunai, -kawari ni, wake nai, moshimoshi, bikkuri shita, ki o tsukete, ireru, tariru, okoru, -sasete, dou iu); all joined existing chunks.
No pitch-accent numbers: the recorded audio carries accent; guessed accents were the main error source in earlier lists.
